issues.title: 'Region' is one vendor pool per region, collinear with vendor, pay, training, language, display hardware and annotator team, so the causal 'cultural contexts / mental models' reading is not identified
issues.claim: Each region is a single vendor-sourced annotator pool on monthly contracts, and hourly pay differs about threefold between them. Region is therefore perfectly collinear with vendor or site, pay, training cohort and trainer, task language, working hours and timing, and display hardware and viewing environment. Pools are not replicated within a region, so the effective sample size for any inference about a region-level cause is 5. No annotator-level culture measures were collected (self-identified background, residence history, own skin tone). Display is a plausible instrumental cause in its own right. The task is colour matching against rendered swatches or orbs, yet no monitor, calibration, brightness, white point, ambient light or browser colour management is reported for either arm. Site-issued hardware is constant within a region and differs between regions, which produces exactly the observed pattern: high within-region agreement plus a systematic between-region shift. Because MST steps are perceptually very unequal, a display shift of a few ΔE can move a judgement by one category in some parts of the scale and not in others, which mimics region × category 'mental model' differences. Pool size per region is also unreported, so the effect may come from a few individuals (see C02). No US crowd pool was included, although the oracle and the scale are US/Americas-centred. Only the descriptive claim that annotations differ by sourcing pool survives. The Limitations section concedes that background and language were not considered, but the Abstract and Conclusion keep the causal wording.
issues.paper_evidence: Conclusion p.10: “We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations.” Abstract p.1: “annotators from different geographic regions rely on different mental models of MST categories resulting in annotations that systematically vary across regions”. App. K p.28: “Crowdsourced annotators were contracted by the sourcing vendor to work for monthly increments.”; “Payment rates are determined by fair market value in the different regions.” Limitations p.9: “it does not consider other aspects of annotator identity and background, or other factors such as the language used in the task”. App. A.2 p.17: “The MST scale was designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas”. Absent: §§4–7 and Apps C, D and K describe no vendor sites, per-region training or trainers, crowd task language, annotation timing, or any display, monitor, calibration or viewing conditions (full-text search, design:M2).
issues.external_evidence: App. K pay table: India ~$6/h, Philippines ~$11/h, Ghana/Brazil ~$13/h, Hungary ~$19/h (about 3x), so region is collinear with at least one non-cultural factor. Adjacent CIEDE2000 between the official MST orb PNGs (median opaque pixel, sRGB→CIELAB D65): 2.65, 5.83, 7.89, 13.49, 12.71, 7.47, 7.63, 8.12, 3.65, so the largest step is 5.1x the smallest. Caveat: the orb renders include shading, and the values assume an sRGB-calibrated display, which is exactly what was not controlled.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (c), first sentence. The Abstract's 'different mental models'. §7's inference that regional cultural contexts shape perception. The recommendations to diversify regions and to match annotator region to the deployment region. The descriptive finding that pools differ is not affected.
issues.severity_disagreement: design:M1 banded this critical; stat:M3, design:M2 and data:D6 banded it major. Major is chosen because the descriptive pool difference survives and the immediate remedy is re-wording. The defect removes the causal interpretation, not the data.
issues.suggested_fix: Re-word (c) and the Abstract as an associational 'annotations differ systematically across sourcing pools'. To identify culture: (i) recruit 2 or more independent vendors or pools per region, or use one vendor across regions with identical training material, language and hardware specification; (ii) record annotator-level covariates (display model and calibration, time of day, training cohort, self-described background, self-reported skin tone); (iii) report display hardware per site, and re-run a subset (e.g. the Golden and Challenging sets) on calibrated or loaner displays, or add physical colour-patch control trials, to test whether regional offsets persist; (iv) fit mixed models with annotator nested in site and region, and test whether a region effect survives the covariates; (v) add a US crowd pool; (vi) report regional differences per scale position rather than in pooled MST units.

verdicts.reasoning:
Textual check. Every quote in the issue is verbatim. The core textual claim holds: the paper uses causal, culture-based wording that a design with one pool per region cannot support.

1. Causal wording is present and not hedged in three places. Conclusion (c) says "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations." The practitioner bullet says "In our case cultural differences across geographic regions influenced skin tone annotations." The Abstract says "we also find evidence that annotators ... rely on different mental models." §6 ("suggests that the shared mental models ... may vary") and §7 ("suggesting that regional cultural contexts influence") are softer, but they still read the result as cultural.

2. The paper does not remove the confound anywhere. The Intro frames location as "a proxy for cultural context and lived experience", which admits it is a proxy but never tests or isolates it. The Limitations section mentions only "other aspects of annotator identity and background" and "the language used in the task". It says nothing about vendor or pay differences, display or viewing conditions, training cohort, or the fact that region is a pool-level variable with n=5. The Ethics paragraph confirms that no annotator-level measures were collected ("beyond general geographic region"). Appendix L ("Addressing previous reviews") does not raise the issue at all. A search of the full text finds zero mentions of monitor, display, calibration or screen. App D describes the crowd task interface only in a figure and does not state the crowd task language; the English statement applies to the photographers only. App K documents the roughly threefold pay gap ($6/h to $19/h) and says crowd workers were vendor-contracted on monthly terms. §6 says five annotators were "randomly selected from a broader pool ... within each market" and gives no pool size. The released metadata (mst-e_image_details.csv and the golden/adversarial IDs) contains no crowd annotations or rater IDs, so pool size cannot be checked from the data.

3. Where the issue overstates (hence partially upheld):
(a) App K says "the sourcing vendor" (singular) for the crowd workers. The plural "relevant sourcing vendors" covers GLG for the photographers plus the crowd vendor. So vendor identity may be the same in every region and is not shown to be collinear with region. Only the site, team or contract terms plausibly differ.
(b) "Perfectly collinear with training cohort/trainer, language, hours/timing, display hardware" is an inference from what the paper leaves out, not a documented fact. The defensible statement is that each pool-level factor is unmeasured and, by design, cannot be separated from region.
(c) The Abstract sentence is introduced with "We also find evidence that", a hedge the issue's excerpt omits.
(d) The co-location recommendation is already labelled a hypothesis: "We hypothesize ... although more careful study of this is needed."
(e) The "diversify regions" recommendation and the finding that the global median lands close to the oracle rest on the descriptive pool differences, not on a cultural cause. Those parts survive.
(f) The Limitations section does concede language, so that factor is partly acknowledged.

Severity: major. The defect removes the causal "cultural context / mental model" reading of contribution (c) and of the Abstract. It leaves contributions (a), (b), (d) and (e) and the descriptive between-pool difference untouched, and the fix is mainly rewording plus a fuller limitations paragraph. It does not invalidate the paper's central reliability findings or the dataset, so critical is not justified.

verdicts.corrections:
1. Vendor: App K uses the singular "the sourcing vendor" for crowd workers, so the paper suggests one vendor across all five regions. Describe the confound as pool, site or contract per region, not as vendor identity.
2. "Perfectly collinear" with training cohort/trainer, task language, timing and display hardware is not documented. The paper is simply silent on these. Restate them as unmeasured pool-level factors that the design cannot separate from region; only pay and contract terms are documented as differing.
3. The Abstract sentence is hedged with "We also find evidence that". Quote it in full. The unhedged causal statements are Conclusion (c) and the practitioner bullet "In our case cultural differences ... influenced skin tone annotations". The issue should cite that bullet, which it omits.
4. The Intro already frames location as "a proxy for cultural context and lived experience". The co-location recommendation is already flagged as a hypothesis needing "more careful study". Credit both.
5. The Limitations section partly concedes language (and identity/background), but not pay, vendor/site, display or the pool-level n=5 problem.
6. The "diversify regions / replicate more" recommendation follows from the descriptive between-pool differences and the median-to-oracle agreement, so it survives without the cultural reading. Remove it from the affected claims; keep only the co-location rationale and the "mental models / cultural contexts" wording.
7. Pool size per region cannot be checked from the released metadata, which has no crowd annotations or rater IDs. The point stands only as "unreported".

verdicts.reasoning:
The central methods point is correct and well established. Region is a cluster-level factor. The paper samples one annotator pool per market ("randomly selected from a broader pool of annotators within each market", §6) and has no replicate pools inside a region. So every pool-level attribute (site or team, training delivery, pay, task language, hardware, timing) is perfectly aliased with region. That is a design fact, and it holds whether or not those attributes actually differ. At least one of them does differ, as documented: App. K hourly wages run from ~$6 to ~$19, a ratio of 3.17, so "about threefold" is right. For any claim about why pools differ, the inferential unit is the pool, so n=5 with no replication. In Hurlbert's terms the culture attribution is pseudo-replicated. No annotator-level culture measures were collected, and the ethics paragraph says nothing was collected "beyond general geographic region". Pool size per region is not given, and the data card leaves "Number of unique annotations" blank. The Limitations section concedes that identity, background and task language were not considered. A competent methods reviewer at a top venue would accept the core criticism: the paper's evidence (MANOVA on region, Mann-Whitney on experts, V² on Open Images) shows that pools differ, not that culture causes the difference.

The overclaim is in headline places. The Abstract says annotators "rely on different mental models". Conclusion (c) says "We show that cultural contexts ... influence". The first practitioner bullet says cultural differences "influenced" annotations. The body hedges: §6 says "suggests ... may vary", §7 says "suggesting", and the co-location bullet says "We hypothesize ... more careful study of this is needed". So this is a real but fixable attribution error in a core stated contribution. Major fits only at the low end. The dataset, the reliability results and the replication guidance are untouched, and the remedy is mainly rewording to "sourcing pool" or "location-confounded" language. Critical would be too strong.

Where the issue overstates:
(1) Vendor. The paper uses both "the sourcing vendor" (singular) and "the relevant sourcing vendors" (plural). Whether the vendor differs across regions is therefore undetermined. Collinearity with site or team holds; collinearity with "vendor" is not established.
(2) Training cohort, trainer, timing and hardware are unreported, not shown to differ. "Site-issued hardware is constant within a region and differs between regions" is an assumption.
(3) The display argument is overstated. The skin image and the MST reference swatches appear on the same screen, so a gamma, white-point or brightness shift applies to both and largely cancels in a relative match. A shift of a few ΔE in the stimulus against a fixed reference does not follow. What survives are second-order effects: black-level crush or ambient glare that compresses the dark MST 8–10 steps, plus non-uniform transfer curves. These could produce category-specific shifts, so display remains a plausible uncontrolled factor. "Exactly the observed pattern" is not supported.
(4) The unequal-step point holds. I computed CIEDE2000 between the official flat MST hex swatches (sRGB→Lab, D65): 1.95, 5.56, 4.02, 7.66, 18.76, 14.01, 10.87, 11.83, 5.00, so the largest step is about 9.6x the smallest. The issue's orb-based figures (5.1x) could not be reproduced from local files, but the qualitative claim is, if anything, stronger with flat swatches. The hex values are taken from the public MST palette, not from the paper.
(5) Affected claims. The recommendation to diversify regions does not depend on the causal mechanism. If pools differ for any reason (culture, site, display, pay), pooling several sources averages out pool-specific bias, so that advice survives, reframed as diversifying sources. Only the recommendation to match annotator region to deployment region rests on the cultural mechanism, and the paper already labels that one a hypothesis.
(6) The missing US crowd pool and the US-centred oracle are tangential to identification here.

verdicts.corrections:
(1) "Single vendor-sourced pool ... collinear with vendor": the paper calls the sourcing vendor both singular and plural, so whether the vendor differs across regions is unknown. One pool per market is supported; vendor differences are not.
(2) Training cohort and trainer, timing and display hardware are listed as if known to differ. They are unreported and possibly different. Only pay is documented to differ, about 3.2x.
(3) The display mechanism is overstated. Image and reference swatches share the same display, so first-order calibration shifts largely cancel in a relative match. Only second-order effects remain plausible, such as dark-end compression from black level or ambient glare and non-uniform transfer curves. "Produces exactly the observed pattern" is speculation.
(4) The ΔE figures could not be reproduced from local files. Flat official MST swatches give adjacent CIEDE2000 of 1.95–18.76 (about 9.6x), so the unequal-steps point stands with different numbers.
(5) The "diversify regions" recommendation survives the confound, since averaging over heterogeneous pools helps regardless of the cause. Only the co-location recommendation depends on the cultural reading, and the paper already marks it as a hypothesis.
(6) The body text (§6, §7) is hedged. The unhedged causal wording sits in the Abstract, Conclusion (c) and the first practitioner bullet.

issues.title: The crowd region MANOVA has an undefined (apparently impossible) unit of analysis, ignores annotator and image clustering, reports no effect size or df, and states the inference backwards
issues.claim: With 'MST annotations for each subject' as the DVs, every observation row needs values for all 19 subjects. But images are nested in subjects and annotators were drawn at random for each image, so no natural unit carries 19 DVs. The rows must therefore be annotators who rated every subject (not shown), aggregates, or arbitrarily index-matched images, and each choice changes what the test means. If the rows are annotations or images, this is pseudo-replication: within-image and within-annotator dependence is ignored and the p-value is anti-conservative. Neither the number of unique annotators per region nor any annotator ID is released, so a 'region' effect cannot be separated from a few idiosyncratic annotators. 'Annotations predict region' is backwards for a MANOVA with region as the IV, and it does not answer the question of interest: how far, and in which direction, each region shifts annotations, and at which scale positions. Pillai's trace = 1.97 comes with no F, df, N, exact p or post-hoc contrasts. The maximum is 4, so 1.97 implies a mean squared canonical correlation of about 0.49. That is a very large effect, hard to reconcile with within-region ICCs of 0.86–0.94, with every region's median sitting within 1 of the oracle, and with the small Open Images effect. It fits an inflated or aggregated unit of analysis with 19 DVs. MANOVA assumptions (multivariate normality, equal covariance matrices) are not credible for bounded 10-level ordinal data with heavy ties. The claim of 'enough statistical power' comes with no power analysis.
issues.paper_evidence: §6 p.8: “with annotator region as the independent variable and MST annotations for each subject as the dependent variable”; “We found that the subject annotations were a significantly high predictor of the region of the annotators (Pillai’s trace = 1.97, p < 0.05).”; “in this setting we have enough statistical power to explicitly test the effect of the annotator’s region on MST annotation”. §6 p.7: “Five annotators were randomly selected from a broader pool of annotators within each market to annotate each image.” Data card p.23: the crowd field “Number of unique annotations:” is left blank. App. C: the released annotation fields are subject, image, region and annotation only (“region, Ghana, Region where the annotation came from”). No F, df, N, unit of analysis or annotator-ID field appears anywhere in §6 or Apps C–L.
issues.external_evidence: For 5 regions, Pillai's trace is bounded by min(p, g−1) = min(19, 4) = 4. A value of 1.97 therefore means a mean squared canonical correlation of about 0.49 (computed independently by stat:M2 and design:M3).
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (c), first half, and the Abstract's 'systematically vary across regions'. Whether a region-level (as opposed to annotator-level) effect exists at all. The claim that Open Images regional differences are 'consistent with' MST-E. Practitioner advice that depends on the size and direction of regional shifts.
issues.severity_disagreement: None; both sources banded it major.
issues.suggested_fix: State the unit of analysis, N, F, df and exact p, or replace the MANOVA with a cumulative-link (ordinal logit) mixed model on individual annotations: region (fixed) + lighting + pose + (1|subject/image) + (1|annotator), optionally with a region × oracle-MST interaction. Report region contrasts as signed latent and predicted MST shifts with CIs per scale position, and likelihood-ratio tests with df. Add a leave-one-annotator-out check and, as robustness, per-image regional medians compared pairwise with clustering by subject. Report the number of unique annotators per region and their rating counts, and release pseudonymous annotator IDs.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the issue holds. The paper's only explicit test of the crowd regional effect is one sentence in §6 (p.8). It names region as the IV and "MST annotations for each subject as the dependent variable", then reports only "Pillai's trace = 1.97, p < 0.05". It gives no F, df, N, exact p, univariate or post-hoc contrasts, direction or size of shifts, or unit of analysis.

I searched the main text, Limitations, Suggestions for practitioners, the data card (App. C), Apps D–K and App. L ("Addressing previous reviews"). Nothing defines the observation rows, deals with clustering by image or annotator, or backs up the power claim with a power analysis. App. L's "Analytic Clarifications" paragraph covers only the "average median distance" and the 1-point threshold. App. L also asserts "properly powered analyses later in the paper" without showing any calculation.

The released metadata supports the point that no natural unit exists. Images per subject range from 55 (subject_15) to 112 (subject_12), so rows made by index-matching images across the 19 subjects would be unbalanced. Rows must therefore be aggregates or annotators, and the paper says neither. Annotator count and annotator IDs are never reported. The paper gives a privacy reason ("We chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about ... our annotators, beyond general geographic region"). That explains the gap but does not fix the analysis.

A Pillai's trace above 1 requires at least 2 DVs and at least 3 groups, which is consistent with per-subject DVs. With 5 regions and 19 DVs the maximum is 4, so 1.97/4 is about 0.49, as the issue says.

Contribution (c), the Abstract's "systematically vary across regions" and the practitioner advice rest mainly on this test. The other support is weak: the exploratory expert Mann-Whitney tests give 3 of 36 uncorrected p < 0.05, and the Open Images V² is under-specified. This materially weakens a core claim, so the severity is major. It is not critical: regional differences may well be real, but the paper does not credibly establish their size, direction or inferential basis.

Several parts of the issue are overstated or wrong (see corrections), so the verdict is partially_upheld rather than fully upheld.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
1) §6 p.8, verbatim: "with annotator region as the independent variable and MST annotations for each subject as the dependent variable".
2) §6 p.8, verbatim: "We found that the subject annotations were a significantly high predictor of the region of the annotators (Pillai's trace = 1.97, p < 0.05)".
3) §6 p.8, verbatim: "in this setting we have enough statistical power to explicitly test the effect of the annotator's region on MST annotation".
4) §6 p.7, verbatim: "Five annotators were randomly selected from a broader pool of annotators within each market to annotate each image."
5) App. C, p.23, crowd card: "Number of unique annotations:" is blank. The expert card reads "19".
6) App. C, p.21 fields: "region, Ghana, Region where the annotation came from". The fields are subject, image, region and annotation only.
7) §6 p.8: "average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition".
8) App. L p.29–30: "use the results from this work to establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later in the paper".
9) Limitations p.10: "We chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about ... our annotators, beyond general geographic region".
10) §6 p.8, Open Images: "(V 2 = 0.0766, p < 0.05), consistent with the MST-E annotations".
verdicts.corrections:
(a) "Reports no effect size" is wrong as stated. Pillai's trace is itself a multivariate effect-size statistic (V/s works like a partial eta-squared), and the issue derives about 0.49 from it. What is actually missing is F, df, N, exact p, and per-subject or post-hoc contrasts that show direction and size.

(b) "States the inference backwards" is overstated. MANOVA is the dual of discriminant analysis, and Pillai's trace is a symmetric sum of squared canonical correlations, so "annotations predict region" is loose wording, not a logical error. The real gap is that the test says nothing about how far, or in which direction, regions shift.

(c) "Apparently impossible" unit is overstated. Annotators were contracted monthly, so per-annotator means for each of the 19 subjects would be a plausible unit, and the issue itself lists this. "Undefined" is accurate. "Impossible" is not.

(d) "Hard to reconcile with within-region ICCs of 0.86–0.94" is faulty reasoning. A within-region ICC is unaffected by offsets between regions. Low residual variance within regions means even sub-1-point consistent shifts can give a large Pillai's trace. So 1.97 is not by itself evidence of an inflated unit, though pseudo-replication remains a live concern.

(e) "Every region's median sitting within 1 of the oracle" misquotes the paper. It reports the AVERAGE median distance as below 1 for every region, and 94.7% within-1 agreement only for the global pool.

(f) The blank data-card field is "Number of unique annotations", not annotators. The claim that the annotator count is unreported is still true from the rest of the paper.

(g) The paper says "dependent variable" (singular), so "19 DVs" is an inference, though Pillai > 1 confirms more than one DV.

(h) Comparing the Open Images V² = 0.0766 with Pillai's trace mixes different statistics and datasets, so it is weak evidence of inconsistency.

No reviewer-directed imperative text was found in the sections examined.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of C02 holds up against the text. Several of its secondary arguments are overstated or wrong.

What holds:
(1) The unit of analysis is never defined. §6 calls the DV 'MST annotations for each subject', which means each row needs 19 values. The text says annotator groups changed from image to image ('Five annotators were randomly selected... As the group of annotators was not consistent from image to image'). Nothing in §6 or the appendices says which row could carry all 19 values: annotators, index-matched images, replicate slots, or aggregates. This matters for interpretation, not just completeness. For example, if the rows were the 25 region×replicate slots, then N=25, p=19, error df=20, and the null expectation of Pillai's V = p·ν_h/(ν_h+ν_e) = 19·4/24 ≈ 3.2. An observed 1.97 would then be unremarkable. The meaning and significance of 1.97 therefore depend entirely on that undefined choice.
(2) No F, df, N or exact p is reported, and there are no per-subject or post-hoc contrasts.
(3) A one-factor MANOVA has no annotator or image random effects. Whatever the rows are, within-annotator or within-image dependence is unmodelled unless the rows are annotators.
(4) The released fields are subject, image, region and annotation only (App. C). There is no annotator ID, and the crowd 'Number of unique annotations' field is blank. Readers therefore cannot separate a region effect from a small number of idiosyncratic annotators. The pool size per market is also unreported.
(5) 'Enough statistical power' comes with no power analysis.
(6) This test is the main support for the abstract's 'systematically vary across regions', for contribution (c) first half, and for the practitioner advice. The expert Mann-Whitney evidence is weaker still: 3 of roughly 36 per-image tests were significant at p<.05, with no correction. A competent methods reviewer would require these items to be fixed, so 'major' is right for the regional-difference claim. The MST-E release keeps its value regardless.

What is overstated or wrong:
(a) The arithmetic is correct: s = min(19, 4) = 4, so V/s = 1.97/4 ≈ 0.49. But that same arithmetic shows Pillai's trace is itself a multivariate effect size (multivariate η² = V/s). 'Reports no effect size' should read 'reports no df, F, N, or interpretable per-subject or directional effect'.
(b) 'States the inference backwards' is mostly pedantic. A one-way MANOVA is equivalent to a canonical correlation or discriminant analysis between group dummies and the DVs, so Pillai's test is symmetric. Saying 'annotations predict region' is loose wording but tests the same hypothesis. The valid remaining point is that the test gives no magnitude or direction per subject. Even that is partly addressed descriptively by the Fig. 8 confusion matrices across annotator pools (figure missing, so not verifiable).
(c) The claim that 1.97 is 'hard to reconcile' with the ICCs of 0.86–0.94 is a non sequitur. A one-way ICC with subject as the random effect compares between-subject variance with within-subject variance. A consistent regional shift of about 0.5 MST, with residual SD of about 1, adds up across 19 DVs to a large Mahalanobis separation (D² ≈ 19·0.28 ≈ 5) and a sizable canonical correlation. The same applies to the 'median within 1 of oracle' result: a ±1 shift is large relative to that residual noise. The Open Images V² = 0.0766 is a different statistic on different data with mostly unique individuals, so it is not comparable. A high V can arise from aggregation or a small N, but it does not by itself signal inflation.
(d) The MANOVA-assumption concern for 10-level ordinal data is fair but minor. Pillai's trace is the most robust of the MANOVA statistics. The real problems are the clustering and the undefined unit.

Net: the regional-difference finding is unverifiable as reported and may be confounded with individual annotators. That materially weakens a headline claim but does not show it is false, which is why I rate it major rather than critical.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §6 p.8: "with annotator region as the independent variable and MST annotations for each subject as the dependent variable" (L399-401). §6 p.8: "the subject annotations were a significantly high predictor of the region of the annotators (Pillai's trace = 1.97, p < 0.05)" (L401-402). §6 p.8: "we have enough statistical power to explicitly test the effect of the annotator's region" (L398-399). §6 p.7: "Five annotators were randomly selected from a broader pool of annotators within each market to annotate each image." (L380). §6 p.7: "As the group of annotators was not consistent from image to image, we use a one-way random" (L381-382). App. C p.21: "region, Ghana, Region where the annotation came from" (L1079-1080); the fields listed are subject, image, region and annotation only. Data card p.23, crowd: "Number of unique annotations:" followed by a blank (L1217-1218). Abstract: "annotations that systematically vary across regions" (L49-50). Contribution c): "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations." (L541). Open Images: "V 2 = 0.0766, p < 0.05" (L447). Fig. 8 caption: "median value selected by crowdsource annotators across subsets of images and different annotator pools" (L1358-1360).
verdicts.corrections:
1. 'Reports no effect size' is wrong. Pillai's trace is a multivariate effect size, and V/s = 1.97/4 ≈ 0.49 (multivariate η²) follows directly from it. The real gap is the missing F, df, N, exact p, and per-subject or directional contrasts.
2. 'States the inference backwards' is overstated. A one-way MANOVA is mathematically equivalent to canonical correlation or discriminant analysis between region dummies and the DVs, so 'annotations predict region' tests the same null hypothesis. This is loose wording, not a reversed inference.
3. The claim that 1.97 is 'hard to reconcile' with within-region ICCs of 0.86–0.94, with medians within 1 of the oracle, and with the Open Images V² does not follow. The ICC measures between-subject versus within-subject variance and says nothing about region shifts. Shifts of 1 point or less, consistent across 19 DVs, can produce large canonical correlations. The Open Images V² = 0.0766 is a different statistic on different data. A large V is consistent with an aggregated or small-N unit, but it is not evidence of one.
4. 'Does not answer direction or magnitude' needs softening. Fig. 8 reportedly shows median versus oracle confusion matrices across annotator pools, which gives descriptive direction (figure missing, unverified).
5. The MANOVA normality and homogeneity concern is minor, because Pillai's trace is the most robust MANOVA statistic. The clustering and unit-of-analysis problems carry the issue.
6. The pseudo-replication charge is conditional. If the rows were annotators who each rated all 19 subjects, annotator would be the correct unit. The paper's text makes that unlikely but does not rule it out.

issues.title: The reference standard is 19 subject-level integers from one non-blind co-author (the scale's creator) who approved an author's pre-annotations; its reliability is never assessed
issues.claim: Every accuracy claim is scored against one rater's labels. Dr. Monk, the scale's creator and a co-author, approved labels another author had already proposed, which is a textbook anchoring set-up. The paper does not say whether he was blind to those proposals or how many he changed. It reports no test-retest, no second-expert check and no uncertainty for the oracle. He also chose each Golden image as the one that 'best represents' his label, so agreement on the Golden set is partly built in. The whole reference standard is 19 integers, one per subject, applied to roughly 1,500 images. The image-level metric therefore weights subjects by their image counts (55–112), and an annotator–oracle disagreement cannot be split into annotator error and oracle error. The scale was designed around the Americas and the oracle is US-based. In a paper whose thesis is that perception is culturally situated, regional distance from this oracle may partly measure cultural distance from one reference point rather than error; for example, US experts sat closer to the oracle than Indian experts on the showcase subject. 'Aligns with an expert' therefore means alignment with one anchored, unvalidated label set.
issues.paper_evidence: §3 p.4: “Images were first annotated by an author and sent to Dr. Monk for final golden annotations.” §3 p.4: “Dr. Monk selected an image for each subject that best represents their skin tone (called the Golden Images set) and approved the corresponding MST annotation.” App. C: “Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value.”; “Number of unique annotations: 19”. §4 p.5: “we have MST annotations provided by the creator of the MST scale.”; “the average median distance, the expected difference between the median annotation from a group of annotators and the oracle computed across all images”. App. A.2 p.17: “designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas”. No oracle test-retest, blinding or second-expert agreement appears in §3, §4 or Apps C, F or L (App. L adds only his name and credentials).
issues.external_evidence: In the released mst-e_image_details.csv the MST column is constant within each subject, giving 19 distinct subject-level values that match the data card's 'Number of unique annotations: 19'. These values match App. E's MST column for all 18 subjects listed there (e.g. S12 = 10; S16 and S18 = 1).
issues.affected_claims: The Abstract's 'aligns with an expert in the MST scale'. Conclusions (a), (b) and (c), wherever 'match the original intention' is the yardstick. Every within-±1 and average-median-distance result in §§5–6. Reading regional deviations as error.
issues.severity_disagreement: None; all three sources banded it major.
issues.suggested_fix: Report whether Dr. Monk saw the author's pre-annotations and how often he changed them. Have him re-annotate blind, on several images per subject, and report test-retest. Add at least 2–3 independent MST-trained experts, ideally from different regions, and report their agreement with each other and with Dr. Monk. Score annotators against a consensus or latent-class reference that carries uncertainty, and present regional results relative to several references. Report subject-level (n=19) metrics with the image weighting made explicit, and treat Golden-set results as an upper bound. Frame 'alignment with intent' as alignment with one perspective, and disclose the co-author conflict of interest next to the oracle definition.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the whole paper: abstract, §§3–8, Limitations, and Appendices A.2, B, C (data card), E, F, G and L. The core facts in the issue hold.

1. **What the paper says about the reference labels.** The oracle is one person's label for each subject. That person is Dr. Monk, a co-author and the scale's creator. An author annotated first, and Dr. Monk "approved" the label. The paper never says:
   - whether he saw the proposed labels;
   - how many labels he changed;
   - whether anyone assessed test-retest or second-expert agreement.

   §3 also says images were "annotated using the MST scale by the authors as well as the MST creator". So author labels existed, but no author-versus-Monk agreement is reported.

2. **Nothing in the paper resolves this.**
   - The Limitations section covers only the 19-subject count, the region and annotator-type variables, the ±1 threshold and the number of annotators.
   - App. L shows earlier reviewers objected to what "credentials they possessed to establish ground truth on skin tone, a characteristic we highlight as subjective". The response only names Dr. Monk and lists his credentials. The paper was challenged on this exact point and did not deal with reliability or blinding.

3. **The released data match the issue.** The MST value is constant within each subject, giving 19 distinct values. Per-subject row counts run from 55 to 112, though these counts include videos (1,546 rows = 1,515 images + 31 videos).

**Why this is only partially upheld, and why the severity is lower than claimed.**

- **The paper frames the target as creator intent.** It consistently calls the oracle the "intended annotations", "Dr. Monk's intent" or "the scale creator's intent", not objective truth. A creator-approved label is that construct by design. The real weak points are possible anchoring on an author's pre-label and the lack of any stability check, not the fact that there is only one rater.

- **Oracle noise would lower agreement, not raise it.** The crowd and photographer annotators label independently of the oracle. Random error in 19 oracle integers would reduce agreement within ±1 rather than create it. So the high agreement reported (18 of 19 subjects for the pooled crowd; median distance about 0.78) is, if anything, conservative with respect to oracle noise. Anchoring changes whose label the reference really is. It does not inflate agreement unless the pre-annotating author shares a bias with the annotators, and nothing suggests that.

- **Several core results do not use the oracle at all.** These include all the ICC/reliability results, the MANOVA region effect, the Open Images V² and ICC results, and the Spearman-Brown replication results. Conclusion (a) mostly rests on ICC. Conclusion (b) rests partly on ICC and partly on the oracle distance (0.78 for both lighting conditions). Only conclusion (c) and the abstract's "aligns with an expert" depend directly on the oracle.

- **The cultural-distance argument is selectively supported.**
  - Subject 14 does show US experts (MST5–7) closer to the oracle (MST6) than Indian experts (MST3–5).
  - In aggregate, though, Indian experts were closer to the oracle than US experts (median distance 0.78 vs 0.84). Their within-±1 rate was also higher (88.9% vs 83.4%).
  - None of the five crowdsourced regions is the US.

  So the paper's own numbers do not back the idea that a US-based oracle favours US-like perception.

- **The paper does not read regional deviation as error.** It describes regional differences as different "mental models" shaped by "regional cultural contexts". It even suggests using annotators from the same region as the data. It only uses the oracle to say the pooled median is close.

- **The Golden-set point is speculative.** Choosing the best-lit, most representative image is the stated purpose of a reference set. The paper reports Golden and Challenging results separately.

- **Image weighting is overstated.** It affects only the average median distance, which is computed across all images. The crowd within-±1 figure (94.7%) is per subject, i.e. 18 of 19.

**Net assessment.** This is a real, unaddressed gap in reporting and validation that should be fixed: say whether Dr. Monk was blind to the proposed labels, how many he changed, and how stable his labels are, and give an author-versus-Monk check. It limits how strongly "aligns with an expert" or "matches the original intention" can be read. But it does not materially undermine the paper's core reliability or regional-variation findings, and noise would bias agreement downward. Severity: minor (bordering on moderate), not major.

**No injected instructions aimed at reviewers were found in the sections I read.**

verdicts.corrections:
1. **"Non-blind" is an inference.** The paper says an author annotated first and Dr. Monk "approved" the label, which strongly suggests he saw it. It never states that he was not blind, so the title should say "blinding not reported".
2. **"'best represents' his label" misquotes the paper.** The text says the image "best represents their skin tone".
3. **The Subject 16 example is wrong.** S16 does not appear in App. E, which lists 18 subjects and leaves out one because of a programming error. S16 = 1 comes only from the CSV. App. E lists S18 alone at MST1.
4. **The per-subject counts of 55–112 include videos.** The CSV has 1,546 rows, which is 1,515 images plus 31 videos.
5. **Image weighting applies to only one metric.** It affects the average median distance. The crowd within-±1 result (94.7%) is per subject.
6. **The US-oracle example cuts against the issue in aggregate.** Indian experts were closer to the oracle overall than US experts (0.78 vs 0.84; 88.9% vs 83.4% within ±1), and no crowdsourced region is in the US.
7. **"Reading regional deviations as error" misstates the paper.** It treats regional differences as cultural mental models and even recommends annotators from the same region as the data.
8. **Not all of conclusions (a) and (b) depend on the oracle.** They rest largely on the ICC results, which do not use it.
9. **Missing: oracle noise lowers measured agreement.** Random error in the oracle would bias agreement downward, so the reported alignment is conservative with respect to that error. The issue's real force is about interpretation (anchoring, whose label the reference is, and unreported stability), not inflated accuracy.

verdicts.reasoning:
The facts in the issue are correct, and the text forces me to accept them. §3 says an author annotated first and Dr. Monk "approved" the labels. That wording implies he saw the proposed labels, so this is a non-independent, anchoring-prone process. The paper does not say how many labels he changed. It reports no test-retest, no second-expert check and no uncertainty for the oracle anywhere: §3, §4, Apps C, F and L. App. L only names him and gives his credentials. The data card also leaves out the author pre-annotation step: it says the images were "annotated ... by the MST creator". That is a provenance gap in a Datasets & Benchmarks release. I checked the released CSV. MST is constant within every subject, giving 19 subject-level values. Each subject has 55 to 112 rows, 1546 rows in all (images plus videos). All 18 subjects listed in App. E match the CSV. A methods reviewer would rightly ask for a description of the oracle procedure and some reliability evidence. Under STARD and QUADAS-2 thinking, this is a recognised weakness of the reference standard.

The materiality is overstated, though, and several supporting arguments are weak.

(1) Random error in a reference standard lowers observed agreement; it does not raise it. Oracle unreliability alone cannot produce the reported result: 18 of 19 subjects within ±1, and a mean distance of 0.78. Only systematic error could inflate agreement, for example anchoring on a pre-annotating author whose perceptions resemble the annotators'. On a 10-point scale with a ±1 tolerance, that inflation is plausibly small.

(2) The paper scopes the claim honestly. It defines the target as the "intended" annotation, the "scale creator's intent". The abstract says "an expert", in the singular. So "aligns with one expert" is literally the claim, and for that construct the creator is the natural reference. A second expert would change the construct rather than validate it. Test-retest would still be desirable.

(3) Two headline findings do not depend on the oracle at all: the reliability results (ICC) and the regional differences (MANOVA and Mann-Whitney). The dataset's images also keep their value. The issue affects only the alignment sub-claim and the second half of Conclusion (c).

(4) A constant label per subject is a design choice, not a defect. The construct is the person's skin tone, photographed within 4 hours, and annotators are meant to be invariant to lighting. The real statistical consequence is that the effective n is 19. That clustering problem with missing confidence intervals is a separate issue.

(5) The weighting point is small. Only the average median distance is computed per image. The crowd headline of 94.7% equals 18/19, which is per subject. Image counts vary only about 2x across subjects.

(6) The Golden "built-in agreement" applies only to the Golden set. The all-image and per-subject metrics are unaffected, and the paper reports 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly-lit images.

(7) The cultural-distance argument rests on one cherry-picked subject. In aggregate, Indian experts were closer to the oracle than US experts: 88.9% vs 83.4% within ±1, and a distance of 0.78 vs 0.84. There is no US crowd pool to test proximity to a US reference point.

On balance this is a legitimate documentation and limitation issue that should be disclosed and caveated. It is unlikely to reverse any headline conclusion, so I downgrade it from major to minor, at the upper end of minor.

Arithmetic checks: 94.7% = 18/19 ✓. 88.9% = 16/18 ✓. 83.4% does not match k/18 exactly (15/18 = 83.3%); this is a rounding nit. As a tangent, the data card's per-MST images sum to 1512 and its videos to 34. The CSV has 34 mp4 files. The text says 1515 images and 31 videos.

verdicts.corrections:
1. The issue says the paper "does not say whether he was blind" to the author's proposals. In fact, "approved the corresponding MST annotation" implies he saw them. The text supports "not blind", which matches the issue's own title. What remains unknown is how many labels he changed.

2. The external evidence lists "S16 and S18 = 1" as matching App. E. S16 is not in App. E; it was excluded from the expert study by a programming error (footnote 4). Only S18 appears there at MST1. S16 = 1 is in the CSV and is consistent with the data card (2 subjects at MST1). All 18 App. E values do match the CSV.

3. Subject weighting by image count affects only the average-median-distance metric. The crowd within-±1 headline of 94.7% is 18/19 subjects, computed per subject. Counts range from 55 to 112 (about 2x), so the distortion is modest. The more serious statistical problem is clustering (effective n = 19, no confidence intervals), which is a separate issue.

4. Random oracle error would lower observed agreement, not raise it. Unreliability alone therefore cannot explain the high agreement; only systematic or anchoring error could inflate it.

5. The Golden-selection effect applies only to the Golden set. It does not affect the per-subject or all-image metrics.

6. The cultural-distance example (Subject 14) is cherry-picked. In aggregate, Indian experts were closer to the oracle than US experts (88.9% vs 83.4%; 0.78 vs 0.84), and there was no US crowd pool.

7. The paper does not explicitly read regional deviations as error. It frames them as cultural and recommends co-located annotators, so that "affected claim" is overstated.

8. One label per subject is intentional, since the construct is a person's lighting-invariant skin tone. It is not in itself a flaw.

9. The paper explicitly scopes alignment to "an expert" and "the scale creator's intent", so the abstract's claim is narrower than the issue suggests.

10. The issue misses one point that supports it: the data card attributes the annotations to Dr. Monk alone and omits the author pre-annotation step.

issues.title: 'Invariant to lighting (with training)' is inferred from equal unsigned averages and overlapping ICC ranges, on a Golden/Challenging contrast confounded with pose, mask, outcome-based selection, session order, unreported skips and repeated exposure to the same 19 people
issues.claim: INFERENCE. Invariance is an equivalence claim, yet no lighting effect is estimated, no paired within-subject signed shift is computed and no equivalence margin is set. The evidence consists of (a) identical average median distances (0.78 for well-lit and poorly-lit images), which are unsigned and could hide opposite shifts at different scale positions (e.g. poorly-lit images rated darker for light subjects and lighter for dark subjects), and (b) overlapping ICC ranges (Golden 0.90–0.96, Challenging 0.82–0.95). With n=19, those ICCs have CIs of roughly ±0.06–0.12, and the drop itself suggests some lighting sensitivity. The 0.78 figure cannot equal k/19 (15/19 = 0.789), so its unit (images or subjects) is unstated. The pooled well-vs-poorly-lit crowd comparison mixes subjects whose poorly-lit share ranges from 19% to 74%, which is a Simpson-type risk, and images are nested in 19 subjects with no clustering. 'With training' and 'learn' imply a training effect, but there is no untrained or pre-training arm (training is undescribed; see C12). DESIGN. (i) The oracle chose each Golden image as the one that best represents his label, so the Golden set is selected on the outcome. (ii) The Challenging set was curated with no stated rule by people who knew the targets. (iii) Pairs differ beyond lighting: pose differs in 15 of 18 resolvable pairs, and mask status differs for S15 and S16. (iv) Experts always rated Golden first and Challenging a week later with new distractors, so lighting is confounded with session, order, practice and anchoring on the same 18 recognisable people. The distractors were never analysed, and one subject was dropped for a 'programming error'. (v) The binary lighting label is never defined and its provenance is unknown. (vi) Crowd pools rated 55–112 images of each of 19 people. How often an annotator saw the same person is unreported, so cross-lighting consistency may partly reflect recognising the person, which cannot happen in the wild. (vii) Skips and 'difficult' flags were allowed but are not reported by lighting. Differential skipping of poorly-lit images would leave the easier cases and inflate apparent invariance. (viii) All lighting variants were staged within one 7–19-minute studio session per subject on one device family (see C18).
issues.paper_evidence: Conclusion p.10: “with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions.” §7 p.9: “We find that annotators are able to learn to be invariant to environmental factors such as lighting quality”. Abstract: “annotators can reliably annotate skin tone in a way that aligns with an expert in the MST scale, even under challenging environmental conditions”. §3 p.4: “We curated a corresponding Challenging Images set which mirrored the Golden Images set with different lighting conditions.” §6 p.7: “The Golden Images ICC ranged from 0.9 to 0.96, and Challenging Images ICC ranged from 0.82 to 0.95 – a comparatively lower range but still significant and consistent.” §6 p.8: “The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images.” §5 p.6: “Participants first annotated the Golden Images set and distractor images. Approximately one week later, participants annotated the Challenging Images set”. Footnote 4: “One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error.” §6 p.7: “the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators.” App. C: “Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators.” The data card defines lighting only as “lighting, well_lit, Lighting condition of the image”.

All 18 resolvable Golden images are well_lit and all 19 Challenging images are poorly_lit. Pose matches only for S0, S9 and S13; the other 15 pairs differ (e.g. S2 facing_camera vs side). S15's Challenging image has mask=1 and S16's Golden image has mask=1. Poorly-lit share by subject: S0 46/62 = 0.74 (24/40 = 0.60 once the 22 DNG duplicates in C16 are removed), S8 52/90 = 0.58, S5 20/80 = 0.25, S10 13/67 = 0.19. Pose 'side' has 635 rows, the same as poorly_lit (635); these were not cross-tabulated and the match may be coincidental. Filename timestamps put each subject's shoot within 6.6–18.4 minutes, all on 2022-09-22. Caveat: the boundary between 'frontal' and 'facing_camera' in the released labels may be fuzzy.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (b). The Abstract's 'even under challenging environmental conditions'. Contribution (e), which motivates MST-E as training for invariance. The Discussion's invariance claim. 'Similar average accuracy under staged lighting' is supported; 'invariant' and the training-causal wording are not.
issues.severity_disagreement: stat:M6, meas:MV3, meas:MV4, design:M7 and data:D7 banded it major. design:m1 banded the expert-only session-order confound minor, because the expert study is exploratory and (b) rests mainly on crowd data. The merged issue is major because the crowd-side inference defects alone suffice.
issues.suggested_fix: Fit a lighting fixed effect, with pose and mask as covariates, in an ordinal mixed model on all still images, with random effects for subject, image and annotator. Report per-subject paired signed differences (poorly − well lit) in individual and median annotations with bootstrap CIs clustered by subject, and a TOST against a margin fixed in advance (e.g. ±0.5 MST). Use pose- and mask-matched pairs, or several pairs per subject. Define the lighting label and report who assigned it and how reliably. Report Golden-set results as an upper bound. Report the distribution of annotator × subject exposures, and re-estimate on each annotator's first exposure only, or randomise so that a subject's well-lit and poorly-lit images go to different annotators. Report skip and 'difficult' rates by lighting × region, with missing-not-at-random sensitivity analyses. Counterbalance or interleave expert sessions and analyse the distractors. Add an untrained arm or drop the 'learn' / 'with training' wording. State whether 0.78 is signed or absolute and whether it is averaged over images or subjects. Weaken 'invariant' to 'similar consensus accuracy under the tested (staged) lighting conditions' unless equivalence is shown.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked every cited passage against the manuscript. All are verbatim apart from ligatures, have the right page numbers and are quoted in fair context. Nothing in the main text, the Limitations section, the data card, the footnotes or Appendix L ("Addressing previous reviews") deals with how the lighting contrast was designed or inferred. The Limitations paragraph covers annotator identity, UI and language, the 19-subject sample and the exploratory status of the expert study. Appendix L is about the MST citation, Dr. Monk's credentials, the choice of photographers, the definition of "average median distance", scope and the 19-subject limit. Lighting comes up in neither.

The paper does make an equivalence-type claim in strong form, in Conclusion (b) and (e), the Discussion ("learn to be invariant") and data-card item 3 ("Trains annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions"). The Results section is more cautious: "some evidence" and "a comparatively lower range". So the strong wording in the Conclusion and Discussion goes beyond the paper's own Results.

The paper also partly contradicts its invariance claim, which the issue does not mention. The Replications paragraph says "For more challenging images, two annotators per region is beneficial", advises "filtering for images with good lighting conditions", and recommends 10 annotators on low-quality images. The Limitations section repeats "10 annotators per image if image quality is unknown". The authors therefore concede that single-rater reliability drops under poor lighting. "Invariant" can at most describe consensus-level accuracy, and the pooled, unsigned 0.78 figure does not establish even that.

No untrained arm exists. Crowd training is mentioned only as "provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task", and Appendix D describes only the photographers' task. The photographers are never described as trained, yet they were also consistent across conditions. "With training" and "learn" therefore have no causal support.

I re-checked the data claims myself (scripts/c04_check.py). All 18 resolvable Golden images are well_lit and all 19 Challenging images are poorly_lit. Pose matches only for S0, S9 and S13. S15's Challenging image and S16's Golden image carry mask=1. The raw counts match the issue: S0 46/62, S5 20/80, S8 52/90, S10 13/67, and side=635=poorly_lit.

The core point stands: "invariant" and the training-causal wording are unsupported, while "similar average consensus accuracy under staged lighting" is supported. Several sub-points are overstated (see corrections). Rewording would fix the problem, but it affects a listed contribution, the Discussion and the dataset's stated purpose, so I rate it major, at the lower end of that band.

Limitations p.9: "This work suggests the use of 10 annotators per image if image quality is unknown." — same.
§5 p.6: "Participants first annotated the Golden Images set and distractor images. Approximately one week later, participants annotated the Challenging Images set" — verbatim.
§5 p.6: "the time delay reducing the likelihood that participants would annotate the Challenging set based on their memory" — addresses memory but not order or practice.
Footnote 4 p.6: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error." — verbatim.
§6 p.7: "the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators." — verbatim; a mitigation is claimed but not quantified.
§7 p.9: "crowdsourced annotators who were provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task" — the only description of training.
App. C p.21: "Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators." — verbatim.
App. C p.20: "lighting, well_lit, Lighting condition of the image" — verbatim.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Point (ii), "no stated rule", is overstated. The paper gives a minimal criterion: the Challenging set "mirrored the Golden Images set with different lighting conditions" (§3) and was "selected with worse lighting conditions" (App. B). What is missing is an operational selection procedure, meaning why this one poorly-lit image was chosen from the 13–56 available per subject.

2. Point (iii), "pose differs in 15 of 18", counts 7 pairs (S1, S6, S11, S14, S15, S16, S17) that differ only as frontal vs facing_camera, which may be label noise. Only 8 pairs differ on side vs non-side (S2, S3, S4, S5, S7, S8, S10, S12).

3. The 'side' = 635 = poorly_lit match is coincidental and can be dropped. In the deduplicated data, side × poorly_lit is only 253.

4. The k/19 argument is weak. If the 0.78 is averaged over region-by-image medians, or over all images carrying each lighting label, it can come out at 0.78 (for example 74/95). The valid point is only that the averaging unit is unstated.

5. Some confounds work against invariance rather than inflating it. Choosing Golden images on outcome, and pose differences that make the Challenging images harder, both reduce apparent invariance. Those confounds mostly blur what the contrast can be attributed to. The ones that would inflate apparent invariance are differential skipping, repeated exposure, session order and practice, and signed shifts cancelling in an unsigned average.

6. The Golden/Challenging confounds (i)–(iv) bear on the ICC comparison and the expert study. The crowd figure of 0.78 appears to compare all images by their lighting label rather than the 19-image sets, so the Simpson-type and clustering concerns are what apply to it.

7. The issue misses supporting evidence. The paper's own Replications paragraph and Limitations section concede lower reliability under poor lighting by recommending 2 annotators per region (10 in total) for challenging or unknown-quality images. This contradicts "invariant" directly.

8. The "with training" critique gains from the fact that the photographers are never described as trained, yet they too were consistent across lighting conditions.

9. The Abstract's "even under challenging environmental conditions" claims alignment with the expert, which the similar consensus distances do support. The overclaim is the "invariant" and "learn/with training" wording in Contributions (b) and (e), the Discussion and the data card.

verdicts.reasoning:
The main point holds, and a methods reviewer at a top venue would accept it. "Invariant" is an equivalence claim, and the paper never tests it.

(1) The ICCs on the Golden and Challenging sets measure agreement between raters within each condition. They do not measure consistency across conditions. If poorly-lit images shifted every rater's judgement by the same amount, the ICC would not change. So overlapping ICC ranges say nothing direct about invariance.

(2) "0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images" is an unsigned average over units the paper does not state. There is no paired, within-subject comparison of signed shifts, no confidence interval and no equivalence margin.

(3) "With training" and "learn to be invariant" imply a training effect, but the study has no untrained or pre-training comparison group.

(4) The paper's own advice contradicts invariance. It recommends extra annotators for challenging images and filtering for good lighting. The Challenging ICC floor is lower (0.82 vs 0.90). My one-way ICC(1,1) confidence intervals (n=19, k=5) are 0.82 [0.69, 0.92] and 0.90 [0.82, 0.95]. They overlap, so the data can neither establish a drop nor rule one out.

(5) The data claims check out. All 18 resolvable Golden images are well_lit and all 19 Challenging images are poorly_lit; S18's Golden ID is missing from the details file. Pose matches only for S0, S9 and S13. S15's Challenging image has mask=1 and S16's Golden image has mask=1. Poorly-lit shares are S0 0.74, S5 0.25 and S10 0.19. Each subject's shoot spans 6.6–18.4 minutes, all on 2022-09-22. The data card defines lighting only as a label.

Several supporting points are overstated or point the wrong way.
- (i) Choosing the Golden image as the one that best fits the oracle label would lower Golden distance. If anything, that works against finding equal distances, so it does not inflate invariance.
- (iii) Pose and mask differences between pairs add nuisance variation. They prevent attributing any effect to lighting alone, but unless effects happen to cancel, they make equality harder to find, not easier.
- The "15 of 18" pose mismatches depend on treating 'frontal' and 'facing_camera' as different. If they are merged, 10 pairs match, and only 8 of 18 differ through a 'side' pose.
- The expert session-order confound applies only to an exploratory study. The paper partly mitigated it with a one-week gap and new distractors.
- For the crowd, the paper explicitly mixed the images into a larger set to prevent face recall. Exposure counts are not reported, but this concern is speculative.
- Differential skipping by lighting and the Simpson-type risk from unequal poorly-lit shares are plausible but not shown.

The Abstract's weaker wording, "reliably annotate… aligns with an expert… even under challenging environmental conditions", is reasonably supported: Challenging ICC is at least 0.82 and median distance is below 1. Only "invariant", "learn" and "with training" are unsupported.

Severity: major, not critical. "Invariant" appears in Contribution (b), Contribution (e) and the data card's motivating factors ("Trains annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions"), so the lack of support materially weakens a stated core contribution and the dataset's stated purpose. The fix is rewording, or a paired signed-shift analysis on the released annotations. The value of the MST-E release does not depend on this claim.
