verdicts.corrections:
1. Point (i), outcome-based Golden selection, would bias Golden distance downward. That works against finding equal distances, so it does not inflate apparent invariance.
2. Point (iii), pose and mask differences, limits attributing any effect to lighting alone. These differences add nuisance variation and do not inflate invariance unless effects happen to cancel.
3. "Pose differs in 15 of 18" depends on treating 'frontal' and 'facing_camera' as different poses. Merging them leaves 8 of 18 pairs that differ through a 'side' pose.
4. "0.78 cannot equal k/19" holds only if values were rounded. 15/19 truncated gives 0.78, and 14/18 = 0.778. The point that the unit is unstated still stands.
5. ICC 95% confidence intervals at n=19, k=5 are asymmetric. Half-widths run from about 0.02–0.04 at ICC 0.96 to about 0.10–0.13 at ICC 0.82, so "roughly ±0.06–0.12" understates the spread at both ends.
6. S8's poorly-lit share is 52/92 = 0.57 when its videos are counted; 52/90 = 0.58 excludes them.
7. The Abstract's "reliably… aligns with an expert… even under challenging environmental conditions" is reasonably supported. It should not be listed alongside the unsupported "invariant" wording.
8. Face recall among crowd annotators was explicitly mitigated by mixing images into a larger set, so (vi) is speculative rather than a demonstrated defect.
9. The expert session-order confound in (iv) applies only to the exploratory 18-subject expert study, not to the crowd evidence.
10. One addition the issue missed: an ICC computed within a condition cannot detect a lighting shift shared by all raters. This is the strongest technical reason the ICC evidence does not bear on invariance.

issues.title: Oracle agreement is reported only as heavily aggregated, saturating median metrics on n=18–19 subjects, with no CIs, exact agreement, signed bias, individual-level accuracy, chance baselines or stated median rule
issues.claim: Every alignment claim rests on 18–19 subjects, because the oracle is one value per subject. 'Average median distance' is averaged over images, which weights subjects by their 55–112 images and treats nested images as independent. The headline 94.7% pools every annotation across a subject's images (about 1,400–2,800 labels per subject). That mainly measures central tendency and mixes lighting conditions in proportions that vary by subject (well:poorly lit from 16:46 to 54:13). The median-within-±1 metric saturates. In simulation, a 5-rater median with unbiased per-annotation error up to SD 1.15 MST falls within ±1 of the oracle 99–100% of the time, so 83%, 89% and 95% say little about annotator quality. The median's exact-match rate does discriminate (0.62–0.83 in the same simulations) but is not reported. Also missing: single-annotator accuracy (the relevant figure under the 3-annotator status quo the paper criticises), image-level crowd within-±1, signed bias (median − oracle) by region and MST level, and a weighted κ or ordinal Krippendorff's α against the oracle. Signed bias is the natural effect size for (c), and it would show whether the 'diverse pool matches intent' result arises from opposite regional biases cancelling. No CI is given for any proportion, and the India-vs-US contrast is within noise. Chance baselines are missing; the results beat them clearly, so this concerns interpretability, not validity. The paper does not state how even-count medians after skips are handled or whether half-step medians are rounded. At MST1 and MST10 the ±1 window covers only two categories and errors can only go one way, so endpoint subjects are biased toward the centre by construction. The App. G pixel baseline is judged only visually, using RGB L2 distance.
issues.paper_evidence: §5 p.7: “88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States”. §6 p.8: “Using the global pool, the consensus annotation agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%).” §4 p.5: “when calculating the consensus MST annotation for an image we use the median MST annotation from the responses.” §6 p.7: “we look at the annotations Per Subject - meaning annotations across all images of a single subject”. App. G p.26: “finding the closest MST point based on the L2 distance in RGB space to the reference colors [14]”. App. C: “Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators.” No CI, exact-match rate, signed bias, chance baseline, median tie rule or boundary treatment appears in §§4–6 or App. F.
issues.external_evidence: Wilson 95% CIs: 18/19 = 0.947 (0.754, 0.991); 16/18 = 0.889 (0.672, 0.969); 15/18 = 0.833 (0.608, 0.942). Exact Clopper–Pearson (data:D3): 74.0–99.9, 65.3–98.6 and 58.6–96.4. Simulation (stat:M1/M7; normal error around the oracle, rounded and clipped, 5 raters, 400 replications): median-within-1 = 1.00/1.00/0.99 and median exact = 0.83/0.69/0.62 for error SD 0.7/1.0/1.15. Chance: uniform-random within-±1 = 5.4/19 = 28.4%; always MST2 (or MST3) = 7/19 = 36.8%; uniform-random MAE = 3.29. Images per subject in the released CSV: 55–112.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (a) ('aligns with an expert'). Contribution (c), second half ('a diverse geographical pool … match[es] the original intention'). Contribution (d): the k recommendation rests on reliability projections, not on how accuracy changes with k. The Abstract's alignment claim.
issues.severity_disagreement: stat:M7 and meas:MV6 banded it major. meas:MV11 banded the baseline, median-rule and endpoint-truncation sub-points minor, because the results clearly beat chance.
issues.suggested_fix: For each region and for the pooled consensus, report per-subject (n=19, equally weighted) exact-match rate, within-1 rate, MAE and signed bias (median − oracle), with bootstrap CIs clustered by subject. From the released annotations, report single-annotator and median-of-k accuracy curves for k = 1..25 by region and lighting. Add weighted κ or ordinal Krippendorff's α against the oracle. Put chance and constant-guess baselines next to every figure. Plot signed bias against oracle MST level and run leave-one-region-out analyses. State the median rule for even n. Report endpoint subjects separately or use an ordinal model that handles truncation. Quantify the App. G baseline against the oracle in CIELAB/ΔE2000.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the main text, Appendices A–L, the limitations section, the data card and the footnotes. The core of the issue holds. Every agreement-with-oracle figure is given as a bare percentage or mean, with no CI or other uncertainty measure (the only inferential statistics are the ICC p-values, the MANOVA and the Mann-Whitney tests). There is no chance baseline, no single-annotator accuracy, no numeric exact-match rate and no numeric signed-bias summary. Reliability is reported only as ICC, never as agreement with the oracle (no weighted κ or ordinal α). The paper never says how ties or half-step medians are handled. It does say annotations can be skipped (App. C), so ties are possible. The oracle is one value per subject (data card: "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value"), so the 94.7% headline rests on 18/19 subjects. Recommendation (d) uses only Spearman-Brown reliability projections and never shows how agreement with the oracle changes with k.

I confirmed the data claims with the released CSV. Rows per subject run 55–112. The lighting split runs from 16 well-lit : 46 poorly lit (subject_0) to 54:13 (subject_10). Rerunning the simulation reproduced it: median-within-±1 of 1.00/0.996/0.987 and exact match of 0.83/0.69/0.61 at SD 0.7/1.0/1.15.

All of this weakens the strength of the Abstract's claim, contribution (a) and the second half of contribution (c) without invalidating them. 18/19 within ±1 clearly beats chance, and even the Wilson lower bound (about 75%) supports loose alignment. What the paper lacks is any metric that could tell good annotators from mediocre ones. It also has nothing showing that the diverse pool beats a single-region pool, since every region also had an average median distance below 1.

The issue overstates several points, so I rate it partially upheld:
1. App. F / Fig. 8 gives confusion matrices of Dr. Monk's value against median annotations "across subsets of images and different annotator pools". By construction these show exact agreement (the diagonal) and the direction of error by MST level and by pool. The information is therefore displayed, just not summarised numerically or with uncertainty. The issue's "No … exact-match rate, signed bias … appears in … App. F" is wrong as stated.
2. The paper never claims India and the US differ in alignment. It says both markets align, so the India-vs-US contrast "within noise" rebuts a claim the paper does not make.
3. The paper partly hedges. It acknowledges the small n ("small number of subjects (19)"). It calls the ±1 threshold a convention from prior work ([33, 34]; Limitations; App. L). It labels the expert study exploratory (App. L). None of this addresses saturation, CIs or baselines.
4. The 5-rater simulation applies to the expert medians and the image-level crowd medians. It does not apply to the per-subject pooled 94.7%, where random error averages out entirely and the metric tests only systematic bias of more than one category. Also, the observed 83–89% for experts is below the simulated ceiling of 99–100%. So the metric did flag 2–3 real misses, and "say little" overstates the case.

The sub-points on baselines, the median rule, endpoint truncation and the App. G pixel baseline are minor.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
All of the issue's quotes match the manuscript verbatim and keep their context:
- §5 p.7: "88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States"
- §6 p.8: "Using the global pool, the consensus annotation agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%)."
- §4 p.5: "when calculating the consensus MST annotation for an image we use the median MST annotation from the responses."
- §6 p.7: "we look at the annotations Per Subject - meaning annotations across all images of a single subject"
- App. G p.26: "finding the closest MST point based on the L2 distance in RGB space to the reference colors [14]"
- App. C: "Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators."

Other passages I checked:
- §4 p.5: "the average median distance, the expected difference between the median annotation from a group of annotators and the oracle computed across all images (ideally less than 1)"
- §6 p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
- App. F p.26/27 (Fig. 8): "Comparisons between the intended MST value as annotated by the MST creator and the median value selected by crowdsource annotators across subsets of images and different annotator pools."
- Limitations p.10: "While we use thresholds for agreement (e.g., 1-point discrepancy) that are in line with prior work when describing the resulting annotations as reliable"
- Limitations p.10: "The MST-E dataset has a small number of subjects (19)"
- §7 p.9: "This is a very large jump from the status quo of 3 annotators per image"
- §7 p.9: "This suggests that a geographically diverse annotator pool provides annotations that are in line with the intended use"
- App. L p.29/30: "We also more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory"
- Data card p.23: "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value."
verdicts.corrections:
1. Fig. 8 (App. F) gives oracle-versus-median confusion matrices by image subset (Golden, Challenging, per subject) and by annotator pool. These show exact agreement and error direction by MST level and by region graphically. What is missing is a numeric summary with CIs, so "exact-match rate / signed bias not reported" should read "not quantified".
2. The paper makes no India-versus-US alignment contrast. The sentence that it is "within noise" should be dropped or recast as a caution that 88.9% and 83.4% should not be compared.
3. The expert denominator is not stated. 83.4% matches neither 15/18 (83.3%) nor 30/36 (83.3%), so the Wilson intervals that assume n=18 rest on an assumption. This mismatch is itself a small reporting inconsistency.
4. The 5-rater simulation fits the expert medians and the image-level crowd medians. It does not fit the per-subject pooled 94.7%, which tests systematic bias only. The experts' 83–89% sits below the simulated saturation level of 99–100%, so the metric did detect failures. "Say little about annotator quality" is too strong.
5. The figure of 55–112 per subject counts video rows. Still images alone run from 52 (subject_15) to 111 (subject_12).
6. The paper partly acknowledges small n and the conventional ±1 threshold, citing [33] and [34] (Limitations; App. L), and frames the expert study as exploratory. None of this addresses saturation, CIs or chance baselines.
7. The "average median distance" weighting critique applies to the crowd analysis only. The expert analysis used only Golden and Challenging images.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of C05 is technically correct, and a competent methods reviewer would raise it. I checked each numeric claim myself.

1. The data claims hold. In mst-e_image_details.csv the oracle MST is constant within each subject, so there are only 19 independent reference values (18 for the expert study). Rows per subject run from 55 to 112. Well:poorly-lit ratios run from 16:46 (subject_0) to 54:13 (subject_10).

2. The interval arithmetic holds. Wilson intervals: 18/19 gives 0.754 to 0.991, 16/18 gives 0.672 to 0.969, and 15/18 gives 0.608 to 0.942. Clopper–Pearson: 74.0 to 99.9, 65.3 to 98.6, and 58.6 to 96.4. The paper reports no interval for any proportion.

3. The chance baselines hold. Uniform-random within ±1 is 5.4/19 = 28.4%. Always answering MST2 or MST3 gives 7/19 = 36.8%. Uniform-random MAE is 3.29.

4. The saturation claim holds. I re-ran it with 4,000 replications per subject, normal error, rounding and clipping, and a median of 5. Median within ±1 was 1.000, 0.996 and 0.988 at error SD 0.7, 1.0 and 1.15. Exact match was 0.83, 0.68 and 0.62. These match the issue.

5. The issue understates its own case. The crowd consensus is a median of 25 annotations. For a 25-rater median with no rater bias, within ±1 is 1.000 even at SD 1.5, and the average absolute median distance is only 0.00 to 0.16. The paper's reported 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly-lit images is what a systematic shift of about 0.8 MST per image produces (simulated 0.82 to 0.91). The paper's "ideally less than 1" yardstick is therefore lenient for a 25-rater median. It hides that the consensus often misses Dr. Monk's exact category.

6. Consequences for the claims. The ±1 consensus metric can only detect a systematic shift of about 1 point or more. It cannot support the Abstract's wording that annotators "reliably annotate… align[ing] with an expert". The paper reports no single-annotator agreement with the oracle, although it names a 3-annotator status quo. The diverse-pool claim in contribution (c) has no comparative support. The paper reports average median distance below 1 for every region, so single-region pools also pass. The within-±1 figure is given only for the global pool. Signed bias or a per-pool comparison would be needed to show that diversity is what produces the alignment.

7. Why this is not critical. The qualitative claim survives. Even the lowest CI bounds (59 to 75%) are well above chance (28 to 37%). The ±1 convention is cited from prior work [33, 34] and acknowledged in the Limitations section. The MST-E release has value regardless.

8. Why partially upheld rather than fully upheld. Several sub-points are overstated, wrong or peripheral. App. F's Figure 8 does show oracle-versus-median confusion matrices, so exact agreement and error direction by MST level are shown graphically. The paper never contrasts India against the US. The endpoint-truncation point gets the direction wrong for the ±1 metric. Image-weighting a descriptive mean is a defined choice, not an inferential error. The lighting-mix confound is partly answered by the separate well-lit and poorly-lit figures. The pixel baseline in App. G is a side illustration. The tie-rule, endpoint and baseline sub-points are minor.

Overall: major for the core (a lenient metric on the consensus only, no uncertainty, no exact or individual-level agreement, no comparative evidence for the diverse pool). Minor for the rest.

No imperative text aimed at reviewers was found in the manuscript.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§4 p.5: "when calculating the consensus MST annotation for an image we use the median MST annotation from the responses."
§4 p.5: "the average median distance… computed across all images (ideally less than 1)."
§5 p.7: "88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States".
§6 p.7: "we look at the annotations Per Subject - meaning annotations across all images of a single subject".
§6 p.8: "the consensus annotation agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%)."
§6 p.8: "less than 1 for every region and image condition. The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
§7 p.9: "When combining the annotations across a variety of regions, we find that the median of the annotations are consistently close to Dr. Monk's annotations."
§7 p.9: "a very large jump from the status quo of 3 annotators per image".
§7 p.10 (Limitations): "we use thresholds for agreement (e.g., 1-point discrepancy) that are in line with prior work".
App. C: "Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators."
App. F p.26: "Figure 8 shows confusion matrices of Dr. Monk's annotations compared to the median annotations".
App. G p.26: "closest MST point based on the L2 distance in RGB space to the reference colors [14]".
verdicts.corrections:
1. The issue says no exact-match rate or signed bias "appears in §§4–6 or App. F". This is overstated. App. F's Figure 8 gives oracle-versus-median confusion matrices for Golden, Challenging and Per-Subject across annotator pools. Exact agreement and error direction by MST level are therefore shown graphically. What is missing is numeric summaries, CIs and kappa/alpha.

2. "The India-vs-US contrast is within noise" targets a claim the paper does not make. The paper says only that both markets are high.

3. 83.4% is not 15/18 (which is 83.3%). The expert denominator is ambiguous. Experts annotated Golden and Challenging images in two sessions, so the figure may be over 36 images (32/36 = 88.9%, 30/36 = 83.3%). There are still only 18 independent oracle values.

4. Saturation is understated, not overstated. The crowd consensus is a 25-rater median, and the per-subject pool runs to about 1,400–2,800 labels; saturation is stronger there than at 5 raters. The paper's own average median distance of 0.78 for 25-rater medians implies about 0.8 MST of systematic deviation. A 25-rater median with no rater bias gives 0.00–0.16 even at SD 1.5.

5. Conversely, "83%, 89% and 95% say little about annotator quality" is too strong. Values below the roughly 99–100% ceiling expected without bias do signal subject-level systematic bias on 1–3 subjects.

6. Endpoint truncation: clipping at MST1/MST10 makes within-±1 easier, because errors past the end pile onto the endpoint. It does not penalise endpoint subjects. "Biased toward the centre" applies to signed bias or MAE, which the paper does not report.

7. "55–112 images" counts videos too. There are 1,546 rows, 1,515 images plus 31 videos; subject_15, for example, has 52 images and 3 videos.

8. That 94.7% pools all of a subject's annotations, rather than taking a median of image medians, is an inference. The paper does not state the aggregation rule.

9. Image-weighting and nesting in "average median distance" matter only for inference. The paper defines the metric explicitly and draws no inference from it, so this sub-point is minor.

10. The lighting-mix confound is partly addressed: separate well-lit and poorly-lit distances are reported (0.78 each).

11. The App. G RGB-L2 point is valid; CIELAB ΔE would be standard. But App. G only illustrates that pixel methods are inadequate and is peripheral to the alignment claims.

12. The contribution (d) point, that the k recommendation rests on Spearman–Brown reliability rather than accuracy against the oracle, is valid but is a separate issue.

issues.title: High ICCs mainly reflect the full-range spread of 19 targets; they are tested against zero, lack CIs and ICC type, and within-region one-way ICC is blind to the regional shifts the paper reports
issues.claim: Every ICC takes the subject (or one image per subject) as its target. That gives 19 targets chosen to span all ten MST levels (oracle SD 2.89, variance 8.33), so between-target variance dominates the denominator. Testing ICC against 0 ('significant, p < .05') is uninformative. Back-calculated from the reported values, single-annotation ICCs of 0.82–0.96 fit a per-annotation error SD of about 0.6–1.35 MST steps. In simulation, ICCs of 0.87–0.94 coexist with only 30–41% exact agreement between two annotators. So 'reliably annotate' overstates fine-grained, category-level precision. A one-way ICC within a region also ignores any shift shared by all of that region's raters: biasing every rater by +1 MST gave ICC 0.92 while the median matched the oracle only 17% of the time. Within-region ICC therefore cannot detect the regional differences the paper reports, yet it is offered as evidence of a 'shared mental model', which sits awkwardly beside claim (c). The paper does not say whether the expert ICC(2,1) measures absolute agreement or consistency; consistency would drop rater offsets, the very effect of interest. Numeric expert ICCs are never given. The per-subject crowd ICC is a one-way ICC on unbalanced data (55–112 images per subject) that folds image and lighting variance into error. The 10-point ordinal scale, whose steps are perceptually unequal, is treated as interval. Partial mitigation: Open Images ICCs (0.875–0.91) stay high despite its light-skewed, narrower range.
issues.paper_evidence: §5 p.6: “Each expert reviewed each image, so we use a two-way random, single score ICC where the subject and annotator are viewed as random effect”; “Figure 3(a) shows significant, p <.05, intraclass correlation in both markets and in both image quality conditions.” §6 p.7: “For every region, the ICC is very high with Per Subject ICC ranging from 0.86 to 0.94.”; “Figure 3(b) shows significant, p< 0.05, ICC values for each region and annotation task.”; “we find that non-expert annotators also consistently annotate skin tone on the MST, using a shared mental model of the MST categories.” No CI, absolute-vs-consistency choice or numeric expert ICC appears in §5, §6, the Fig. 3 caption or Apps C–L.

Simulation (normal error around the oracle, rounded and clipped to 1–10, 5 raters, 400 replications): SD 0.7 gives ICC 0.94, pairwise exact 0.41, within-1 0.88; SD 1.15 gives ICC 0.87, exact 0.30, within-1 0.70; all raters biased +1 with SD 0.8 gives ICC 0.92 and median = oracle in 0.17 of cases. issues.affected_claims: Contribution (a) ('skin tone can be annotated reliably'). The Abstract's 'reliably annotate'. The 'shared mental model' wording.
issues.severity_disagreement: stat:M1 banded it major; meas:MV14 and design:M10 banded it minor (framing and precision, partly answered by the high Open Images ICC). Major is kept because ICC is the only individual-level reliability evidence for (a), the implied category-level precision (exact agreement of about 30–40%) materially qualifies 'reliably', and within-region ICC cannot support the 'shared mental model' reading.
issues.suggested_fix: Report the ICC type (absolute agreement, ICC(A,1)) with McGraw–Wong CIs, tested against a meaningful threshold (e.g. ICC > 0.75) rather than 0, and give the numeric expert ICCs. For each region and pooled, add ordinal Krippendorff's α or quadratic-weighted κ, plus pairwise exact and within-1 rates, with bootstrap CIs clustered by subject. Report the implied single-rater error SD in MST units and agreement stratified by scale position. Decompose variance with a cumulative-link mixed model, annotation ~ region + lighting + (1|subject/image) + (1|annotator), reporting the annotator, region and image-within-subject shares separately from between-subject variance. Drop 'shared mental model' or reconcile it with (c).

verdicts.reasoning:
The quotes are verbatim and in context (§5 p.6, §6 p.7). I checked the data claims against the released metadata. The 19 oracle MSTs have sample SD 2.887 and variance 8.333, and subjects have 55 to 112 images each. Rerunning the simulation reproduces it: SD 0.7 gives ICC 0.94, 42% exact agreement and 88% within 1. SD 1.15 gives ICC 0.864, 29% exact and 69% within 1. A shared +1 bias with SD 0.8 gives ICC 0.923, with the median matching the oracle 17% of the time.

These reporting gaps are real, and nothing in §5, §6, §7, the Fig. 3/5 captions or Appendices C to L covers them:
- No confidence intervals.
- No statement of whether the expert two-way ICC measures absolute agreement or consistency. Citing McGraw–Wong [56] does not settle it.
- Significance is tested only against zero.
- The 10-point scale is treated as interval. Appendix L puts scale length out of scope but does not take up this point.

Several parts of the issue overreach or misread the text:
(1) The paper defines 'reliable' by the 1-point threshold, not by exact-category precision. The Limitations section (p.10) says it uses "thresholds for agreement (e.g., 1-point discrepancy) that are in line with prior work when describing the resulting annotations as reliable". The abstract's "reliably annotate ... in a way that aligns with an expert" rests on consensus within-1 rates (88.9%/83.4% for experts, 94.7% for crowd) and average median distance, not only on ICC. The simulated 30–40% exact agreement still means about 70–88% within 1, which fits what the paper actually claims.
(2) The paper never uses within-region ICC to rule out regional shifts. It tests those separately with MANOVA. §7 explicitly says "although trained annotators have high inter-rater reliability across all regions, there are regional differences". 'Shared mental model within a region, models varying across regions' (p.8: "shared mental models of skin tone may vary significantly across different geographic regions") holds together. It is loose interpretive wording, not a contradiction with claim (c).
(3) The Fig. 3 caption says ICCs were computed "as well as the global pool". A one-way ICC pooled across regions would count regional offsets as error, so it is wrong to say only within-region ICC is offered. The global-pool values are not given in the text, though.
(4) The expert ICC covers 18 subjects, not 19 (footnote 4 excludes one).
(5) The Open Images ICCs (0.875–0.91) are not computed on 19 full-range targets. They stay high despite the light skew shown in Fig. 6, which cuts against the headline that the ICCs 'mainly reflect' spread.
(6) 'Numeric expert ICCs are never given' holds only for the text. Fig. 3(a) is captioned as showing "the ICC scores", and the figure itself is missing, so I cannot confirm they are absent.

Net: the reporting and interpretation criticisms are valid and worth a revision. They qualify how precise the ICC evidence is, but they do not materially weaken contribution (a) as the paper itself operationalizes it. Minor.

verdicts.corrections: (1) The expert ICC covers 18 subjects, not 19 (footnote 4). The data shows the excluded subject is subject_16, at MST1. (2) Not every ICC uses the 19 subjects as targets. The Open Images ICCs are computed over 86,809 faces with a light-skewed, narrower range, and they stay at 0.875–0.91. This undercuts the headline that the high ICCs 'mainly reflect' full-range spread, beyond being a 'partial mitigation'. (3) The Fig. 3 caption reports a 'global pool' ICC across regions, which would count regional offsets as error. The paper therefore does not rely only on within-region ICC, though the global values are not given in the text. (4) The paper does not use ICC to deny regional differences. §7 explicitly sets high IRR against the regional differences and tests the latter with MANOVA. 'Within-region shared mental model, varying across regions' (p.8) is consistent with claim (c), not awkward beside it. (5) The paper ties 'reliable' to the 1-point discrepancy threshold (Limitations, p.10) and to consensus-level alignment, not to exact-category precision. The simulated 30–41% exact agreement does not contradict that claim. (6) 'Numeric expert ICCs are never given' is true of the text only. Fig. 3(a) is captioned as showing the ICC scores, and the figure is unavailable. (7) The exact-agreement figures come from a simulation that assumes Gaussian error around the oracle, not from observed annotations. They are illustrative, not evidence of the paper's actual exact-agreement rate.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the arithmetic myself and it holds. In the released metadata the 19 subjects' oracle MST values have sample SD 2.887 and variance 8.333, and each subject has 55 to 112 images. Implied error SD = sqrt(8.333(1-ICC)/ICC) gives 1.35, 1.16, 0.96, 0.73 and 0.59 at ICCs of 0.82, 0.86, 0.90, 0.94 and 0.96. McGraw-Wong one-way 95% CIs at n=19, k=5 are (0.693, 0.915) at ICC 0.82 and (0.889, 0.973) at 0.94. My own simulation (400 reps) matched the issue's: SD 0.7 gives ICC 0.941, pairwise exact agreement 0.42 and within-1 0.88; SD 1.15 gives ICC 0.868, exact 0.29 and within-1 0.69; a +1 bias with SD 0.8 gives ICC 0.924 with median equal to the oracle in 0.17 of cases.

Four points are technically correct by current reporting standards (Koo & Li; McGraw & Wong):
- A significance test of ICC against 0 is uninformative.
- No CIs are reported.
- The paper does not say whether the two-way expert ICC measures absolute agreement or consistency.
- ICC is relative reliability that depends on between-target spread. It says nothing about category-level agreement or accuracy against the oracle.

A methods reviewer would ask for CIs, the full ICC specification, and an individual-level agreement statistic such as exact or within-1 agreement, ordinal Krippendorff's alpha, or SEM.

Several factors keep this at minor rather than major.

(1) The paper does not use ICC to argue alignment with Dr. Monk. It has a separate oracle-distance analysis (within-1 rates and average median distance). It also hedges the word 'reliable' in its Limitations as tied to 1-point thresholds. The +1-bias simulation therefore shows something the paper never claims.

(2) Even the lower CI bounds (about 0.69 to 0.89) stay in the moderate-to-excellent band. 'Reliably' in its standard psychometric sense of relative reliability is defensible for claim (a).

(3) Within-region ICC and between-region MANOVA together are coherent. The paper explicitly says 'shared mental models of skin tone may vary significantly across different geographic regions'. So within-region consistency plus between-region shifts is the paper's actual thesis, not a contradiction of claim (c). Figure 3(b) also reports a global-pool ICC. In a one-way model that pooled ICC does absorb regional rater offsets into error.

(4) In the per-subject one-way ICC, image and lighting variance does go into error, as the issue says. That makes the ICC conservative, not inflated. A one-way ANOVA ICC on unbalanced groups is also standard.

(5) Treating a 10-point ordinal scale as interval for ICC is conventional, and that objection is pedantic.

(6) The range-spread concern is partly answered by the Open Images ICCs of 0.875 to 0.91 on a light-skewed sample.

(7) The exact-agreement figures of 30 to 41% are not observed values. They come from a simulation that assumes true-score variance equals oracle variance.

One extra point supports the issue's broader idea that ICC cannot see systematic error. The paper reports an average median distance of 0.78 (crowd) and 0.78 to 0.84 (experts). Unbiased noise at the ICC-implied SDs would give only about 0.16 to 0.39. Substantial subject-specific systematic deviation must therefore be present, and ICC cannot detect it. The paper reports that distance itself, though, so the consequence is a framing issue rather than an invalidated claim.

Net: there are real reporting gaps and some loose 'shared mental model' wording. Neither materially undermines contribution (a) as the paper scopes it, nor the value of the MST-E release.

verdicts.corrections:
1. "Numeric expert ICCs are never given": they are absent from the text, but Figure 3(a) is an ICC figure that very likely displays them, and the figures are unavailable here. This should be restated as "not given in the text; can't verify the figure."
2. "Sits awkwardly beside claim (c)": this is overstated. Figure 3(b) also reports a global-pool ICC, and a one-way global ICC does absorb regional offsets into error. Only the generic wording on p.7 is loose, along with inferring a "mental model" from ICC at all.

issues.title: The Open Images generalisation substitutes reliability for validity, reads an unspecified non-significant ICC comparison as equivalence, ignores target-variance and clustering, and rests on an unreported, skin-tone-sensitive face preselection
issues.claim: (1) Open Images has no oracle, so only consistency (ICC) and between-region differences are measured. Yet the Discussion says annotators 'perform similarly' and that recommendations 'likely translate to real-world scenarios', which are validity claims. High agreement can coexist with shared systematic bias (e.g. reading under-exposed faces as darker), and the paper's own regional result shows such bias exists. (2) The ICC comparison (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.99) names no test, df or CIs. The value matches df≈4, which suggests a test across about 5 regional ICC pairs; that has almost no power, and non-significance is not equivalence. (3) ICC depends on between-target variance. Open Images is strongly skewed toward light tones while MST-E spans the scale roughly uniformly, so similar ICCs do not mean similar rater consistency. The light end is also where adjacent MST swatches are perceptually closest. (4) 'V² = 0.0766' is undefined. Read as Cramér's V it is a small effect; read as V², V ≈ 0.28, a moderate-to-large one. With hundreds of thousands to about 2 million non-independent annotations, p < 0.05 is automatic either way. A chi-square on pooled distributions also ignores the paired design (every face rated in every region) and clustering by annotator. (5) The number of annotations per face and the skip rates are not stated. (6) Images were preselected by an unnamed face detector, although the paper itself warns that upstream components miss people unevenly across skin tones. The split, face boxes, size thresholds and sampling frame are not reported. The region confounds in C01 carry over.
issues.paper_evidence: §6 p.8: “the intraclass correlation from the Open Images dataset has no significant differences than crowdsource annotators intraclass correlation in the MST-E dataset”; “This suggests that crowdsource annotators are similarly consistent in MST annotations in controlled datasets and in-the-wild data sets.”; “We also find significant differences between annotation distributions between regions (V 2 = 0.0766, p < 0.05)”; “Overall, this shows that recommendations based on annotator behaviors observed in our controlled studies likely translate to real-world scenarios commonly faced by ML practitioners.”; “We randomly selected a subset of 41,471 images that contained at least one face.” §7 p.9: “find that they perform similarly on the in-the-wild subset of Open Images to the MST-E dataset”; “with the additional analysis of the Open Images dataset, we believe our results will translate to other domains.” §2: “variable performance of upstream components across skin tone groups can lead to missing annotations for underrepresented groups during fairness evaluations”. Fig. 6 caption: “The Open Images dataset has a strong skew towards lighter skin tones.”
issues.external_evidence: Chi-square survival function at 0.26: df1 0.610, df2 0.878, df3 0.967, df4 0.992, df5 0.998. With N ≈ 434k–2.17M annotations (5–25 per face × 86,809 faces), a Cramér's V of 0.077 gives a chi-square in the tens of thousands; Cohen's conventions for df* = 4 are small 0.05 and medium 0.15. 25 × (1,546 + 86,809) ≈ 2.21M annotations in total. Adjacent MST orbs at the light end differ by about 2–6 CIEDE2000 units, against about 13 mid-scale, so Open Images agreement is measured mostly in a perceptually different part of the scale from MST-E.
issues.affected_claims: The Discussion's 'perform similarly' and 'likely translate to real-world scenarios'. The Limitations' 'translate to other domains'. Contribution (b)'s extension to in-the-wild data. The Open Images corroboration of (c). The practitioner recommendations in (d) that are carried over from MST-E. §4 frames the Open Images study as testing whether controlled findings generalise, but only reliability was tested.
issues.severity_disagreement: stat:M8, meas:MV8 and data:D4 banded it major; design:m5 banded it minor. Major is kept because the only in-the-wild evidence for the generalisation claims is mis-specified and cannot address validity.
issues.suggested_fix: Obtain expert or panel reference labels for a random Open Images subsample stratified by exposure and lighting, and report within-1 accuracy and signed bias against them, or restrict the claim to reliability. Name the ICC-comparison test and df. Report each ICC with CIs and use an equivalence test or bootstrap difference against a stated margin. Compare reliability with metrics that do not depend on target variance (pairwise exact and within-1 disagreement, residual annotator variance), or re-weight Open Images to the MST-E tone distribution. Fit the ordinal mixed model with face and annotator random effects and a fixed region effect, and report region shifts in MST units. If Cramér's V is kept, name it and give N, df and the table dimensions. Report replication count and skip rates per face. Name the face detector and report its recall by skin tone, along with the split, box and size thresholds.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked every quote against the manuscript. All are verbatim apart from ligatures, and none is taken out of context. No part of the paper covers the Open Images (OI) gaps. Appendix L ("Addressing previous reviews") never mentions Open Images. The data card (App. C) describes only MST-E. Appendix D shows only the annotation UI, and Appendix K covers only pay. The words "Cramér", "equivalence" and "validity" appear nowhere, and no test is named for χ² = 0.26. The core of the issue therefore stands.

(1) Reliability standing in for validity: §6 states its OI hypotheses only in terms of consistency and region effects ("we expect that crowdsource annotators will still consistently annotate ... and that geographic region will have a significant effect"). That scoping is fair. The paragraph then ends with "Overall, this shows that recommendations ... likely translate to real-world scenarios". The Discussion adds "perform similarly", in the same sentence as "invariant to environmental factors such as lighting", and the Limitations section uses OI to answer the 19-subject limitation ("we believe our results will translate to other domains"). OI has no oracle, so the validity-based recommendations, such as a diverse pool's median matching Dr. Monk, cannot be tested on it. The overreach is real. The wording is hedged ("likely", "we believe", "is possible"), which tempers it somewhat. §4 does note that inter-rater reliability is "Typically ... the only available indicator of annotation quality", but the paper never draws the limitation that follows for OI.

(2) The test is unnamed, with no df or CIs. A survival-function check gives p = 0.992 at df = 4, consistent with about five regional ICC pairs. Treating a non-significant result as "similarly consistent" is a textbook equivalence error. The issue's "almost no power" claim is an inference: if the test had used the face-level N (86,809 faces against about 1.5k images), even 0.03 ICC gaps would probably have come out significant. That makes the inference plausible but not established.

(3) ICC does depend on between-target variance, and Fig. 6 confirms the light-tone skew. The point is valid. One caveat: a restricted range usually lowers ICC, so the bias is not shown to favour the paper. The CIEDE2000 figures are external and I could not verify them here.

(4) "V 2 = 0.0766" is never defined. A pooled chi-square over hundreds of thousands of non-independent annotations makes p < 0.05 meaningless, and the paired, clustered design is ignored. Valid.

(5) This point is overstated. §6 begins with "We collected annotations for the entire MST-E dataset and a subset of the Open Images dataset ... Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image", so the nominal number of annotations per face is stated for both datasets. Only the skip rates go unreported; the data card mentions skips only qualitatively, and only for MST-E.

(6) This point is also overstated. The paper says only that images "contained at least one face" and never says a face detector was used. Faces may have come from Open Images' existing human-verified face boxes. The real problem is that the selection mechanism, box source, size thresholds and sampling frame are not reported. The skin-tone-sensitive detector is a hypothesis, not a fact, though the paper's own §2 warning makes it a fair concern.

Severity: the abstract and the main MST-E claims do not depend on OI. However, OI is the paper's only in-the-wild evidence, §4 states its purpose as testing generalisation, and the Limitations section uses it to offset the small, controlled MST-E. Its weakness therefore materially weakens the generalisation claim. I rate this major, at the low end of that band.

verdicts.corrections:
(a) "Likely translate to real-world scenarios" is in the §6 Results paragraph, not the Discussion. The Discussion says "perform similarly", and the Limitations section says "translate to other domains".
(b) Item (5) is partly wrong. §6 states 5 annotations per region, 25 per image, in a paragraph that covers both MST-E and OI. Only skip rates and realised counts are unreported. The issue's own "5–25 per face" is inconsistent with its "25 × (1,546 + 86,809)".

The mechanism, which could be Open Images' existing human-verified face boxes, is unreported. A detector-induced skin-tone bias is a plausible concern, not a documented fact.
(d) The "almost no power" claim in (2) is an inference from χ²≈0.26 being consistent with df≈4. The test is unnamed, so the actual df and N are unknown.
(e) The paper lists research questions (a)–(c) only. There is no contribution "(d)"; the practitioner recommendations sit under (c) and §7.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the manuscript text, the released metadata and the arithmetic.

What holds up:
(1) Reliability is not validity. Open Images has no oracle, so §6 measures only ICC and between-region differences. The Limitations sentence ("our results will translate to other domains") and the §6 sentence ("recommendations ... likely translate to real-world scenarios") go beyond that evidence. Nothing on Open Images tests whether pooled medians match the scale's intended values in the wild.
(2) The χ² = 0.26, p = 0.99 test is not named, and no df or CIs are given. The p-value does fit df = 4 (survival function 0.992; df = 5 gives 0.998, which would round to 1.00). Either way, a non-significant result is not equivalence. Any test against the MST-E ICCs would be limited by the wide CIs that come from about 19 subjects.
(4) "V² = 0.0766" is undefined. With roughly 2.17M annotations (25 × 86,809) and df* = 4, V = 0.0766 already implies χ² ≈ 51k. V = √0.0766 = 0.277 implies χ² ≈ 665k. So p < 0.05 tells us nothing, and the pooled test ignores pairing and annotator clustering.
(6) The sampling frame for the 41,471 images and 86,809 faces is not reported: how faces were found, size thresholds, which split. The Open Images annotations are also not in the release; the data folder holds only MST-E files.

What is overstated or wrong:
(3) It is true that ICC depends on between-target variance. But the argument works in the paper's favour. A light-skewed target pool has less between-face variance, which pushes ICC down for the same absolute error. Reaching a similar ICC (0.875–0.91) therefore implies equal or smaller absolute error, not hidden inconsistency. The light-end perceptual point cuts the same way. I recomputed CIEDE2000 between adjacent MST orbs: 1.9, 5.6, 4.0, 7.7 at the light end against 18.8, 14.0, 10.9, 11.8 mid-scale. Harder distinctions would lower agreement, yet the ICC stayed high.
(5) The number of annotations is stated. The §6 opening covers both datasets and says each task was replicated 5 times per region, giving 25 per image. The issue's own 25 × 86,809 calculation depends on that sentence. Only skip rates, and per-image versus per-face for images with several faces, are missing.
(6) The paper never mentions a face detector. It says only that images "contained at least one face", which could equally mean Open Images' human-drawn face boxes. Saying the pool was "preselected by an unnamed face detector" is an inference, not a reported fact.
(1, example) The "under-exposed faces read as darker" shared bias is speculative. MST-E's controlled lighting comparison gives the same median distance to the oracle, 0.78, for well-lit and poorly lit images. That partly addresses lighting-driven bias, though only in controlled conditions.
The df ≈ 4 / "5 regional ICC pairs" reading is a guess.

Why minor, not major:
- The headline contributions are reliability, the MST-E regional differences, MST-E oracle agreement and the MST-E release. None of them depend on the Open Images analysis.
- What the Open Images analysis can support it does support, even setting the badly reported tests aside: ICC is high across markets, and regional differences replicate.
- The carried-over recommendations are mostly reliability-based. The 10-rater Spearman-Brown advice and the geographic-diversity advice are exactly what ICC and between-region evidence address.
- The overreach is confined to hedged Discussion and Limitations wording ("likely", "we believe", "suggesting ... possible"). It is fixed by rewording to reliability, naming the test, defining V, giving CIs and an effect size, and describing the face sampling frame.
That is a reporting and wording problem worth fixing, not one that materially weakens a core claim.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §6 p.8: "the intraclass correlation from the Open Images dataset has no significant differences than crowdsource annotators intraclass correlation in the MST-E dataset ( χ2 = 0.26, p = 0.99 > 0.05)". §6 p.8: "significant differences between annotation distributions between regions (V 2 = 0.0766,p < 0.05)". §6 p.8: "recommendations based on annotator behaviors observed in our controlled studies likely translate to real-world scenarios". §6 p.8: "We randomly selected a subset of 41,471 images that contained at least one face." §6 p.7: "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image." §6 p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images." §7 p.9: "find that they perform similarly on the in-the-wild subset of Open Images to the MST-E dataset". §7 p.10: "with the additional analysis of the Open Images dataset, we believe our results will translate to other domains." §4: "Typically, the only available indicator of annotation quality is a measure of inter-rater reliability." Fig. 6 caption: "The Open Images dataset has a strong skew towards lighter skin tones." §2: "variable performance of upstream components across skin tone groups can lead to missing annotations".
verdicts.corrections:
- (5) is wrong on the count. The paper does state the number of annotations: the §6 opening covers both MST-E and Open Images and says 25 annotations per image (5 per region). Only Open Images skip rates, and per-image versus per-face counts for multi-face images, are missing. The issue's own 25 × 86,809 figure relies on that sentence.
- (6) The paper does not say a face detector was used. It says only that images "contained at least one face", which could mean Open Images' human-annotated face boxes. The valid point is that the sampling frame, box source and size thresholds are unreported.
- (3) The target-variance and light-end perceptual arguments push ICC down, not up. A similar ICC on a light-skewed, perceptually compressed pool implies equal or better absolute consistency, so these points do not undermine the reliability claim. Recomputed adjacent-orb CIEDE2000: light end 1.9 / 5.6 / 4.0 / 7.7; mid-scale 18.8 / 14.0 / 10.9 / 11.8. The darkest pair is also about 5.0, which the issue leaves out.
- (2) "df ≈ 4, about 5 regional ICC pairs" is a guess. df = 4 is consistent with p = 0.99 (survival function 0.992), but the test is unknown.
- (1) The under-exposure shared-bias example is speculative. MST-E shows the same 0.78 median distance to the oracle in well-lit and poorly lit conditions.
- The recommendations that carry over (number of raters via Spearman-Brown, geographic diversity) rest on reliability and between-region differences. The Open Images analysis does address those, so "only reliability was tested" undermines the validity-flavoured generalisation sentences, not the recommendations as a whole.
- Severity should be minor, not major. The overclaims are hedged Discussion and Limitations wording, and core contributions (a), (c) and (e) rest on MST-E.
- Arithmetic checks out: χ² survival function at 0.26 for df 1–5 is 0.610, 0.878, 0.967, 0.992, 0.998. Implied χ² is about 51k (V = 0.0766) or about 665k (V = 0.277) at N ≈ 2.17M with df* = 4.

issues.title: The diversity and same-region recommendations do not follow from the analyses and pull against each other; the oracle-distance metric cannot discriminate diverse from single-region pools
issues.claim: Every single region already has an average median distance below 1, so the chosen metric cannot separate diverse pools from single-region ones. No pooled-vs-single-region comparison at equal k is reported. Geographic diversity is therefore shown to be neither necessary nor beneficial for oracle alignment. 'At least five regions' simply equals the number of regions sampled; the number of regions was never varied. 'Use annotators from the same region' as the data has no supporting analysis, because subject or image regions are not known or matched. It also conflicts with the 'diversify' advice and with the oracle-alignment rationale: if region shapes perception, local annotators would by design pull labels away from the US-based 'intended' annotations. The paper never says whether the target is the creator's intended categories or region-specific perception, and never reports which regions sit closer to or further from the oracle, or in which direction. The Spearman-Brown basis for the replication counts is treated in C09.
issues.paper_evidence: §6 p.8: “we find the average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition.” §7 p.9: “This suggests that a geographically diverse annotator pool provides annotations that are in line with the intended use of the MST scale”. Suggestions p.10: “have at least two annotators in at least five different geographical regions (10 ratings per image), particularly for challenging images.”; “If you know the geographical region of your data or deployment scenario, it may be wise to use annotators from the same region.” App. A.2 p.17: “designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas”.
issues.external_evidence: None beyond the paper's own statement that every region falls below 1. design:M5's Spearman-Brown computations are reported under C09.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (c), second sentence (a diverse pool matches the intended MST). Contribution (d)'s actionable suggestions on diverse vs co-located pools. The Abstract's 'use a diverse set of annotators'.
issues.severity_disagreement: None; both sources banded it major.
issues.suggested_fix: Using the released ratings, for budgets k = 1..25, compare oracle MAE, within-1 rate and reliability for (a) k raters from one region and (b) k raters spread across 2–5 regions, with CIs. Report per-region signed bias against the oracle. Either drop the causal 'diversity → alignment' wording or support it with that comparison. Drop the same-region advice or test it on data whose subject region is known. State the target explicitly and make the recommendations consistent with it, e.g. diversity for a scale-intended consensus and locality for a deployment-specific perception target.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the main text, the appendices (A.2, C data card, E, F, K, L) and the limitations. The central point holds. §6 states that the average median distance to oracle is below 1 "for every region and image condition". §7 then attributes oracle alignment to geographic diversity ("This suggests that a geographically diverse annotator pool provides annotations..."), and Contribution (c) repeats this. The paper's own numbers therefore show that single-region pools also meet the paper's 1-point criterion. The paper reports no pooled-versus-single-region comparison at equal k, no per-region within-1 percentages (94.7% is given for the global pool only), and no per-region distance values in the text. The Spearman-Brown analysis uses k = total replications across all regions. Its "one rater per region" and "at least five different geographical regions" advice simply mirrors the design (5 regions × 5 raters), and the number of regions was never varied. Nothing in Appendix L, the limitations, or the data card addresses this. Appendix L's "Analytic Clarifications" only redefines average median distance and the 1-point threshold.

The tension the issue identifies is also real. The diversity advice rests on matching Dr. Monk's intent; Monk is at Harvard, and per A.2 the scale was "designed... across the Americas". The same-region advice, by contrast, aims at "relevant data" for a local deployment. The paper never reconciles which target it means: §5 says the goal is "skin tone annotation in images that aligns with social perception".

Several parts of the issue are overstated, so I partially uphold rather than fully uphold:
(1) The metric can discriminate in principle. Continuous average median distances or within-1 percentages could differ between pooled and single-region pools. The problem is that the paper reports only a binary "<1 for every region" statement and runs no comparison, not that the metric itself cannot separate them.
(2) "Shown to be neither necessary nor beneficial" goes too far. Under the paper's threshold, the data show diversity is not necessary. They do not show it brings no benefit; they simply do not test for one.
(3) The issue omits the paper's explicit hedge on the same-region advice ("it may be wise", "We hypothesize... although more careful study of this is needed"). The paper concedes the advice is an untested hypothesis, which weakens the "no supporting analysis" criticism, although the conflict is still left unresolved.
(4) "Never reports which regions sit closer or further" is too strong. Figure 8's caption covers comparisons across "different annotator pools", which may include per-region confusion matrices (the figures are unavailable). For the experts, per-region distances (India 0.78, US 0.84) and a direction (India lighter, US darker for S14) are reported.
(5) The diversity recommendation does have a separate, plausible rationale in the MANOVA finding of regional variation. The Suggestions bullet ("Diversity of annotators is important... cultural differences across geographic regions influenced skin tone annotations") and the abstract's "Given this" both point to variation, not to oracle alignment. It is not wholly a non sequitur, but no analysis tests it.

Severity is major rather than critical. Contribution (c)'s literal statement remains true, since the pooled median does align. What is unsupported is the implied claim that diversity is what produces the alignment, together with the specific "at least five regions" prescription. This materially weakens the paper's headline practitioner advice, but the core reliability and regional-variation findings are untouched.

Data check: the released metadata contains only image details and the oracle MST, with no per-region crowd annotations. Per-region distances therefore cannot be recomputed from it.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§6 p.8: "we find the average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition" (verbatim; next sentence: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images", with no per-region values).
§6 p.8: "Using the global pool, the consensus annotation agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%)" (global pool only).
§6 p.8: "one rater per region likely suffices (5 total annotators). For more challenging images, two annotators per region is beneficial."
§7 p.9: "This suggests that a geographically diverse annotator pool provides annotations that are in line with the intended use of the MST scale" (verbatim).
Suggestions p.10: "have at least two annotators in at least five different geographical regions (10 ratings per image), particularly for challenging images." (verbatim)
Suggestions p.10: "If you know the geographical region of your data or deployment scenario, it may be wise to use annotators from the same region." (verbatim; continues "We hypothesize that co-located annotators may have a better cultural context... although more careful study of this is needed.")
§8(c): "when collecting annotations from a diverse geographical pool, annotators are able to provide annotations that match the original intention behind the MST scale."
App A.2 p.17: "designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas" (verbatim).
§5: "0.78 in India and 0.84 in the United States" (expert per-region distances).
App F / Fig 8 caption: "median value selected by crowdsource annotators across subsets of images and different annotator pools".
App L "Analytic Clarifications": "more clearly define 'average median distance' and describe the '1-point discrepancy' threshold" (does not address the diverse-vs-single comparison).
verdicts.corrections:
(1) "The chosen metric cannot separate diverse pools from single-region ones" is overstated. Average median distance and within-1 percentage are continuous and could separate them. The paper only reports the binary "<1 for every region" statement and runs no pooled-versus-single comparison; the failure lies in what is reported, not in the metric.
(2) "Geographic diversity is therefore shown to be neither necessary nor beneficial" should read "not shown to be necessary (under the 1-point criterion) or beneficial". The data do not demonstrate an absence of benefit.
(3) The issue omits the paper's explicit hedge on the same-region advice ("We hypothesize... although more careful study of this is needed"). The authors themselves present it as an untested hypothesis.
(4) "Never reports which regions sit closer to or further from the oracle, or in which direction" is too strong. Figure 8 (unavailable) reportedly shows confusion matrices for "different annotator pools", and for the expert study per-region distances (India 0.78, US 0.84) and the direction of difference (India lighter, US darker for S14) are reported. It holds for the crowdsourced text only.
(5) The abstract's diversity advice is grounded textually in the regional-variation finding ("Given this"), not in oracle alignment. That rationale is plausible but untested, not absent.
(6) "US-based 'intended' annotations" is an inference from Monk's Harvard affiliation and A.2's Americas framing. The paper never states it as such.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the issue holds, and it rests on the paper's own text. §6 says the average median distance to the oracle is "less than 1 for every region and image condition". So any single 5-rater regional pool already meets the criterion the paper uses to call annotations "in line with intended use". That means the §7 inference and Contribution (c) ("However, when collecting annotations from a diverse geographical pool... match the original intention") do not separate diversity from simply having annotators. The global-pool figures are confounded with pool size: 18/19 = 94.7% within 1 point and 0.78 distance come from a median over k=25, while each region's median is over k=5. No per-region values and no pooled-versus-single-region comparison at equal k are reported. The Abstract's "Given this, we advise practitioners to use a diverse set of annotators" is therefore a normative step that the analyses do not test.

The other points also hold. "At least five regions" is just the number of regions sampled; region count was never varied. The Spearman-Brown projection runs over total k and treats raters as interchangeable, so it cannot justify any split across regions (the details are C09). The same-region advice has no supporting analysis because subject and image provenance is never stated or matched. The paper never says whether its target is Dr. Monk's intended categories or local social perception (§5 says "social perception"), and the oracle-alignment rationale sits uneasily with region-specific annotation. A competent methods reviewer would ask for per-region distances and signed bias, plus an equal-k comparison between mixed-region and within-region subsamples. That analysis is cheap, and the authors' data could support it. The released metadata I checked (mst-e_image_details.csv) holds only the oracle MST per image, with no per-region crowd labels, so I could not compute these numbers myself.

Why this is only partly upheld and sits at the low end of major:
(1) The paper hedges the same-region bullet ("may be wise", "We hypothesize... although more careful study of this is needed"). It is also a conditional ("if you know the region"), so it creates tension with the diversity advice rather than a contradiction.
(2) The metric is continuous, so it could separate pools. What fails is the paper's thresholded reporting (<1) and its missing per-region values.
(3) "Shown to be neither necessary nor beneficial" goes too far. The data show diversity is not needed to clear the <1 bar, but whether it helps was never tested, not shown to be absent. There is a reasonable bias-cancellation argument (in the spirit of the diversity prediction theorem) that the paper could have tested.
(4) The expert study does report which region sat closer to the oracle (India 0.78 and 88.9% vs US 0.84 and 83.4%). Fig 4 with App E also gives direction for S14 (oracle MST6; India MST3–5, lighter). Taken at face value, the US experts were not closer to the oracle (n=5 per region), which weakens the claim that local annotators would "by design" drift away from it. Every crowd region also stays within 1 point.
(5) Fig 8's caption mentions "different annotator pools", so per-pool confusion matrices against the oracle may exist in the missing figures.

The release (MST-E) and the reliability and lighting claims (a, b, e) are unaffected. The flaw materially weakens Contribution (c)'s second sentence, part of (d), and the Abstract's main recommendation to practitioners. I rate it major on that basis, though it is fixable and borderline.

§6 p.8: "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image" (p.7).

verdicts.corrections:
1) "The oracle-distance metric cannot discriminate" overstates it. Average median distance is continuous and could separate pools. The flaw is that the paper reports only the <1 threshold per region, gives no per-region values, and compares the k=25 global pool with k=5 regional pools.
2) "Geographic diversity is therefore shown to be neither necessary nor beneficial" should read "not shown to be necessary or beneficial". The data show it is not needed to meet the <1 criterion; any benefit (for example, regional biases cancelling out) was untested, not disproven.
3) "Never reports which regions sit closer to or further from the oracle, or in which direction" holds only for the crowdsourced main text. The expert study reports per-region distance (India 0.78, closer, vs US 0.84). Fig 4 with App E shows direction for S14, where Indian experts rated lighter than the oracle (MST6). The paper never says the oracle is US-based; it only says the MST was designed for the Americas. Its own data bound any pull: every region is within 1 point, and US experts were not closer to the oracle than Indian experts.
6) None of this affects the value of the MST-E release or the reliability and lighting-invariance claims.

issues.title: The Spearman-Brown replication advice assumes exchangeable raters, which the regional finding contradicts, sets no reliability target, and projects the reliability of a mean while the consensus is a median
issues.claim: Spearman-Brown projects the reliability of the mean of k parallel, exchangeable raters. Here k is the 'total number of replications over all regions', while the paper argues that regions differ systematically, so raters are not exchangeable. Regional effects that interact with MST level or lighting do not average out, and the formula cannot yield a per-region allocation. The projection is for a mean, but every consensus in the paper is a median. Reliability is also not accuracy: Spearman-Brown says nothing about how stable the k-rater median category is, whether it hits the oracle, or how it depends on the regional mix. No target reliability is stated. With the reported single-rater ICCs (≥ 0.82), Spearman-Brown already gives ≥ 0.93 at k=3 (the status quo the paper argues against), ≥ 0.958 at k=5 and ≥ 0.979 at k=10, above every conventional benchmark. So 'one rater per region suffices', 'two per region is beneficial' and '10 ratings per image' do not follow without an unstated criterion. The input ICC (per-region or global pool) is unstated. The per-subject 'consensus across multiple images' gains from averaging over images as well as raters, which Spearman-Brown over raters does not model, and it does not carry over to typical fairness datasets with one image per person.
issues.paper_evidence: §6 p.8: “We use the Spearman-Brown prediction formula to determine inter-rater agreement over k replications”; “the total number of replications over all regions (See Figure 5)”; “for datasets containing high quality images or annotations of a single individual based on a consensus across multiple images, one rater per region likely suffices (5 total annotators). For more challenging images, two annotators per region is beneficial.” §7 p.10: “have at least two annotators in at least five different geographical regions (10 ratings per image), particularly for challenging images.” §4 p.5: “we use the median MST annotation from the responses.” No target reliability appears in §6, §7 or the Fig. 5 caption.
issues.external_evidence: Spearman-Brown: single-rater 0.82 gives k=3 0.932, k=5 0.958, k=10 0.979; 0.86 gives k=5 0.968, k=10 0.984; 0.90 gives k=3 0.96, k=5 0.978, k=10 0.99 (stat:M5; the same figures were independently computed in design:M5). Wong & Paritosh [83], whom the paper cites, argue for estimating k-rater reliability empirically by resampling.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (d), especially '10 ratings per image' and 'one rater per region suffices'. The Abstract's 'higher replication count' advice.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source banded major; design:M5, merged in C08, independently flags the same point as major).
issues.suggested_fix: Use the released 25-annotation data directly. For each k and each regional composition (1–2 per region across 5 regions, k from a single region, etc.), resample annotators without replacement and report: (i) agreement of the k-rater median with the full 25-rater median (exact and within 1); (ii) agreement with the oracle; (iii) variance of the median category. Bootstrap CIs over subjects. State a target in advance (e.g. 90% exact agreement with the 25-rater median) and derive k from it. Report leave-one-region-out sensitivity, state which ICC was the Spearman-Brown input, and derive single-image replication guidance from single-image, single-exposure data.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked every quote against the full manuscript, including Appendix C (data card), Appendix K, Appendix L ("Addressing previous reviews") and the Limitations section. The main points of C09 hold, and nothing in the paper addresses them.

What holds:
(1) The paper uses Spearman-Brown with k as "the total number of replications over all regions". It never states a target reliability or decision rule in §6, §7, Limitations, the Fig. 5 caption or any appendix. Statements such as "one rater per region likely suffices", "two annotators per region is beneficial" and "10 ratings per image" therefore lack a stated criterion. Raising k always raises Spearman-Brown reliability, so "beneficial" is vacuous unless a threshold is given. The arithmetic in the issue is correct. With 0.82 for one rater, Spearman-Brown gives 2.46/2.64 = 0.932 at k=3, 4.1/4.28 = 0.958 at k=5 and 8.2/8.38 = 0.979 at k=10. So the reported per-region ICCs already give high projected reliability at the k=3 status quo that the paper argues against.
(2) The paper does not say which single-rater ICC feeds Fig. 5. Section 6 reports per-region one-way ICCs (Per Subject 0.86 to 0.94, Golden 0.9 to 0.96, Challenging 0.82 to 0.95). Fig. 3(b) also mentions a "global pool" ICC, but its values are not in the text.
(3) Every consensus in the paper is a median (§4: "we use the median MST annotation from the responses"; §7 and Fig. 8 refer to the median). Spearman-Brown projects the reliability of a mean. The paper never links k-rater reliability to its own accuracy metrics, the within-1-point percentage and the average median distance, as a function of k. The Limitations text ("future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations") is a general caveat and does not address this.
(4) Appendix L lists prior-review responses on the MST citation, the identity of the expert, the expert sample, analytic clarifications, scope and dataset size. None concerns replications or Spearman-Brown. Limitations admits that 10 annotators is costly ("a very large jump from the status quo of 3") but does not question how the number was derived.

What is overstated:
(a) The exchangeability argument is stated too strongly. If Fig. 5 uses the global-pool one-way ICC, raters are treated as random draws from the pooled population and regional variance sits in the error term. Spearman-Brown is then a defensible rough approximation, and stratifying one rater per region would make it conservative, not optimistic. The real problem is that with a fixed set of five regions, region-by-subject effects become reproducible "signal". That inflates reliability relative to accuracy. Because the input ICC is unstated, the direction of the error cannot be settled from the text.
(b) The per-region allocation, "at least five regions", is motivated mainly by the regional-difference finding and by the observation in §7 that the median across regions sits close to Dr. Monk's annotations. It does not rest on Spearman-Brown alone. Only the step from one to two raters per region depends on Spearman-Brown.
(c) The recommendations are hedged and conditional: "likely suffices", only "for datasets containing high quality images or ... consensus across multiple images", "particularly for challenging images", and "if image quality is unknown" in Limitations. The issue's list of affected claims drops these hedges.

Severity: this is bounded to the quantitative replication-count part of contribution (d) and the Abstract's "higher replication count" advice. Findings (a) to (c) and (e) are unaffected, and the diversity recommendation survives on other evidence. Spearman-Brown is still the only quantitative support for the 10-per-image figure, a recommendation the paper itself calls costly, and that figure is unsupported without a criterion. That materially weakens a headline practitioner recommendation, so I rate it major, at the lower edge.

One note on the manuscript: I found no imperative text addressed to reviewers in the sections I read.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§6 p.8 (l.412-413): "use the Spearman-Brown prediction formula to determine inter-rater agreement over k replications, where k is the total number of replications over all regions (See Figure 5)" — verbatim.
§6 p.8 (l.413-416): "for datasets containing high quality images or annotations of a single individual based on a consensus across multiple images, one rater per region likely suffices (5 total annotators)" — verbatim.
§6 p.8: "For more challenging images, two annotators per region is beneficial." — verbatim.
§6 p.8 (l.418-419): "practitioners can then annotate with 10 annotators on just those low quality images" — verbatim (not cited in the issue).
