verdicts.reasoning:
The data claim is accurate. I re-ran the released CSV: 1,546 rows, of which 893 are well_lit, 635 poorly_lit and 18 video. There are 19 subjects, and none has more than one MST value. So every poorly-lit image does carry its subject's single label, and the oracle is subject-level and lighting-invariant by construction.

The core argument fails, though. It claims the paper is torn between two incompatible constructs and never resolves which one it means. The paper's text does resolve it. Section 5 defines the intended task as photographers "assessing the skin tone in the image while correcting for extraneous image features". The experts were also chosen for experience with "reviewing and editing skin tone in color correction software". Removing illumination effects is exactly what colour correction does. Section 3 and the data card add that the dataset's goal is "consistent skin tone annotation across environment capture conditions". So the construct is the perceived tone of visible skin with lighting discounted, which is ordinary human colour constancy. That target is coherent and well-defined in colour science, and it is compatible with social perception: people do not see someone's skin tone change category when the room light changes.

The issue says this is "close to the dermatological stance" the paper rejected. That runs two different things together. The dermatologists were set aside for guessing at skin that is not in the image (under clothing, or not exposed to sun), which is constitutive pigmentation. Discounting the light on skin that is visible is a different operation. The dilemma "if intrinsic, the case for photographers falls away" therefore does not hold. Colour-correction expertise is the right qualification for a lighting-invariant target.

Penalising poorly-lit deviations as error is internally consistent with the stated goal. Conclusions (b) and (e) are about invariance, and that is what the metric measures. The paper also reports the same average median distance (0.78) for well-lit and poorly-lit images. Within the paper's own framing, that is evidence for invariance, not an artefact of the scoring.

Three points survive, none of them material to the headline claims.
1. "Social perception" is used loosely and never defined against the alternative of the image as rendered.
2. The paper never argues why a person-level, lighting-invariant label is the right one for fairness evaluation. It does recommend MST-E for evaluating models "over varying lighting conditions", where the pixels as rendered matter. Slicing by a person-level attribute is standard practice, so this is a framing gap, not a validity failure.
3. The documentation is ambiguous about who labelled what. Section 3 says images were first annotated by an author and that the golden-image value is the oracle "for the images". The README says Dr. Monk "annotated the images". The data card says "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value" and gives "Number of unique annotations: 19". Read closely, these agree (images were reviewed, and one value was assigned per subject), so this is an ambiguity, not a contradiction.

Severity: minor. For a Datasets & Benchmarks paper, the release is useful whichever construct a user wants, and the main text, data card and released labels make the subject-level labelling clear. A methods reviewer would ask for a sentence justifying invariance as the fairness target, not reject the paper.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §5 p.6: "photographers tended to approach the task as designed, assessing the skin tone in the image while correcting for extraneous image features." §5 p.6: "dermatologists interviewed in the pilot study were more likely to attempt to assess skin tone beneath clothing which was not depicted." §5 p.6: "had previous experience reviewing and editing skin tone in color correction software". §3 p.4: "The goal of this dataset is to enable and test consistent skin tone annotation across environment capture conditions." §3 p.4: "Dr. Monk selected an image for each subject that best represents their skin tone ... and approved the corresponding MST annotation." §3 p.4: "We refer to these annotations as the oracle or intended annotations for the images." App. C p.23: "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value." App. C p.23: "Number of unique annotations: 19". §6 p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images." §7 p.9: "evaluate performance of models over varying lighting conditions and poses." App. L p.29: "some dermatologists tended to devise the skin tone under clothing which was not depicted in the image (or skin untouched by sun)." Abstract: "Perceived skin tone is affected by technical factors, like lighting conditions".
verdicts.corrections:
1. "The paper never resolves which it is" is wrong. Section 5 defines the task as assessing tone "in the image while correcting for extraneous image features". Section 3 and the data card state that consistency across capture conditions is the dataset's goal. Together these make the target perceived tone of visible skin with lighting discounted.

2. "Close to the dermatological stance" conflates two things. The dermatologists were set aside for inferring skin that is not depicted (constitutive pigmentation). Discounting illumination on visible skin is colour constancy, which is part of everyday social perception.

3. "The case for photographers falls away" does not follow. The photographers were chosen for colour-correction expertise, which matches a lighting-invariant target.

4. The claim that the main text and data card disagree on whether images or subjects were annotated is overstated. Both describe images being reviewed and a single per-subject value being assigned, and the released CSV confirms one value per subject. At most this is ambiguous wording, for example "oracle ... for the images" in §3 and "Dr. Monk then annotated the images" in the README.

5. The residual valid point is narrower than the issue states. The paper does not explain why a person-level, lighting-invariant label suits fairness evaluation of models judged on rendered pixels, and "social perception" is left undefined. Severity should be minor, not major.

6. The external evidence is accurate: 893 + 635 + 18 = 1,546 rows, and every subject has a single MST value.

issues.title: Crowd training is undescribed while MST-E is advertised as the training instrument: possible train/test contamination, and no untrained baseline for the 'with training' claims
issues.claim: The crowd is described as trained in MST annotation, and MST-E is presented as the training dataset. Yet the paper never describes the training: materials, duration, feedback, qualification threshold, language, or whether it differed by region. It also never says whether MST-E subjects, Golden images or oracle labels were used. If they were, the oracle-agreement results on MST-E (Golden, Challenging and per-subject) are contaminated by subject-to-label learning. The face-recall precautions show the authors saw recall as a risk, but train/test separation is not addressed. With no untrained or pre-training comparison, the claims that training produces invariance and that MST-E trains it are untested. Training differences between regions would also feed the region confound (C01).
issues.paper_evidence: Abstract p.1: “MST-E is designed to help train human annotators to annotate MST effectively.” §7 p.9: “crowdsourced annotators who were provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task”. Conclusion p.10: “with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions.” Suggestions p.10: “The MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training.” Absent: §§4 and 6 and Apps C, D and K give no training protocol or materials.
issues.external_evidence: None.
issues.affected_claims: Conclusions (b) and (e). Crowd-side (a), since oracle agreement may reflect memorised labels. The dataset's stated value as a training tool. Impact on (a)–(c) is conditional on overlap.
issues.severity_disagreement: design:M6 banded it major; meas:MV10 banded it minor (impact conditional on overlap). Major is chosen because the paper itself positions MST-E as the training material, which makes overlap a live possibility, and no disclosure at all is given for a design element every crowd accuracy result depends on.
issues.suggested_fix: Describe the training protocol and materials fully, including per-region differences, and state whether any MST-E subject, image or oracle label appeared in training. If any did, re-evaluate on held-out subjects only. To support the training claims, run a small randomised comparison (no training vs generic MST training vs MST-E training) on held-out subjects and on Open Images faces with a reference standard, or remove the training-causal wording.

verdicts.reasoning:
I searched the full text for train, qualif, instruct, guideline, familiar, onboard, recall, memor, calibrat, pilot, practice, exemplar and teach. That covered the main text, Limitations, Suggestions, Conclusion and Appendices C, D, I, K and L. No passage describes the crowd training: no materials, duration, feedback, qualification threshold, language or regional differences. The paper also never says whether MST-E images, Golden or Challenging images, or Dr. Monk's oracle labels were used in that training.

The only mentions are labels. §4 calls the crowd a "larger pool of trained crowdsourced annotators". Fig. 4's caption mentions "trained annotators". §6 says annotators had no domain expertise "outside of the instructions they received for this task". §7 says they were "provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task". Appendix D's caption says "trained crowdsourced annotators". Appendix L, which answers the earlier FAccT reviews, does not raise training at all. Appendix K covers pay only. The released metadata (README and CSVs) has no training information either. The image filenames are dated 2022-09-22, so MST-E existed before the crowd annotation and could have been used in training.

The paper makes training-causal claims with no test behind them. §7 says "annotators are able to learn to be invariant to environmental factors". Conclusion (b) says "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions". Conclusion (e) says MST-E helps "train annotators to be invariant". No condition is untrained or pre-training, and no experiment trains with MST-E and measures the effect. The invariance result can stand (median distance 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly-lit images), but crediting it to training, or to MST-E, is untested.

§7 also uses the "trained annotators" to argue that "subject matter experts are not necessarily needed". That practical recommendation cannot be acted on or replicated if the training is unknown. It also matters for reading the results if the training used MST-E oracle labels.

The face-recall precaution in §6 only covers recall within the annotation task: "mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall". It says nothing about exposure during training, so the train/test question is still open. The contamination prong is speculative, and the issue rightly flags it as conditional. But the paper invites the question by presenting MST-E as an annotator-training tool. The oracle labels are per subject, so any exposure would leak labels to every image of that subject.

Overall: a material reporting gap that weakens contributions (b) and (e) and the scalability recommendation, and leaves the crowd–oracle agreement open to a contamination question. I rate it major, not critical, because the reliability and regional-difference findings do not depend on how the crowd was trained.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
All four of the issue's quotes are verbatim and fairly represent their context.
- Abstract (line 45): "MST-E is designed to help train human annotators to annotate MST effectively."
- §7 (lines 462–463): "crowdsourced annotators who were provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task"
- Conclusion (b) (lines 539–540): "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions."
- Suggestions (line 531): "The MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training."

Additional passages checked:
- §6: "professional data annotators without specific domain expertise outside of the instructions they received for this task"
- §6: "the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators"
- §7: "We find that annotators are able to learn to be invariant to environmental factors such as lighting quality"
- §4: "extending to a larger pool of trained crowdsourced annotators located in five different geographical regions"
- Limitations: "it does not consider ... other factors such as the language used in the task, different UI improvements"
- Data card (App. C): "Trains annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions."
- §5: "with the time delay reducing the likelihood that participants would annotate the Challenging set based on their memory" (this precaution applies to the photographers, not the crowd)
verdicts.corrections:
1. Training is not completely unmentioned. §6 refers to "the instructions they received for this task", and §4, the Fig. 4 caption and Appendix D call the crowd "trained". The gap is the missing protocol and content, not the absence of any mention.

2. The paper never says the study crowd was trained on MST-E. Calling MST-E the training instrument describes its intended use by practitioners, not a disclosed fact about this study. Contamination is therefore an undisclosed possibility, not something the text implies. Its effect on crowd agreement with the oracle (Golden, Challenging and per-subject) stays conditional on overlap, as the issue says.

3. The Limitations section does admit that "the language used in the task" was not considered. That partly overlaps with the point that task presentation, and possibly training, may have differed by region (C01). It does not address training content.

4. The 5-photographer panels in India and the US are a partial non-crowd comparison: they got no stated MST training and still landed within 1 point of the oracle. They are not an untrained-crowd baseline, though. They are a different population and annotated only the Golden and Challenging sets, so the "no untrained baseline" criticism stands.

5. The figures are missing, so I cannot rule out that the Appendix D task screenshot shows on-screen instructions. Its caption and text describe only the annotation interface, not a training procedure.

verdicts.reasoning:
The text supports the factual core of the issue. Training is mentioned twice and never described: §7 says annotators "were provided training", and §6 says they had no expertise "outside of the instructions they received for this task". §§4 and 6 and Appendices C, D and K give no materials, duration, feedback, qualification threshold, language, or regional consistency. They also do not say whether MST-E images or Dr. Monk's labels were used. The data card lists annotator training as a "Motivating factor" for MST-E, so overlap is a fair question. Reporting the annotator training protocol is a standard expectation in crowdsourcing and annotation reporting (e.g., Geiger et al. 2020, data statements). Without it, a practitioner cannot reproduce the crowd results, and the paper explicitly recommends that practitioners copy its setup. The "untrained baseline" point is also correct as far as it goes. Every crowd annotator was trained, so the design has no contrast that could show training causes invariance. §7's wording ("annotators are able to learn to be invariant") is causal language with no learning measurement behind it. MST-E's value as a training tool (abstract, conclusion (e), suggestions) is stated as intent and never tested.

Three things argue against "major".
(1) The contamination charge depends on a fact that cannot be confirmed. The paper never says MST-E was used for training. Every released image has a capture date of 2022-09-22 in its filename (1542 of 1542 in mst-e_image_details.csv). So contamination is possible only if crowd training happened after that date, and the timing is undisclosed either way. The released crowd annotations are not in the local data, so I could not check whether Golden images show inflated oracle agreement compared with other well-lit images.
(2) The oracle-agreement metric is lenient: the median of 25 ratings within ±1 on a 10-point scale, against 19 subject-level labels. The photographers, for whom no training is reported, reached similar levels (88.9% and 83.4% within 1 point; mean median distances of 0.78 and 0.84). The crowd reached 94.7% (18 of 19 subjects) and 0.78. Crowd agreement is therefore not anomalously high, which argues against a large memorisation effect. This is not a clean untrained control, because the photographers are experts and saw a different image set. Still, it weakens the claim that crowd conclusion (a) is undermined.
(3) The headline findings do not depend on whether training worked: high ICC, regional differences, and median-of-pool closeness to the oracle. The "with training" qualifier in conclusion (b) can be read as describing the sample ("trained annotators were approximately invariant") rather than as a causal claim. Conclusion (e) is a statement of release intent, which is normal for a Datasets & Benchmarks release whose value as a controlled, oracle-labelled evaluation set stands without the training claim.

Net: a valid reporting omission plus overreaching causal wording. Fixing it needs disclosure (the protocol, and whether MST-E or oracle labels were used) and softer language ("learn to", "with training"). It does not invalidate or materially weaken a core empirical claim unless overlap is shown, so I rate it minor. If the authors confirm that MST-E Golden images with oracle labels were used in training, the oracle-agreement results for the Golden set and per subject would become major.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
Abstract p.1: "MST-E is designed to help train human annotators to annotate MST effectively." (confirmed)
§6 p.7: "professional data annotators without speciﬁc domain expertise outside of the instructions they received for this task" (the only other description of training)
§6 p.7: "the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators" (confirmed)
§7 p.9: "crowdsourced annotators who were provided training in MST skin tone annotations prior to the annotation task" (confirmed)
§7 p.9: "We ﬁnd that annotators are able to learn to be invariant to environmental factors such as lighting quality" (causal wording, no learning measured)
§7 Suggestions p.10: "The MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training." (confirmed)
Conclusion (b) p.10: "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions." (confirmed)
App C data card: "Trains annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions." (listed as a motivating factor)
§5 p.7: "88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States... 0.78 in India and 0.84" (photographers, no training reported)
§6 p.8: "agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%)" (18/19 = 94.7%, arithmetic checked)
verdicts.corrections:
1. The contamination is conjecture and the issue should label it that way. The paper says nothing either way, and every released MST-E image is dated 2022-09-22 by filename, so overlap would require crowd training after that date. That timing is undisclosed.
2. The issue says there is no comparison of any kind. In fact the photographers, for whom no training is reported, give an informal non-crowd comparison. Their oracle agreement (83–89% within 1 point; 0.78–0.84 distance) is close to the crowd's (94.7%; 0.78). This argues against large memorisation effects, although the two groups differ in expertise and image set.
3. "MST-E trains it" and conclusion (e) are statements of intent for the release, not empirical results. The "untested" criticism applies fully only to §7's "able to learn to be invariant" and, read causally, to conclusion (b).
4. The issue omits that §6 itself describes the crowd's preparation as "instructions they received for this task". This suggests the "training" may have been only task instructions, which makes the "with training" claims weaker and contamination less likely.
5. The link to the region confound (C01) is speculative. Nothing in the paper shows that training differed by region.
6. Severity should be minor (a required disclosure plus softer wording), not major. It would become major only if the authors confirm that MST-E or oracle labels were used in training.

issues.title: 'Experts are not necessary' rests on comparing non-identical expert and crowd designs, with no head-to-head or non-inferiority test
issues.claim: The expert and crowd arms differ in stimuli (18 Golden + 18 Challenging images vs 1,515 images), replication (5 per country vs 25 per image), ICC model (two-way vs one-way), training (crowd trained; expert training not described), task UI and context (survey vs thumbnail-plus-box tool), language (English stated only for experts), session structure and incentives. The 'experts' are photographers, not MST experts. No statistical comparison on a common footing is reported, so 'not necessarily needed' is a non-inferiority claim made without a non-inferiority analysis. A matched comparison was feasible: crowd ratings exist for the same Golden and Challenging images, including from India.
issues.paper_evidence: §7 p.9: “suggesting that subject matter experts are not necessarily needed for MST skin tone annotation tasks.” §5 p.6: “we use a two-way random, single score ICC”. §6 p.7: “we use a one-way random, single score ICC”; “Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image.” App. D p.24: “The task was presented in English and all photographers were fluent English speakers.”
issues.external_evidence: None.
issues.affected_claims: Conclusion (a) as a comparative claim. The Discussion's scalability argument that trained crowds can replace experts.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, major).
issues.suggested_fix: On the identical 18 Golden and 18 Challenging images, compare the 5 Indian experts with repeated random draws of 5 Indian crowd raters (and of other regions) on within-1 rate, MAE to the oracle and ICC computed with the same model. Report bootstrap CIs and a non-inferiority margin fixed in advance. Describe any expert training or briefing and the expert task UI.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked every quote the issue cites against the manuscript. All are verbatim and accurately described. The design differences the issue lists also hold up:
- **Stimuli:** experts saw 19 images per session, with one subject dropped (fn. 4), so 18 Golden and 18 Challenging images. Crowds annotated "the entire MST-E dataset".
- **Replication:** 5 experts per country, against 5 raters per region × 5 regions (25 per image).
- **ICC model:** two-way for experts, one-way for crowds.
- **Training:** stated for crowds (§7, abstract), not described for experts.
- **Task format:** experts took "two 30 minute surveys" for a GLG honorarium (App. K). Crowds used a thumbnail-plus-box tool and were contracted monthly.
- **Language:** English is stated only for the photographers (App. D).
- **Comparison:** no expert-vs-crowd statistical test is reported anywhere.

Those facts are accurate. The issue's framing goes too far, for four reasons.

1. **The claim is not a non-inferiority claim against photographers.** The reference standard is Dr. Monk's oracle, not the photographers. The §7 argument checks each group separately against fixed benchmarks: significant ICC, at least 1-point agreement, and average median distance below 1. Crowds meet those benchmarks on their own: 94.7% within 1 point; average median distance 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly lit images; and "less than 1 for every region and image condition." That evidence alone supports "trained crowds are adequate, so experts are not needed." The expert arm is not the comparator the claim depends on, so a missing non-inferiority test against photographers does not undermine the claim much.

2. **The wording is hedged.** The text says "suggesting" and "not necessarily needed", not "crowds are equivalent to experts."

3. **The issue misreads Conclusion (a).** It says skin tone can be annotated reliably "by both" groups. That is a statement about each group, not a comparison between them.

4. **The paper already covers parts of the issue:**
   - It calls the expert study a "qualitative survey" (§4).
   - It names the expert analyses as "more limited" (Limitations, p.10) and as "exploratory" hypothesis-generation (App. L).
   - It puts "experts" in scare quotes, says they are photographers, and explains why it chose them (§5, App. L).
   - It names "language used in the task" and "different UI improvements" as factors it did not consider (Limitations).
   - It reports crowd results on the same Golden and Challenging subsets: ICC 0.9–0.96 and 0.82–0.95, and Figure 8, which is described as covering "different annotator pools". So the stimulus mismatch is partly addressed descriptively.

**What remains valid:**
- The text makes informal comparative statements without a common-footing analysis: "Consistent with our results from professional photographers" (§6) and "similar to the expert photographers" (§6).
- It sets numbers side by side that are not comparable. For example, the crowd's 94.7% is per subject from a 25-rater global pool, while the experts' 88.9% and 83.4% are per image from 5 raters.
- The asymmetries (training, replication, UI, incentives) are never acknowledged as confounds for any expert-versus-crowd reading.
- A matched comparison, such as India crowd against India photographers on the same 36 images, appears feasible from the paper's own description. I could not check this against the released local metadata, which contains no crowd annotations.

**Severity: minor.** These are presentation and inference-hygiene problems. The core "experts not necessary" conclusion rests mainly on the crowd-vs-oracle results, which are directly reported, so it is weakened only modestly.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§7 p.9: "suggesting that subject matter experts are not necessarily needed for MST skin tone annotation tasks." Verbatim.
§5 p.6: "so we use a two-way random, single score ICC where the subject and annotator are viewed as random effect". Verbatim.
§6 p.7: "we use a one-way random, single score ICC to measure inter-rater reliability". Verbatim.
§6 p.7: "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image." Verbatim.
App. D p.24: "The task was presented in English and all photographers were fluent English speakers." Verbatim.
§5 fn.4: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error."
§4 p.5: "The first is a qualitative survey with a group of skin tone 'experts', photographers".
§8 (a): "skin tone can be annotated reliably on the MST scale by both trained crowdsourced annotators and subject-matter experts".
§6 p.8: "crowdsource annotators, similar to the expert photographers, arrive at consensus MST annotations".
§6 p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
Limitations p.10: "the exploratory analyses of annotations from photography experts is more limited than the scale achieved with crowdsourced annotators".
Limitations p.9: "other factors such as the language used in the task, different UI improvements".
App. L p.29–30: "more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory and use the results from this work to establish hypotheses".
App. K: "participation in two 30 minute surveys".
verdicts.corrections:
1. Conclusion (a) is not a comparative claim. It says annotation is reliable "by both" groups, so listing it as an affected comparative claim misreads it.
2. The paper does not need a non-inferiority test against photographers to say experts are "not necessarily needed". Its reference is Dr. Monk's oracle, judged with fixed thresholds (ICC significance, 1-point discrepancy, average median distance below 1), and crowds meet those thresholds directly. The claim is also hedged ("suggesting", "not necessarily").
3. "Stimuli differ (36 vs 1,515)" overstates the mismatch. The paper reports crowd ICC and distance results separately for the same Golden and Challenging subsets (Fig. 3b, Fig. 8, §6), so a descriptive like-for-like view exists. What is missing is a formal test.
4. The paper is open that the "experts" are photographers, not MST experts. It puts the word in scare quotes in §4, explains the choice in §5 and App. L, and treats Dr. Monk as the MST expert. It also calls the expert arm exploratory and limited (§4, Limitations, App. L) and names task language and UI as factors it did not study.
5. That a matched comparison was feasible follows from the paper's own description of the crowd data. It cannot be checked against the released local metadata, which has no crowd annotations.
6. Proposed severity "major" is too high. This is a minor inference and presentation problem: informal "similar to" comparisons and side-by-side numbers that are not comparable, with no confound acknowledgment.

verdicts.reasoning:
The factual inventory of design differences checks out against the text. Experts rated 18 Golden plus 18 Challenging images (19 subjects, one excluded per footnote 4) in two 30-minute English surveys, with 5 raters per country, scored with a two-way ICC. Crowd annotators rated all 1,515 images in a thumbnail-plus-box tool, 5 per region and 25 per image, scored with a one-way ICC, and were described as trained. They were paid monthly, while the experts received an honorarium. No formal statistical test compares the two arms. A matched comparison was feasible from the paper's own design: the crowd annotated the full MST-E set in India, and Figure 3(b) reports crowd Golden and Challenging ICCs per region. The released metadata folder holds no crowd annotations, so I could not run that comparison.

The methodological framing of the issue is still mostly wrong, which keeps the severity low.

(1) The section 7 inference does not logically need a non-inferiority test against photographers. The photographers are not the reference standard; Dr. Monk's oracle labels are. The argument holds or fails on whether the trained crowd meets an absolute adequacy criterion against that oracle, and the paper reports this on the same Golden and Challenging images: 94.7% of subjects within 1 point, and an average median distance of 0.78 for both lighting conditions, below 1 for every region. Testing the crowd for non-inferiority to a 5-person photographer panel would be a weaker and less relevant design, and with n=18 images it would be badly underpowered. The proper critique is that the adequacy criteria are weak (ICC significance tested against zero, a 1-point margin, no confidence intervals). Those are separate issues.

(2) Conclusion (a) is not comparative as written. It says both groups can annotate reliably, which is a conjunction of two absolute claims. The issue misreads it.

(3) The claim is hedged ('not necessarily needed'). The paper also flags the photographer arm as exploratory and underpowered (section 4: 'small scale study'; section 7 Limitations; Appendix L).

(4) The ICC model difference follows from the designs and is correctly chosen for each. ICC(1,1) and ICC(2,1) both estimate absolute agreement and differ little in practice, so this is not a material bias.

(5) The 'photographers, not MST experts' point is disclosed in the paper, which puts 'experts' in scare quotes and justifies the choice.

What survives:
- The sentence presents the expert arm as evidence for a replacement claim when that arm contributes almost nothing inferentially.
- 'Subject matter experts' is generalised from 10 photographers of a single discipline.
- Any reading of 'crowd is as good as experts' is unsupported, because the arms differ in stimuli, UI, language, training and incentives, and nothing compares them on common ground.
- Experts' training is not described.

This is a Discussion-level overreach in wording, not a flaw that undermines the dataset release or the headline findings on oracle alignment and regional differences. I rate it minor, not major.

Arithmetic note (not part of this issue): 88.9% matches 16/18 or 32/36, but 83.4% does not match any k/18 or k/36 (the nearest is 83.3%).
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§7 p.9: "suggesting that subject matter experts are not necessarily needed for MST skin tone annotation tasks" -- confirmed.
§5 p.6: "we use a two-way random, single score ICC where the subject and annotator are viewed as random effect" -- confirmed.
§6 p.7: "we use a one-way random, single score ICC" and "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image" -- confirmed.
App. D p.24: "The task was presented in English and all photographers were fluent English speakers" -- confirmed.
§5 p.6: "Experts were asked to annotate a total of 50 images, 19 from the MST-E Golden Images or Challenging Image sets"; fn 4: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error."
§6 p.8: "Using the global pool, the consensus annotation agreed within 1 point for all but one subject (94.7%)"; "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
§8 (a): "skin tone can be annotated reliably on the MST scale by both trained crowdsourced annotators and subject-matter experts such as professional photographers" -- not comparative.
§4 p.5: "The second study expands on the results of the small scale study"; §4: photographers are labelled skin tone "experts" in quotes.
App. K: experts were paid "a token honoraria not exceeding $500 by GLG for participation in two 30 minute surveys."
§7 Limitations p.10: "the exploratory analyses of annotations from photography experts is more limited than the scale achieved with crowdsourced annotators."
verdicts.corrections:
1. Conclusion (a) is not a comparative claim. It says both groups can annotate reliably, which is two absolute claims joined together. The only sentence that implies replacement is in section 7, and it is hedged ('not necessarily').

2. Calling this a 'non-inferiority claim made without a non-inferiority analysis' misidentifies what the inference needs. The reference standard is Dr. Monk's oracle, not the photographers. The paper does report crowd adequacy against the oracle on the same Golden and Challenging images, per region and per lighting condition. So the gap is weak adequacy criteria, not a missing head-to-head test against photographers. Such a test, with n=18 images and 5 raters, would be underpowered and the less relevant comparison anyway.

3. 'No statistical comparison on a common footing' overstates the gap. Same-image descriptive metrics are reported side by side for both arms (Golden and Challenging ICC in Fig. 3a vs 3b; within-1-point and median distance figures). Only a formal test is missing.

4. The paper itself discloses the photographer and non-MST-expert status, and the exploratory nature of the expert arm.

5. The ICC model difference follows from each design, is appropriate for it, and biases the comparison little.

6. The released metadata contains no crowd annotations, so the matched comparison cannot be checked from the release. The paper's text does confirm that crowd ratings exist for those images.

7. Recommended severity is minor, not major. The overreach is limited to the wording of a Discussion sentence and the broad generalisation to 'subject matter experts'.

issues.title: The ±1 tolerance, imported from 6-point FST, spans a perceptual distance that varies about 5x along the MST scale and is never tied to downstream fairness use
issues.claim: The ±1 threshold and the 'average distance < 1 guardrail' are justified only by FST precedent. On MST, one step is not a constant perceptual quantity. Adjacent orbs differ by between 2.65 and 13.49 CIEDE2000, and the colour range a ±1 window admits roughly triples from oracle MST2 (ΔE ≈ 8.5) to MST5 (ΔE ≈ 26.2). At the light end L* is not monotone, so MST1–3 differ mainly in yellowness (b*), exactly what illuminant colour temperature and white balance shift. The same '±1 hit' therefore means very different perceptual accuracy depending on scale position, and lighting robustness is a different task at the light end. In fairness to the paper, ±1 on 10 points (3 of 10 categories) is stricter as a share of the scale than ±1 on FST (3 of 6); the problem is non-uniformity and lack of validation, not leniency. Prior work set a per-item tolerance, which the paper repurposes as a ceiling on mean distance. It never asks what agreement level keeps MST-bucketed disaggregated metrics unbiased, though its Limitations note the gap.
issues.paper_evidence: §4 p.5: “This threshold of 1-point discrepancy has continued to be used when comparing skin tone annotations between crowdsource annotators and experts [34].” §5 p.7: “the average median distance from the oracle annotation was not above the 1-point guardrail established in previous research [33, 34]”. §7 p.10: “While we use thresholds for agreement (e.g., 1-point discrepancy) that are in line with prior work when describing the resulting annotations as reliable”.
issues.external_evidence: Computed from the official MST_1..10.png orbs (median of opaque pixels, sRGB→CIELAB D65, CIEDE2000). Adjacent ΔE: 2.65, 5.83, 7.89, 13.49, 12.71, 7.47, 7.63, 8.12, 3.65 (largest 5.1x smallest). ±1-window span for oracle k = 2..9: 8.5, 13.7, 21.4, 26.2, 20.2, 15.1, 15.7, 11.8. Orb L*: MST1 80.4, MST2 82.3, MST3 81.0. Uniform-chance within-±1: 44% on a 6-point scale vs 28% on 10 points.
issues.affected_claims: Conclusions (a) and (c), and every within-±1 and average-median-distance result. 'Aligned' is not comparable across scale positions, or between MST-E and the light-skewed Open Images, and has no demonstrated link to valid fairness disaggregation.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, major). Note: design:M10 (merged in C06) treated threshold leniency as a minor framing issue, but MV5's point is non-uniformity, not leniency.
issues.suggested_fix: Report exact-agreement rates and full confusion matrices with counts. Report error in perceptual units (ΔE2000 between the orbs of the annotated and oracle categories) and accuracy separately for the light, mid and dark ranges. Simulate how the observed confusion matrix affects a disaggregated metric (e.g. an error-rate gap across MST buckets such as 1–3/4–7/8–10) to show what tolerance is enough for fairness use.

verdicts.reasoning:
Textual fidelity: all three quoted passages are verbatim and fairly represent their context.

1. "Justified only by FST precedent" is accurate. The ±1 threshold is supported solely by [33] (Groh et al., Fitzpatrick 17k) and [34] (Groh et al. 2022, FST annotations in dermatology). Both are FST studies. Appendix L says the authors added a description of the "1-point discrepancy" threshold "citing how they were used in previous research and their purpose in this work". That is a precedent argument, not a validation for MST.

2. "Repurposed as a mean ceiling" is supported by the text. §4 describes [33] at the item level ("crowdsource annotations are typically within 1-point"). §4 then defines average median distance as "ideally less than 1", and §5 calls <1 "the 1-point guardrail established in previous research [33, 34]".

3. Non-uniformity is not addressed anywhere. I searched the main text, Limitations, the data card, Appendices E/F/G and Appendix L. The paper never claims MST steps are perceptually uniform; it says only that the scale's "color selection and gradations" were designed to capture ethnoracial diversity. Appendix L explicitly calls scale length (10-point vs other lengths) "out of scope". Appendix G uses RGB L2 distance to the reference colours but never discusses step spacing.

4. "Never tied to downstream fairness use" is already conceded in the Limitations ("future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis"), as the issue itself admits. That part adds nothing new.

Why severity is not major: the paper's claims are ordinal and category-level. It says consensus falls within one MST category of Dr. Monk's intended category, and it frames this as alignment with "the scale creator's intent". It never reads ±1 as a fixed perceptual accuracy. The downstream use the issue invokes (MST-bucketed disaggregated metrics) also works in category units, so category agreement is the relevant unit for that use, not ΔE. Perceptual non-uniformity is a legitimate interpretive caveat. Confusion may cluster at the light end, where MST1–3 differ mainly in b*. Aggregate metrics, like the 0.78 average median distance for both well-lit and poorly lit images, could hide position-specific errors. But this does not invalidate or materially weaken "within 1 category of the creator's intent". Figure 8 (Appendix F) reports per-position confusion matrices, which partly expose position-dependence; the figure itself is missing, so I cannot check its content. Conclusion (a), on reliability, rests mainly on ICC, which this issue does not touch.

Numerical check: I re-ran scripts/c14_check.py on data_untrusted/orbs. The qualitative pattern holds:
- Adjacent CIEDE2000 between orbs ranges from 3.17 to 13.42 (about 4.2x).
- With the published hex values the ratio is about 9.6x.
- L* is non-monotone across MST1–3 (80.4, 82.6, 81.0), and b* rises over the same steps (10.1, 13.8, 22.2).
- The ±1 windows for MST2 and MST5 measure about 8.4 and 26.6.
- Uniform-chance within-±1 is 44% on 6 points vs 28% on 10 points.

The issue's exact figures do not reproduce (see corrections).
verdicts.quotes_checked:
1. §4, p.5 (verbatim): "This threshold of 1-point discrepancy has continued to be used when comparing skin tone annotations between crowdsource annotators and experts [34]."
2. §4, p.5: "crowdsource annotations are typically within 1-point of expert dermatologist annotations [33]" (item-level framing)
3. §4, p.5: "the average median distance ... computed across all images (ideally less than 1)"
4. §5, p.7 (verbatim): "the average median distance from the oracle annotation was not above the 1-point guardrail established in previous research [33, 34]"
5. §6, p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
6. §7 Limitations, p.10 (verbatim): "While we use thresholds for agreement (e.g., 1-point discrepancy) that are in line with prior work when describing the resulting annotations as reliable"
7. Appendix B: "The MST scale was designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity" (no claim of perceptual uniformity)
8. Appendix L: "describe the '1-point discrepancy' threshold citing how they were used in previous research and their purpose in this work"
9. Appendix L: "one reviewer raised a question about the effect of scale length ... out of scope for this paper"
10. Refs [33]/[34]: both are Groh et al. studies of Fitzpatrick (FST) dermatology images.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Open Images is wrongly listed among the affected claims. The paper reports no within-±1 or average-median-distance result for Open Images, because there is no oracle there. Open Images is assessed only through ICC and regional chi-square/V². Saying "'Aligned' is not comparable ... between MST-E and the light-skewed Open Images" attacks a comparison the paper never makes. The §7 statement that annotators "perform similarly" on Open Images is based on ICC.

2. The numbers do not reproduce exactly. Re-running the orb computation (scripts/c14_check.py on data_untrusted/orbs) gives:
   - adjacent ΔE: 3.17, 5.70, 7.89, 13.42, 12.74, 7.74, 7.48, 8.12, 3.65, a ratio of about 4.2x, not 5.1x;
   - ±1-window spans for k = 2..9: 8.4, 10.1, 21.1, 26.6, 19.5, 14.6, 14.8, 11.3 (the issue gives 13.7 for MST3);
   - MST2 L* = 82.6, not 82.3.
   The spans are the direct ΔE between window endpoints (k−1 to k+1). With the published MST hex codes, non-uniformity is larger (about 9.6x). The qualitative claim stands, but "about 5x" and the specific values depend on method.

3. "Never tied to downstream fairness use" is already acknowledged in the paper's Limitations. It should not count as an unaddressed defect; at most, the acknowledgement does not fix it.

4. The step from non-uniform ΔE to "materially weakens" is overstated. The paper's claims are category-level agreement with the creator's intended category, and MST-bucketed fairness analysis also works at category level. Perceptual non-uniformity is an interpretive caveat. It is not shown to bias the reported results, and the per-position breakdown is partly available in Figure 8, Appendix F.

5. The light-end point (lighting robustness is a different task for MST1–3 because they differ mainly in b*) is the reviewer's own inference. It is plausible from the orb colorimetry, but no paper data tests it.

verdicts.reasoning:
Checked the paper text and recomputed the colour figures with scripts/c14_check.py, which reuses c01_de.py's CIEDE2000.

What holds:
(1) The ±1 threshold and the "guardrail" are justified only by FST precedent [33, 34]. The paper gives no MST-specific rationale.
(2) MST steps are not colourimetrically uniform. From the median opaque pixel of each orb, adjacent ΔE00 ranges from 3.17 to 13.42, a 4.2x spread. The published MST hex codes give 1.95 to 18.76, a 9.6x spread. The ±1 window span grows from 8.4 at oracle MST2 to 26.6 at MST5, roughly 3x. L* is non-monotone over MST1-3 in both colour sources (orbs 80.4/82.6/81.0; hex 94.2/92.3/93.1), and b* rises over the same range.
(3) The chance arithmetic is right: 44% within ±1 on a 6-point scale, 28% on 10 points.
(4) "Average median distance < 1" repurposes [33]'s per-item within-one accuracy as a ceiling on mean distance. That is an unvalidated reinterpretation, but it adds little, because the within-±1 percentage is reported alongside it.

Why this is not major:
(a) The paper's construct is categorical agreement with the scale creator's labels ("aligns with the scale creator's intent"). It never claims colourimetric or perceptual accuracy. Within-one agreement and MAE in category units are standard ordinal-agreement summaries.
(b) Orb-to-orb ΔE is not the perceptual distance annotators face. They judge photographed skin under varying light against a categorical reference. Orb ΔE is a property of the scale's swatches, not of the annotation error.
(c) For fairness disaggregation, the MST bins themselves are the units of analysis, so the relevant error is category misassignment. The colour distance between adjacent swatches does not change what a one-bin misassignment does to bucketed metrics. Non-uniformity is a real interpretive caveat ("a ±1 hit at MST5 admits more colour range than at MST2"), but it does not undermine conclusions (a) or (c).
(d) The link to downstream fairness use is conceded verbatim in the Limitations section, so it is an acknowledged gap, not a hidden flaw.
(e) With 19 subjects (1-3 per MST level, per the metadata), per-position within-±1 rates would be too noisy to act on. Appendix F / Fig. 8 already gives oracle-vs-median confusion matrices by level.
(f) The idea that light-end lighting robustness is a different task, because MST1-3 differ mainly in b*, is a plausible but untested hypothesis. The paper reports 0.78 average median distance for both well-lit and poorly-lit images and has no per-level lighting data to contradict it.

As a Datasets & Benchmarks paper, the MST-E release's value does not depend on this threshold. A methods reviewer would accept this as a request to justify the threshold and report errors by scale position, which is a minor revision, not a material weakening of a core claim.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §4 p.5: "This threshold of 1-point discrepancy has continued to be used when comparing skin tone annotations between crowdsource annotators and experts [34]." §4 p.5: "the average median distance, the expected difference between the median annotation ... (ideally less than 1)". §5 p.7: "the average median distance from the oracle annotation was not above the 1-point guardrail established in previous research [33, 34]". §6: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images." §7 Limitations p.10: "future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis or mitigations". §2 Related work (manuscript line 859): "crowdsourced annotators had between 71% and 85% within one point accuracy to board-certified dermatologist ratings [33]". §6 Open Images: "we find a high intraclass correlation across markets ranging from 0.875 to 0.91". App. F: "Figure 8 shows confusion matrices of Dr. Monk's annotations compared to the median annotations".
verdicts.corrections:
1) The exact numbers depend on how each orb's colour is extracted. Re-running the stated method (median of opaque pixels, sRGB to CIELAB D65, CIEDE2000) gives adjacent ΔE of 3.17, 5.70, 7.89, 13.42, 12.74, 7.74, 7.48, 8.12, 3.65, a 4.2x spread, not 2.65 and 5.1x. The window span at MST3 is 10.1, not 13.7. The published MST hex codes give a 9.6x spread (1.95 to 18.76). The issue should say non-uniformity is robust across colour sources but its size varies (about 4-10x), not "about 5x" precisely.
2) The statement that "aligned" is not comparable between MST-E and Open Images is inapplicable. The paper reports no oracle-based within-±1 or distance metric for Open Images, only ICC and differences in regional distributions.
3) "Never tied to downstream fairness use" overstates what is hidden. The Limitations section explicitly names this as future work, which the issue partly concedes.
4) The lighting-at-the-light-end argument is a hypothesis. Nothing in the paper or the released metadata shows that errors cluster at MST1-3 or by illuminant.
5) Orb ΔE measures distance between scale swatches, not perceptual accuracy on photographed skin. The paper measures categorical agreement with the scale creator, so non-uniformity is an interpretive caveat, not evidence that ±1 is invalid. Severity should be minor, not major.

issues.title: Usefulness for fairness measurement is never tested, and the lighting-filter budget advice could itself introduce skin-tone-correlated selection bias
issues.claim: No experiment shows that annotations collected the recommended way change or improve any fairness measurement, such as the estimated performance gap of a model across MST groups. The replication advice rests only on Spearman-Brown reliability (C09), and the diversity advice is not supported by the alignment metric (C08). The budget advice to annotate only well-lit (or 'okay'-lit) images could, in the wild, drop under-exposed images, which may disproportionately show darker-skinned people. That would bias the very fairness evaluation the annotations are meant to support. The 'okay lighting' tier is not defined anywhere; the metadata has only two lighting levels. The Limitations acknowledge that downstream usefulness is untested, but not the selection-bias risk.
issues.paper_evidence: §6: “we would suggest filtering for images with good lighting conditions (or even images with okay lighting conditions).” §6: “we find the average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition.” §7: “future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis or mitigations”.
issues.external_evidence: None (the released metadata contains only well_lit and poorly_lit, so the 'okay' tier is undefined).
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (d) and the title's 'for ML Fairness' framing. The lighting-filter recommendation.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, major, confidence 3). The untested-usefulness part is acknowledged by the paper; the unacknowledged selection-bias risk is what keeps this major.
issues.suggested_fix: Run a downstream test: annotate an evaluation set under different designs (1/2/5 per region, single-region vs mixed, lighting-filtered vs not), compute a model's disaggregated metrics under each, and report how far the fairness conclusions change. Check whether lighting filtering shifts the MST distribution of retained Open Images faces. Define the 'okay' lighting tier or remove it.

verdicts.reasoning:
I read the whole paper (main text, Appendices A–L, data card and Limitations) and checked the released metadata.

What holds up:
(1) The paper never tests whether annotations collected the recommended way change any fairness measurement. Its only evidence is reliability (ICC, Spearman-Brown in Fig. 5) and distance to oracle labels.
(2) The lighting-filter suggestion in §6 Replications is quoted verbatim and read fairly. Under a limited budget it says to keep only well-lit (or "okay"-lit) images, and to add poorly-lit images, with 10 annotators, only if they are "necessary".
(3) Nothing in the paper acknowledges that filtering by lighting could drop images unevenly across skin tones. Limitations, Appendix L and the data card are all silent on it. This is an internal inconsistency: §2 criticizes automated pipelines because they "can lead to missing annotations for underrepresented groups during fairness evaluations", but the paper never applies that concern to its own filter.
(4) "Okay lighting" appears only once (line 417) and is never defined. The released mst-e_image_details.csv has only well_lit (893) and poorly_lit (635) for images, plus 18 rows labelled 'video'.

Why the severity is lower than claimed:
(a) The untested-usefulness part is explicitly acknowledged in the Limitations: "future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis or mitigations". The paper never claims its annotations improve fairness estimates. Contributions (a)–(e) are about reliability, lighting invariance, regional effects, practical suggestions and the dataset release. The title's "for ML Fairness" is framing, not a claim of downstream gains.
(b) The lighting filter is a hedged, budget-conditional aside inside one §6 paragraph. It is not among the four bullets in §7 "Suggestions for practitioners". Those bullets instead recommend about 10 ratings per image, "particularly for challenging images". The Limitations likewise say "This work suggests the use of 10 annotators per image if image quality is unknown." So the paper's main advice points away from filtering, which weakens the link the issue draws to contribution (d).
(c) The selection-bias mechanism is a plausible but untested hypothesis. The issue cites no evidence, and the paper's own data cannot show the correlation, because MST-E lighting was set by the photographers and does not depend on skin tone.
(d) The main claims (reliability, lighting invariance, regional differences) do not depend on this one sentence.

Net: an unacknowledged-risk and clarity point about one secondary recommendation. It is a real omission but does not materially weaken a core claim, so I rate it minor rather than major.

No imperative text aimed at reviewers was found. Appendix L is a normal response to the prior FAccT reviews.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§6 Replications (p.8, l.416-419): "if a practitioner's budget is limited, we would suggest filtering for images with good lighting conditions (or even images with okay lighting conditions)." Verbatim.
§6 (l.418-419): "If annotations on images with low quality lighting is necessary, practitioners can then annotate with 10 annotators on just those low quality images." This is the qualifier the issue omits.
§6 Distance (l.407-408): "we find the average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition." Verbatim.
§7 Limitations (p.10, l.504-505): "future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis or mitigations". Verbatim (the issue attributes it to §7, which is correct).
§7 Limitations (l.486): "This work suggests the use of 10 annotators per image if image quality is unknown."
§7 Suggestions bullet: "have at least two annotators in at least five different geographical regions (10 ratings per image), particularly for challenging images." No filter advice appears among the bullets.
§2 (l.171-172): "can lead to missing annotations for underrepresented groups during fairness evaluations". This supports the issue as an internal tension.
§8 (d): "We provide actionable suggestions to practitioners collecting subjective annotations."
Appendix C data card: "lighting, well_lit, Lighting condition of the image". No "okay" tier.
Appendix L: no mention of downstream usefulness or selection bias.
verdicts.corrections:
1. The lighting filter is not among §7's "Suggestions for practitioners" bullets and is not part of contribution (d)'s headline advice. It sits only in the §6 Replications paragraph.
2. The issue leaves out the qualifier in the very next sentence of that paragraph: poorly-lit images that are needed should be annotated with 10 annotators.
3. The paper's main recommendation is 10 annotators per image when image quality is unknown, which points away from filtering.
4. The selection-bias mechanism (under-exposed images disproportionately showing darker-skinned people) is speculative. The issue gives no evidence for it, and MST-E cannot test it because lighting there was set by the photographers.
5. The metadata's lighting column holds well_lit and poorly_lit plus 18 'video' rows. The claim that there are only two lighting levels for images is correct.
6. The untested-usefulness part is already acknowledged in the Limitations and cannot carry major severity. Only the unacknowledged filter risk remains, and it is minor.
7. The claims about C08 and C09 depend on separate issues and were not re-verified here beyond confirming that the replication advice rests on Spearman-Brown in Fig. 5.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the issue holds, but it is overstated, so I rate it minor rather than major.

What holds:
(1) No experiment tests whether annotations collected the recommended way change any downstream fairness quantity, such as gaps in model error across MST groups. The replication advice in §6 rests entirely on Spearman-Brown projections of ICC, computed on the 19-image Golden set and the 19-image Challenging set.
(2) The §6 budget advice reads as a choice: drop poorly lit images, or ("If annotations on images with low quality lighting is necessary") give them 10 annotators. So discarding them is the default option. Any practical filter would select on skin tone. Annotator-judged image quality and automatic brightness or exposure heuristics on face crops are both mechanically confounded with skin luminance. Darker skin is also historically under-exposed by consumer camera pipelines. The paper itself states that models "often perform poorly on images of people with darker skin tones" (l.89). Removing the hardest, poorly lit cases from a fairness evaluation set could therefore make measured gaps look smaller. The paper's Limitations do not mention this risk.
(3) There is also an internal tension that supports the issue. Contribution (b) says annotators are invariant to lighting, and the oracle distance is 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly lit images. So filtering buys only reliability, not accuracy, while it costs coverage. The obvious fix is to allocate more replications to poorly lit images rather than drop them.
(4) The 'okay lighting' tier is undefined. No analysis covers a middle tier: the paper's strata are Golden vs Challenging, and the released metadata has only well_lit and poorly_lit for images.

Why minor rather than major:
(a) The filtering advice is one hedged sentence in §6. It is not repeated in the formal 'Suggestions for practitioners' bullets in §7. Those bullets, and the Limitations, recommend 10 ratings per image 'particularly for challenging images' or 'if image quality is unknown', which is the opposite of dropping images.
(b) The paper explicitly acknowledges the untested downstream usefulness ('future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis'). Leaving this out of scope is standard for an annotation-methodology paper in a Datasets & Benchmarks track. A methods reviewer would not treat the 'for ML Fairness' title as misleading on that basis.
(c) None of the headline claims depend on this sentence: reliability, lighting invariance, regional effects, and the MST-E release are unaffected. The release keeps its value either way.
(d) The skin-tone/lighting correlation in the wild is a plausible hypothesis, not something shown. MST-E cannot test it because its lighting was assigned by design. Poorly lit share by MST level is 0.47, 0.48, 0.62, 0.36, 0.31, 0.39, 0.25, 0.42, 0.31, 0.50 for MST 1 to 10, with no monotone trend. The paper also reports no lighting breakdown for Open Images.

Net: a reviewer would ask for one caveat sentence, plus a rewording to 'stratify and up-replicate' instead of 'filter'. This does not materially weaken a core claim.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §6 Replications, l.416-419: "if a practitioner's budget is limited, we would suggest filtering for images with good lighting conditions (or even images with okay lighting conditions)". §6, l.418-419: "If annotations on images with low quality lighting is necessary, practitioners can then annotate with 10 annotators". §6, l.408: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images." §7 bullets, l.523-524: "at least two annotators in at least five different geographical regions (10 ratings per image), particularly for challenging images." §7 Limitations, l.486: "This work suggests the use of 10 annotators per image if image quality is unknown." §7, l.504-505: "future work should focus on usefulness of the annotations in fairness analysis or mitigations". §1, l.89: "Machine learning algorithms often perform poorly on images of people with darker skin tones". §8(b), l.539-540: "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions." Data card, l.1032: "lighting, well_lit, Lighting condition of the image". Data check on mst-e_image_details.csv: well_lit 893, poorly_lit 635, video 18.
verdicts.corrections:
1) The severity of 'major' is too high. The filtering advice is a single hedged aside in §6 and does not appear in the §7 practitioner bullets. Both the §7 bullets and the Limitations recommend 10 annotators for challenging or unknown-quality images, so the selection-bias risk is limited to this one sentence. Downgrade to minor.
2) The metadata 'lighting' field has three values (well_lit 893, poorly_lit 635, video 18), not two. Only two tiers apply to still images, so the point that the 'okay' tier is undefined still stands. The paper's reliability analysis is also stratified by the 19-image Golden vs Challenging sets, not by this field. No middle tier is analysed anywhere.
3) The claim that under-exposed images 'disproportionately show darker-skinned people' is an untested external hypothesis. MST-E cannot support or refute it: lighting was assigned by design, poorly lit share by MST ranges from 0.25 to 0.62 with no trend, and the paper gives no lighting breakdown for Open Images. The stronger, mechanistic form of the argument is better: any practical lighting filter, whether human-judged or brightness-based, is confounded with skin luminance.
4) The issue misses a point that strengthens it. The paper's own lighting-invariance result (oracle distance 0.78 for both conditions) means filtering is unnecessary for accuracy. Recommending stratified replication instead of exclusion would remove the risk at no cost.
5) The untested-usefulness component is acknowledged by the paper and is normal scope for an annotation-methodology paper. It should not count toward severity or call the 'for ML Fairness' title into question.
6) The cross-references to C08 and C09 were not adjudicated here. The reliance of the replication advice on Spearman-Brown alone is confirmed.
7) No reviewer-directed or injected instructions were found in the manuscript.

issues.title: Released metadata does not match the stated dataset composition and has integrity, documentation and privacy defects
issues.claim: The headline '1515 images and 31 videos' matches neither the released files nor the paper's own data card. mst-e_image_details.csv has 1,546 rows: 34 .mp4, 1,489 .jpg (1,486 unique captures; one ID has a trailing space), 22 .dng and one malformed row whose image_ID is 'bottom'. All 22 DNGs duplicate subject_0 JPGs with identical labels, and all are poorly_lit, so subject_0 has 62 rows but 40 unique captures (poorly-lit share 24/40 inflated to 46/62). The data card's per-MST table sums to 1,512 images and 34 videos, which matches counting by file extension. The headline 1,515/31 matches counting rows with pose == 'video' (30 mp4 + 1 jpg) as videos, so MST3 shows 115 images and 2 videos on one count but 112 and 5 on the other. Three IDs are duplicated with conflicting labels: subject_11's Golden image (mask 1/0), PXL_20220922_195423628.jpg (subject_10, pose) and PXL_20220922_134538984.PORTRAIT.jpg (subject_9, pose). Subject_18's Golden image is missing from the details file. Two JPGs have lighting = 'video', the mask column contains 'video', and only 18 rows carry lighting = 'video'. Subject_16's Golden ('best represents') image is labelled mask=1. Field names diverge: the data card's image_name, mask 'false' and challenge_image_id vs the CSV's image_ID, 0/1 and not_ideal_image_id; the file is 'golden_and_adversarial'; the paper says 'Challenging'. Pose categories are undefined, and the expressions and glasses mentioned in the paper are absent. Data-card errors: the data subject is listed as 'image search queries' (a template leftover), the crowd 'Number of unique annotations' is blank, and 'Annotated by a human expert' conflicts with §3 (an author annotated first). Three subject_15 video filenames contain what appears to be a personal first name, contrary to the stated privacy approach. If the DNG duplicates and duplicated IDs were annotated as separate items, per-subject consensus, per-subject ICC and the per-image average median distance double-weight them. The Golden/Challenging analysis cannot be fully re-run from the metadata.
issues.paper_evidence: Abstract: “containing 1515 images and 31 videos spread across the full MST scale.” Data card p.22: “Images 179 218 112 187 179 165 76 143 142 111” / “Videos 2 5 5 3 4 3 4 2 5 1”. verdicts.reasoning:
I re-ran the counts myself (scripts/c16_verify.py and scripts/c16_mst.py on the released CSVs). Almost every data fact in the issue checks out:
- The CSV has 1,546 rows: jpg 1,488, 'jpg ' 1, mp4 34, dng 22, and one malformed row whose ID is 'bottom'.
- All 22 DNGs are subject_0 rows that duplicate JPGs with identical labels, and all are poorly_lit. Subject_0 has 62 rows and 46 of them are poorly_lit.

- Counting by file extension reproduces the data card's per-MST table exactly (1,512 images, 34 videos). Counting by pose gives 1,515/31, with MST3 at 115/2.

- Three subject_15 mp4 names begin with what looks like a first name.
- The field names differ from the data card (image_ID, 0/1 and not_ideal_image_id), and the file is called golden_and_adversarial.

Textual-fidelity check: nothing in the paper addresses these problems. Appendix H (maintenance), Appendix J (format), Appendix L (previous reviews) and §7 say nothing about known errors, duplicates or DNGs. Appendix J actually makes it worse: it says the download holds ".jpg" images and ".mp4" videos, so the 22 DNG rows contradict the paper's own format description. The data-card quotes in the issue are verbatim and in context.

Why I rate it minor rather than major:
1. The real content of the dataset is intact. MST labels are the same on every row within a subject, and subjects per MST (2,3,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,1) match the data card. The duplicate-ID conflicts only touch pose or mask, never MST. The data card itself says "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value."
2. The headline count is reproducible from the CSV. It is a row count that includes about 29 non-unique or malformed rows, an overcount of roughly 2% of unique stills. That makes it imprecise, not fabricated.
3. Double-weighting is only hypothetical. The crowd annotation file was not checked, so nobody knows whether DNGs or duplicate IDs were annotated as separate items. Since Appendix J lists only jpg and mp4, the DNGs may not be intended dataset items at all. The issue itself concedes that no headline claim reverses.
4. The Golden/Challenging analysis does not depend on the missing subject_18 row. The Golden ID list covers all 19 subjects and the oracle label is per subject, so only that one image's pose, lighting and mask values are lost.
5. These are documentation and hygiene errata that weaken the polish of contribution (e). They do not materially weaken any core claim. The proposed "major" also leans on verification confidence, which is not the same thing as severity.

The privacy point is real but small. The subjects consented to release of their full face images, and it is not established whose name appears in the filenames.

verdicts.reasoning:
I re-ran the checks myself (scripts/c16_verify.py over both released CSVs). Almost every data fact in the issue reproduces:
- 1,546 rows by extension: jpg 1,488, 'jpg ' 1, mp4 34, dng 22, and one row whose image_ID is 'bottom' (row 1352, subject_2).
- All 22 DNGs are subject_0 and poorly_lit, and each duplicates a JPG stem with identical labels. Subject_0 has 62 rows but 40 unique captures, and its poorly-lit count goes from 24/40 to 46/62.
- Non-mp4 rows per MST give [179,218,112,187,179,165,76,143,142,111], sum 1,512. mp4 rows per MST give [2,5,5,3,4,3,4,2,5,1], sum 34. Both match the data card table exactly. Rows with pose != 'video' give 1,515 (MST3 = 115) and pose == 'video' gives 31 (30 mp4 + 1 jpg), so the headline matches neither the table nor any unique-file count.
- Three duplicated IDs carry conflicting mask or pose labels, and subject_18's Golden image is missing from the details file.
- Lighting = 'video' appears on 18 rows (two of them JPGs, and 12 mp4s are labelled well_lit and 6 poorly_lit). Mask = 'video' appears 5 times. Subject_16's Golden image has mask = 1 (so does subject_15's Challenging image).
- Three subject_15 mp4 names begin with a six-letter alphabetic token that looks like a first name.

The data-card quotes ('image search queries', the blank crowd annotation count, the different field names) are verbatim in the manuscript. The paper's own text is internally inconsistent: the snapshot says Images 1515 / Videos 31, while its per-MST table sums to 1,512 / 34.

Methodological weight is another matter, and here the issue overreaches:
1. The MST oracle is per-subject. The data card says "Each subject was annotated with a single MST-E value", and I confirmed every subject has exactly one MST value, with subjects per MST matching the card (2 3 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 1). None of the duplicate or conflict defects touches the outcome label.
2. The conflicts are in mask and pose only. Lighting agrees across every duplicate. The paper's stratified results are by lighting and by Golden/Challenging, never by pose or mask, so no reported stratum changes.
3. The double-weighting is conditional ('If ... annotated as separate items') and was never checked against mste_annotations.csv. Its size is also bounded: 22 rows out of about 1,500 (~1.5%), all for one mid-scale subject (MST3). That cannot plausibly move a per-image average median distance of 0.78 or per-subject ICCs of 0.86 to 0.94 by a material amount. Browser-based crowd tools also rarely serve DNG files, so double annotation is speculative.
4. Golden/Challenging can still be reconstructed. The golden file lists all 19 pairs, and subject_18's oracle (MST1) comes from its other rows. Only the covariate row for one well-lit Golden image is missing.
5. The headline count overstates unique still images by about 29 (~2%). That is an erratum, not a change to the description of the dataset.

For a Datasets & Benchmarks paper, metadata hygiene is in scope and a careful reviewer would ask for an errata release: drop the DNG duplicates, fix the malformed and duplicate rows, add subject_18's Golden row, define the pose categories, rename the PII-bearing files and fix the data-card template text. These are cleanup items, though, not defects that materially weaken the contribution or any headline empirical claim. The issue itself says 'No headline empirical claim is shown to reverse'. 'Major' here rests on speculative double-weighting plus confidence in fixable facts, so I downgrade to minor.

On privacy: a probable first name in three filenames goes against the stated approach in §7 and should be scrubbed. But the subjects are consenting professional models whose faces are released, so the extra identifying risk from a first name is small.
