issues.title: The expert study and all Open Images results cannot be reproduced; the released crowd file omits the fields several analyses need, and replication is costly and account-gated
issues.claim: Only the MST-E crowd CSV (subject, image, region, annotation) is released. Not released: Open Images image IDs, face boxes and annotations; the expert photographers' raw ratings (only Mann-Whitney U statistics are given); the distractor images and the 'much larger set of similar images'; the annotator training materials; any analysis code. The crowd CSV has no annotator ID, difficulty or skip flag, body-part field, or batch or time field. So the region MANOVA (whose unit is undescribed) cannot be reproduced, annotator-level analyses and counts per region are impossible, and the collected 'difficult' and body-part responses cannot be re-analysed. Only the MST-E crowd medians, within-1 rates, one-way ICC and Spearman-Brown are reproducible in principle. Independent re-collection is out of reach for most groups (about $780k spent), and 'open-access' in fact means free with a Google account. Note: the lens did not download mste_annotations.csv; its fields are taken from the data card.
issues.paper_evidence: Data card: “region, Ghana, Region where the annotation came from”; “annotation, MST1, Crowdsourced MST annotation.”; “Crowdsourced annotations for the MST-E dataset has been made available for replication purposes only.” §6: “the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators.”; “We performed a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) [28] with annotator region as the independent variable”. App. K: “Overall, we spent approximately $780k on crowdsourced annotations.” §3: “This paper introduces the open-access MST-E dataset”. §7: “do not allow for anonymous access to the image dataset.”
issues.external_evidence: 25 × 88,355 items ≈ 2.2M annotations, or roughly $0.35 per annotation if the $780k covers only these items. The crowd CSV at storage.googleapis.com/mste/mste_annotations.csv was not downloaded, so its availability and contents are unverified.
issues.affected_claims: Claim (c): the MANOVA (Pillai's trace = 1.97) and the Open Images regional result. All of §5. Claim (b) on Open Images (ICC 0.875–0.91, χ² = 0.26). Independent replication of (c) and (d).
issues.severity_disagreement: data:D5 banded it major; data:D12 (cost and access gating) banded it minor. Major is chosen because the main inferential results for (c) and all Open Images claims cannot be checked.
issues.suggested_fix: Release: Open Images image IDs, face boxes and per-annotation labels; pseudonymous annotator IDs with the difficult/skip and body-part fields; the expert annotation matrix; the distractor image IDs; the annotator training deck; the analysis code. Specify the MANOVA design (unit, DV vector, missing-data handling) or replace it with a mixed model that has annotator random effects. Describe access as 'free with registration', and report cost per annotation and annotator counts so others can plan smaller replications.

verdicts.reasoning:
The facts in the issue hold up against the text. The only artifact released beyond the MST-E images and Dr. Monk's labels is the MST-E crowd CSV (App. L: "We release the annotations with this paper"). Per the data card, that CSV has four fields: subject, image, region, annotation. Nowhere does the paper release or promise any of the following:
- the Open Images subset IDs, face boxes or annotations (§6 gives only the counts 41,471 images and 86,809 faces);
- the expert photographers' raw ratings (App. E lists only per-image U values and p-values);
- the distractor images or the "much larger set of similar images";
- training materials;
- analysis code.

There is no annotator ID, so the region MANOVA cannot be rebuilt. Its unit of observation is never stated: §6 says only that region is the IV and the "MST annotations for each subject" are the DV, and a multivariate observation across subjects implies per-annotator vectors. The Open Images statistics (ICC 0.875–0.91, χ²=0.26, V²=0.0766) cannot be checked by anyone outside the authors. Nothing in the paper, including App. L and the Limitations section, addresses whether these analyses can be reproduced. App. L deals only with releasing the MST-E annotations. All quoted passages are verbatim and fairly represent their context.

The issue overstates several points:
1. The substance of claim (c), that regional differences exist, can still be tested on the released CSV, because it has a region field. For example, one could compare regions within images with images as blocks, which needs no annotator IDs. Only the exact Pillai's trace = 1.97 value cannot be reproduced, so "the main inferential results for (c) cannot be checked" goes too far.
2. The paper labels the expert study "a qualitative survey" (§4) and "exploratory" (§6, Limitations, App. L), and reports per-image test statistics. Its non-reproducibility therefore weighs less than the issue implies.
3. The paper collected "difficult" flags and body-part responses but never reports an analysis of them. Leaving them out of the release affects how useful the data is, not whether any stated result can be reproduced.
4. Skips can be partly recovered: the data card says skipped items yield "less than 25 annotations". Annotation counts per region can also be computed from the region field. Only the number of distinct annotators per region is unrecoverable, and the paper never reports that number anyway.
5. The paper discloses the Google-account requirement openly (data card, App. H). §7 presents it as a deliberate ethical mitigation ("do not allow for anonymous access to the image dataset"). It applies to the images, not to the crowd CSV, which the paper places at a public storage.googleapis.com URL. It has little bearing on reproducing the crowd statistics.
6. The ~$780k figure, the 88,355-item count and the ~$0.35 per-annotation figure are the reviewer's own extrapolation. The $780k may also cover the "much larger set". High cost of re-collection is inherent to annotation studies and is not a flaw in the paper.

Net: the reproducibility gap is real for the Open Images generalization claim, the exact MANOVA statistic and the exploratory expert study. The core MST-E crowd results for (a) and (b), plus a check of the direction of (c), can still be verified from released data. This is a transparency limitation, not something that materially weakens a core claim, so the severity is minor rather than major. Neither the manuscript nor the local data contained any text aimed at reviewers.

verdicts.corrections:
1. Claim (c) is not unverifiable. The released CSV has a region field, so regional differences can be tested with alternative analyses (for example, region compared within images, with images as blocks). Only the exact MANOVA statistic (Pillai's trace = 1.97) cannot be reproduced.
2. Annotation counts per region can be computed from the region field. What cannot be recovered is the number of distinct annotators per region, which the paper never reports. Skips can be partly inferred from images with fewer than 25 annotations, as the data card says.
3. The "difficult" flags and body-part responses are never analysed in the paper. Their absence from the release is a data-utility gap, not a gap in reproducing a reported result.
4. The paper discloses the Google-account gating (data card, App. H) and justifies it as a misuse mitigation (§7). It covers the images; the crowd CSV is placed at a public storage URL. So "'open-access' in fact means free with a Google account" is a framing complaint, not a hidden fact, and it does not block reproducing the crowd statistics.
5. The paper repeatedly labels the expert study qualitative or exploratory and reports per-image U values and p-values. Its non-reproducibility should carry less weight than "the expert study cannot be reproduced" suggests.
6. The 88,355-item count and the ~$0.35 per-annotation figure are reviewer extrapolations, not paper claims (86,809 faces + 1,515 images + 31 videos). The $780k may also cover the undisclosed "much larger set". Cost of re-collection is not a defect of the paper.
7. The proposed severity of major is too high. The core MST-E crowd findings, and a check of (c), are verifiable from released data; what is lost is the Open Images generalization, the exact MANOVA value and the exploratory expert numbers. Minor is the right band.

verdicts.reasoning:
What holds, from the paper's own text: the data card lists only four fields for the crowd CSV (subject, image, region, annotation). The paper never says it releases the photographers' raw ratings; App. E gives only Mann-Whitney U values and p-values. It never says it releases the Open Images face IDs, boxes or MST labels; a web search found no separate public release of MST labels for Open Images. No analysis code, annotator training material or distractor set is released. So the expert ICC/within-1 numbers (88.9%, 83.4%), the Open Images ICC range (0.875–0.91), the χ²=0.26 test and V²=0.0766 cannot be checked from the release. The CSV also has no annotator ID, which blocks any check on annotator clustering or on how many annotators each region had. For a NeurIPS D&B paper, missing code and a partial annotation release are a fair, standard criticism.

Why this is downgraded to minor and only partially upheld:
(1) Claim (c) on MST-E can still be checked. The released CSV supports region-level tests of the regional difference: per-image or per-subject distributions by region, ordinal models with image or subject random effects, and signed regional shifts. The lighting split can be rebuilt by joining on mst-e_image_details.csv, which has a lighting column; I confirmed that locally. What cannot be reproduced is the specific Pillai's trace = 1.97. The main reason is that the paper never says what the MANOVA's unit of analysis is, which is a reporting defect that releasing more data would not fix. The missing annotator IDs then stop anyone from checking whether the effect survives clustering by annotator. That concern belongs to the separate clustering and unit-of-analysis issues. Scoring it again here would double-count.
(2) Not releasing a measurement is not the same as that measurement being wrong. Non-release lowers verifiability but does not by itself weaken any core claim. The paper's main D&B contribution, the MST-E images, Dr. Monk's labels, the golden/challenging IDs and the crowd CSV, is released and can be reused on its own.
(3) Several sub-points do not matter. No reported statistic uses the distractors or the 'much larger set of similar images'. The 'difficult' and body-part responses are never analysed in the paper, so there is nothing to reproduce; that is a loss of potential value, not a reproducibility failure.
(4) The cost argument is overstated. $780k covers the whole crowd effort. On the paper's counts, (86,809 + 1,515) × 25 = 2,208,100 annotations, about $0.35 each. The issue's 88,355 wrongly adds the 31 videos, which the image-level crowd CSV does not cover. At that rate, re-collecting the full MST-E crowd arm (37,875 annotations) costs about $13k. The expert arm cost about $5k (App. K), and the images are released. Only a full-scale Open Images replication is expensive, and a subsample would be enough to test its ICC and regional claims. Expensive data collection is also not a methodological defect in itself.
(5) Account gating is a minor point and does not affect reproducibility. A free Google account is needed for the images, which is a common, disclosed misuse safeguard. The crowd CSV is given as a plain storage.googleapis.com URL with no stated account requirement.

Overall: the factual inventory is right, but only the lack of annotator IDs and the unreleased Open Images labels materially limit verification of headline claims (c) and (b)-in-the-wild. Even these limit verifiability, not validity. Minor.

1) 'Region MANOVA cannot be reproduced': the main blocker is that the paper never states the MANOVA's unit, which is a reporting defect, not a release gap. The substance of claim (c) on MST-E can still be re-tested at region level from the released CSV. What the release cannot support is a test that accounts for annotator clustering.
2) 'Counts per region are impossible' is ambiguous. Annotation counts per region can be computed from the CSV. Only the number of unique annotators per region cannot.
3) The 'difficult' and body-part responses, the distractors and the larger mixing set are not used in any reported analysis. Their non-release does not affect reproducing any reported result.
4) Arithmetic: 88,355 includes the 31 videos. The crowd file is per image, so the count is 86,809 + 1,515 = 88,324, giving 2,208,100 annotations and about $0.353 each. This is an inference: App. K describes monthly salaries, not per-annotation pay.
5) 'Re-collection out of reach for most groups' is overstated. The MST-E crowd arm costs about $13k at the implied rate and the expert arm about $5k (App. K). The MST-E images are released. Only a full-scale Open Images replication is costly, and a subsample would test those claims.
6) The Google-account requirement applies to the image dataset. The paper gives the crowd CSV as a plain public storage URL, so the account requirement does not affect reproducing the crowd analyses. Calling the dataset 'open-access' is loose wording, not a methodological flaw.
7) Severity should be minor, not major. Non-release lowers verifiability rather than weakening the claims, and the material part (no annotator IDs, undescribed MANOVA unit) overlaps with separate analysis findings that should carry that weight.
8) The CSV's actual contents remain unverified; this review, like the original, relies on the data card.

issues.title: MST-E represents 19 hand-picked stock models, each shot in one short studio session on one day with one phone pipeline, which is too narrow for the paper's general claims
issues.claim: Filename timestamps put all 1,542 PXL-named files on 2022-09-22, between about 13:12 and 20:11, with each subject's session lasting only 6.6–18.4 minutes. The stated '4 hours' therefore describes neither the per-subject sessions nor the whole shoot (about 7 hours). Each subject's well-lit and poorly-lit conditions were staged within minutes of each other, so they are not varied environmental conditions. All still filenames follow the Google Pixel naming pattern, and 252 JPGs are Portrait-mode captures, which points to one device family and one image-processing pipeline. Device, location and lighting rig are not reported. The subjects are professional models from one stock agency: 30 candidates were chosen from hundreds by unstated criteria, and 19 were photographed. As 'examples' they are probably prototypical of their MST category, which would make within-1 agreement easier than for people whose tone falls between swatches. No age or other demographic data were collected, so coverage cannot be assessed. (The precision consequences of n=18–19 are covered in C05.)
issues.paper_evidence: §3: “All images and videos of a subject were collected within a short timespan of 4 hours”; “We selected 30 candidate subjects from an initial pool of hundreds of models, 19 of whom were eventually photographed”. Fig. 2: “Each subject has images in a variety of lighting conditions and poses.” Abstract: “even under challenging environmental conditions.” Data card: “Subjects 2 3 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 1”.
issues.external_evidence: Per-subject capture spans from PXL_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS timestamps range from 6.6 min (subject_1) to 18.4 min (subject_9); all files are dated 20220922, earliest 13:12, latest 20:11. 252 of 1,487 well/poorly-lit JPGs are .PORTRAIT. Caveat: timestamps come from the camera clock via filenames, and the device is inferred from the PXL_ naming convention, not from EXIF.
issues.affected_claims: Claims (a) and (b), and the Abstract's 'even under challenging environmental conditions'. Lighting robustness is shown only for staged lighting on one device family. The Limitations admit only that 19 subjects 'do not capture every variation'.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, major). Note that meas:S3, design:S2 and data:S2 rightly count the same tight temporal control as a strength for within-subject contrasts; the defect is the external-validity claim, not the control itself.
issues.suggested_fix: Report camera/device and processing mode, location, lighting rig and subject selection criteria. Re-word 'challenging environmental conditions' as 'staged poorly-lit studio shots'. Future versions should add subjects with intermediate tones, more than one subject per MST point, several devices, and real indoor and outdoor environments.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the data claims against the released metadata (mst-e_image_details.csv) with scratchpad/scripts/c18_verify.py. They hold: all 1,542 PXL_-named files are dated 20220922, running from 13:12:34 to 20:11:59. Per-subject spans run from 6.6 min (subject_1) to 18.4 min (subject_9). For every subject, the well_lit and poorly_lit timestamps fall inside that same span of a few minutes. 252 of the 1,487 well/poorly-lit JPG rows are .PORTRAIT; the 1,487 includes one row whose extension has a trailing space. There are also 22 .dng files. Every still follows the PXL_ pattern.

What the paper says and leaves out:
(1) The paper never reports the capture device, the location, the lighting setup, or how the 30 candidates were chosen from 'hundreds'. No appendix supplies these either: not B, C (data card), H, I, J or L.
(2) The paper does admit that MST-E is controlled. §6 says 'Unlike the MST-E dataset where images were taken in a controlled setting'. The data card calls it 'a controlled set through which to study annotator behavior'. The Limitations say the 19 subjects 'do not capture every variation in skin tone'.
(3) The paper's answer on generalization is the Open Images extension. That analysis tests only inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.875–0.91) and regional differences. It does not test agreement with the expert, and it does not test invariance to lighting, because Open Images has no oracle and no lighting labels. So the abstract's 'aligns with an expert in the MST scale, even under challenging environmental conditions' and contribution (b), 'with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions', rest only on one staged poorly-lit condition per subject, shot minutes apart, in a single one-day shoot. The paper calls that 'challenging environmental conditions' and 'lighting conditions' in general.
(4) The Limitations sentence 'we believe our results will translate to other domains' extrapolates from reliability to the broader claims.

The core external-validity point therefore stands, and the paper does not adequately address it. Several parts of the issue are overstated or speculative, so I uphold it only in part (see corrections). Severity is major but borderline. The within-subject comparison is valid, and the fix is mostly to narrow the claims and disclose the capture details. Even so, a headline contribution (b) and the abstract claim are worded much more generally than the evidence supports.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
All of the following matched the manuscript verbatim, in context:
- §3: "All images and videos of a subject were collected within a short timespan of 4 hours to eliminate skin tone variation" (also repeated verbatim in the data card).
- §3: "We selected 30 candidate subjects from an initial pool of hundreds of models, 19 of whom were eventually photographed".
- Fig. 2: "Each subject has images in a variety of lighting conditions and poses."
- Abstract: "aligns with an expert in the MST scale, even under challenging environmental conditions."
- Data card: "Subjects 2 3 2 2 2 2 1 2 2 1".
- §3: "We curated a corresponding Challenging Images set which mirrored the Golden Images set with different lighting conditions."
- §6: "Unlike the MST-E dataset where images were taken in a controlled setting, Open Images is an 'in-the-wild' dataset".
- §6: "recommendations based on annotator behaviors observed in our controlled studies likely translate to real-world scenarios".
- Limitations: "they do not capture every variation in skin tone"; "we believe our results will translate to other domains."
- Limitations: "We chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about the subjects".
- Appendix L: "this data was explicitly not collected from the models."
- Conclusion (b): "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions."
verdicts.corrections:
1. The '4 hours' statement is loose, not false. It describes each subject ('of a subject'), and 'within 4 hours' is a true upper bound for spans of 6.6–18.4 min. The paper never says the whole shoot took 4 hours. The issue's line that it 'describes neither the per-subject sessions nor the whole shoot' overstates the problem. The real point is that the stated bound hides how tightly the sessions were packed, and that matters for how varied the lighting conditions could be.
2. 'Stock models' and 'professional models from one stock agency' are inferences from TONL being the source. The paper says only 'models' sourced through TONL.
3. 'Probably prototypical of their MST category' is speculation. It fits the 'exemplar' framing and the unstated selection criteria, but nothing shows it, and it should be labeled as a hypothesis.
4. The paper does acknowledge that demographics were not collected, as a privacy choice (Limitations; Appendix L). It also states that subjects 'include individuals of different ethnicities and gender identities'. The issue is right that coverage cannot be checked. It is wrong to suggest the paper says nothing about this.
5. The paper explicitly calls MST-E a 'controlled setting' and offers the Open Images analysis as its generalization check. The issue should say that this check covers only reliability and regional effects, not agreement with the expert or invariance to lighting, rather than imply the paper ignores generalization.
6. The single device family rests on the PXL_ filename convention plus 22 .dng and 252 .PORTRAIT files, not on EXIF. The issue's caveat on this is appropriate.

verdicts.reasoning:
I re-ran the filename checks myself (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-connielam-Documents-Github-modlli-research/258e1bf5-b292-418f-9e28-a4893dc6037a/scratchpad/scripts/c18_check.py and c18_b.py). The figures are right. All 1,542 PXL-named files carry the date 20220922. The earliest is 13:12:34 and the latest is 20:11:59, about 7 hours in total. Per-subject spans run from 6.6 min (subject_1) to 18.4 min (subject_9). For every subject, well-lit and poorly-lit shots are interleaved within the same few minutes. There are 1,487 well-lit or poorly-lit JPGs, 252 of them .PORTRAIT, plus 22 DNGs. The PXL_ prefix is Google Pixel camera-app naming, so inferring one device family is reasonable, though EXIF was not checked.

The part of the issue that holds up: the lighting evidence for contribution (b) comes from one studio, one day, one phone pipeline and a within-minutes well-lit/poorly-lit split. The rig, device and setting are not reported. That supports a within-dataset claim, not "invariant to lighting conditions" in general, and not the Abstract's "even under challenging environmental conditions." The Open Images extension does not close this gap. It reports only ICC and regional differences, with no oracle and no lighting contrast, so it addresses consistency in the wild but not expert alignment or lighting invariance there. A methods reviewer would ask for the Abstract, contribution (b) and the Discussion line "invariant to environmental factors such as lighting quality" to be narrowed. The Limitations section mentions only the subject count. One further concern is plausible but untested: Pixel HDR+ processing could brighten "poorly lit" captures and make the challenge milder than it would be in the wild.

Why I downgraded from major to minor:
1. The paper does not hide that MST-E is controlled. It calls it "a controlled set" and contrasts it with Open Images, which "Unlike the MST-E dataset where images were taken in a controlled setting" is "in-the-wild". The flaw is overbroad wording in the Abstract and contributions, not a hidden design weakness. Rewording fixes it without new experiments.
2. The within-dataset results stand. Median distance is 0.78 for both well-lit and poorly-lit images, and Challenging-set ICC is 0.82–0.95. The tight temporal control is what makes the within-subject lighting contrast valid.
3. For a Datasets & Benchmarks paper, MST-E's stated purpose is annotator training. Exemplar images do not need to be ecologically representative.
4. Several supporting points in the issue are wrong or speculative (see corrections).
5. The n=19 problem is acknowledged in the paper and already covered by C05.
6. Not collecting demographic data was a deliberate privacy choice that the paper discloses.

§3: "All images and videos of a subject were collected within a short timespan of 4 hours to eliminate skin tone variation" (p.4, l.217).
§3: "We selected 30 candidate subjects from an initial pool of hundreds of models, 19 of whom were eventually photographed" (l.213-214).
§3: "a controlled set through which to study annotator behavior" (l.212).

§8(b): "with training, can provide annotations invariant to lighting conditions" (l.540).
§7: "annotators are able to learn to be invariant to environmental factors such as lighting quality" (l.473).
§6: "Unlike the MST-E dataset where images were taken in a controlled setting, Open Images is an 'in-the-wild' dataset" (l.441).
§6: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images" (l.409).

verdicts.corrections:
1. The "4 hours" statement is not contradicted. The paper says each subject was collected "within a short timespan of 4 hours." Per-subject spans of 6.6–18.4 min fall within that bound, so the wording is loose but true. The whole-shoot span of about 7 h is not what the sentence describes.
2. "So they are not varied environmental conditions" goes too far. Well-lit and poorly-lit lighting was varied within each session. What did not vary was location, device, time of day and ambient setting. Short gaps between shots do not mean the lighting barely changed. The rig is unreported, so how far apart the two conditions really are is unknown, not shown to be small.
3. "252 JPGs are Portrait-mode" is 252 of 1,487 lit JPGs (about 17%), so most images are not Portrait-mode. Portrait mode adds little to the single-pipeline point, which rests on the PXL naming and is still inferred, not confirmed from EXIF.
4. The claim that subjects are "probably prototypical of their MST category" is speculation. The paper gives no selection criteria, and the issue offers no evidence of prototypicality. It is a plausible risk, not a finding.
5. The paper discloses that demographic data were deliberately not collected, for privacy (Limitations; reviewer-response appendix). This is a stated design choice, not an omission.
6. The paper does attempt to show generalization, via Open Images ICC and regional differences. That covers in-the-wild consistency but not lighting invariance or expert alignment, so the gap is narrower than "lighting robustness is shown only for staged lighting" implies for claim (a). That sentence does hold for claim (b).
7. The stock-agency and n=19 points overlap with C05 and with the paper's own acknowledged limitation. They should not be counted again here.

issues.title: The licence and terms of use contradict each other, and the promoted model-evaluation use is excluded in two of the paper's own statements
issues.claim: The paper places images and annotations under CC BY, which permits any use including training and commercial use, yet the same paragraph forbids model training, and TONL is credited with 'ALL RIGHTS RESERVED'. Permitted uses also differ between documents. §3 and the data card include model evaluation; App. I and the released README allow only research or annotator training. The Discussion recommends MST-E for model and fairness evaluation, which is either forbidden or unclear under these terms.
issues.paper_evidence: §3 pp.4–5: “The images cannot be used to train machine learning models. The images and annotations are licensed under CC BY.”; “used for research, model evaluations, or annotator-training purposes only.” App. I: “used for research or annotator-training purposes only (Copyright TONL.CO 2022).”; “Annotations provided with the images can be used for research or annotator-training purposes only.” Data card: “Model Evaluation: Can be used to evaluate fairness in computer vision models.” §7: “the MST-E dataset can be used to evaluate fairness over the full MST scale”.
issues.external_evidence: The released README.md in the MST-E zip says: “used for research or human-annotator-training purposes only. The images cannot be used to train machine learning models.” It does not mention model evaluation. CC BY 4.0 grants rights for any purpose, and §2(a)(5)(B) bars imposing additional terms that restrict the licensed rights, so a no-training restriction does not fit a CC BY grant.
issues.affected_claims: Contribution (e) (the dataset release) and the Discussion's model-evaluation use case. Users cannot tell which uses are legally permitted.
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, major).
issues.suggested_fix: Publish one licence that matches the intended restrictions (CC BY cannot carry a no-training clause, so use a custom research licence with explicit terms). Make the paper, data card, README and website consistent. State whether model evaluation, including evaluation of skin-tone estimators and calibration or tuning on MST-E, is permitted.

verdicts.reasoning:
Every quote in the issue is verbatim. The core contradiction is real and nothing in the paper resolves it. I checked §3, §7 including Limitations and Ethical Considerations, the Appendix C data card, App. H, App. I and App. L "Addressing previous reviews". None of them mentions the licence or reconciles the differences.

(1) The CC BY problem. §3 states, in consecutive sentences, "The images cannot be used to train machine learning models. The images and annotations are licensed under CC BY." The Figure 2 caption and the data card say "Copyright TONL.CO 2022 ALL RIGHTS RESERVED". A blanket CC BY grant cannot carry a no-training restriction or an all-rights-reserved notice. App. I and the released README.md never mention CC BY. The 9-line README gives only "research or human-annotator-training purposes only" plus the all-rights-reserved notice.

(2) The permitted uses differ between documents. §3 and the data card list research, model evaluations and annotator training. App. I and the README list only research and annotator training. The Ethics paragraph in §7 also refers only to consent "for research and annotator training purposes".

Where the issue overstates:
(a) Contribution (e) is framed as "help practitioners train annotators ... and support further research". Every document permits that use, so the contribution itself is not undermined. Only the secondary model-evaluation use in the Discussion ("beyond that use case, the dataset can also be used to evaluate models") is inconsistent with App. I and the README.
(b) "Forbidden" is too strong. Model evaluation done as research arguably falls under "research", so the honest description is ambiguous, not prohibited.
(c) The problem is about dataset documentation and legal clarity. It does not touch the paper's empirical findings on annotator agreement or geographic variance, and a text edit to align the terms fixes it. Under the rubric (major = materially weakens a core claim) it is minor. The fix is still mandatory for a dataset release, because users cannot tell which uses are allowed.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§3 l.231-232: "TONL has given permission for these images to be released and used for research, model evaluations," (continues l.242) "or annotator-training purposes only. The images cannot be used to train machine learning models." l.243: "The images and annotations are licensed under CC BY." (verbatim)
Fig. 2 caption l.240-241: "Images by TONL. Copyright TONL.CO 2022 ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Used with permission." (in a caption, not the licence paragraph; the PDF extraction interleaves the two)

§7 Ethics l.512-513: "we have consent from participants to release the MST-E dataset for research and annotator training purposes"
Contribution (e) l.545-546: "We release the MST-E dataset to help practitioners train annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions and support further research."

App. L: no discussion of licence or terms of use.
verdicts.corrections:
1. "Forbidden" is too strong. App. I and the README limit use to "research or annotator-training", and research-purpose model evaluation arguably falls under "research". The model-evaluation use is ambiguous, not clearly prohibited.
2. Contribution (e) is not materially affected. It is framed as annotator training plus "support further research", which every document permits. Only the Discussion's secondary model-evaluation claim conflicts.
3. "ALL RIGHTS RESERVED" appears in the Figure 2 caption and the data card, not in the §3 licence paragraph itself. That paragraph only looks continuous because the PDF extraction interleaves the caption with it. The contradiction still stands across the documents.
4. Severity should be minor, not major. This is a documentation and legal-clarity defect that a text edit can fix, and it does not weaken any empirical claim. The §7 Ethics paragraph also states consent only for "research and annotator training purposes", which is extra support for the inconsistency the issue does not cite.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked every quotation in the issue against manuscript.md and the released README.md, and all of them are accurate. The contradiction is real.

What holds:
(1) In one §3 paragraph (pp.4–5), the paper says the images "cannot be used to train machine learning models" and then says "The images and annotations are licensed under CC BY." CC BY has no non-commercial or use-of-field limits. A licence with a no-training carve-out is therefore not CC BY, and the two statements conflict.
(2) Permitted uses differ across the paper's own documents. §3 and the data card include model evaluation. App. I and the README list only research and (human-)annotator training.
(3) App. I limits annotations to "research or annotator-training purposes only." That conflicts with §3, which puts annotations under CC BY.
(4) The Figure 2 caption and the data card say "ALL RIGHTS RESERVED," which also sits badly with a CC BY grant.
(5) The CC BY version is never stated, which adds ambiguity.

What is overstated:
(a) The issue says model evaluation is "forbidden" by App. I and the README. It is not clearly forbidden. Both allow "research," and fairness evaluation of models done as research falls naturally within that. The real ambiguity is non-research use, such as product or commercial model audits. "Unclear" is accurate; "forbidden" is too strong.
(b) The external argument cites CC BY 4.0 §2(a)(5)(B). That clause restricts recipients, who may not impose extra terms downstream. It does not govern what the licensor itself grants. The right point is that a licensor who adds use restrictions is no longer offering CC BY, and Creative Commons asks licensors not to label modified terms as CC. The conclusion stands, but the cited clause does not support it directly.
(c) The "ALL RIGHTS RESERVED" credit appears in a figure caption and in a data-card attribution line. It reads more naturally as copyright attribution than as a second licence. That is a weak extra contradiction, not an independent one.

Severity: This is a documentation and compliance defect, not a methodological one. It affects none of the paper's empirical findings: annotator variance, regional effects, the medians agreeing with Dr. Monk, or invariance to lighting. The dataset's stated primary purpose, enabling and testing consistent human annotation, is permitted consistently in every document. That purpose is in the data card's Data Description and the README. Research use is also permitted everywhere.

The ambiguity is limited to one secondary use the Discussion promotes (model evaluation outside research) and to the licence label. The fix is a camera-ready text edit: name one custom licence, or drop the "CC BY" label and state the restriction. NeurIPS D&B reviewers do require clear licensing, so this must be fixed. It does not materially weaken a core claim, and it does not reduce the release's value for its main use. I rate it minor, not major.

[the text is split across the page break] / §3: "The images cannot be used to train machine learning models. The images and annotations are licensed under CC BY." / Fig. 2 caption: "Images by TONL. Copyright TONL.CO 2022 ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. Used with permission." / Data card: "Model Evaluation: Can be used to evaluate fairness in computer vision models." and "Model training : The images cannot be used to train machine learning models." / App. I: "used for research or annotator-training purposes only (Copyright TONL.CO 2022)." / App. I: "Annotations provided with the images can be used for research or annotator-training purposes only." / §7: "the MST-E dataset can be used to evaluate fairness over the full MST scale" / README: "used for research or human-annotator-training purposes only. 1. The issue says model evaluation is "excluded" or "forbidden" in App. I and the README. That overstates it. Both permit "research," which plausibly covers fairness evaluation of models in a research setting. Only model evaluation outside research is unclear.
2. CC BY 4.0 §2(a)(5)(B) bars recipients from imposing extra terms downstream; it does not bind the licensor. The correct argument is that a grant with a no-training restriction is not a CC BY licence, and CC asks licensors not to use the CC name for modified terms.

issues.title: The expert 'suggestive evidence' of regional differences (3 of 36 per-image Mann-Whitney tests) is consistent with the global null; p-values are asymptotic and uncorrected, and two of the three hits are the same subject
issues.claim: Appendix E reports 36 tests (18 subjects × Golden/Challenging) at n1 = n2 = 5. Three have p < .05, against 1.8 expected under the global null; P(X ≥ 3 | Bin(36, .05)) = 0.268. The tests are not independent (the same 10 raters appear in every test). Nothing survives correction: the minimum BH-adjusted p is 0.423 (0.24 within Golden alone) and the minimum Holm p is 0.652. The reported p-values match, to six decimals, the normal approximation with tie and continuity correction, which is anti-conservative at 5 vs 5. Whether an exact test removes a specific hit depends on ties. Without ties, U=22 gives an exact p of 0.056, but for tie configurations that reproduce the reported (U, p), the exact conditional p for S14-Challenging ranges over 0.032–0.071. The claim made in meas:MV12 and design:m2 that U=22 'would not pass' an exact test therefore holds only without ties. The robust problem is multiplicity, not exactness. Two of the three hits are Subject 14 (Golden and Challenging) rated by the same experts, so they are not independent replications, and Fig. 4 shows exactly those two. The main text hedges ('suggestive', 'exploratory'), but the Fig. 4 caption generalises to 'consistently measurable differences'.
issues.paper_evidence: §5 p.6: “Differences were significant using p <0.05 for three of the images.”; “The differences observed provide suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation”. Fig. 4 caption p.7: “we found consistently measurable differences in annotator behavior based on region.” App. E rows: “MST2 S13 23.0 0.026888”, “MST6 S14 24.0 0.018119”, “MST6 S14 22.0 0.048632”.
issues.external_evidence: Exact two-sided no-ties p at 5 vs 5 (all 252 splits enumerated): U=22 0.0556, U=23 0.0317, U=24 0.0159, U=25 0.0079 (minimum attainable). Exact conditional permutation p over every 5-vs-5 configuration on a 1–10 scale that reproduces the reported (U, p) (stat:M4): S13-Golden 0.0476 (reported 0.027; 120 configs); S14-Golden 0.0238 (reported 0.018; 3,528 configs); S14-Challenging 0.032–0.071 (reported 0.049; 1,260 configs); S9-Golden 0.119 (reported 0.059); S15-Golden 0.167 (reported 0.071). Binomial P(X ≥ 3) = 0.268. scipy false_discovery_control BH minimum 0.423; Holm minimum 0.652.
issues.affected_claims: The expert half of contribution (c), the hypothesis-generation narrative, and the Fig. 4 framing. Partly mitigated: the authors label the expert study exploratory (§5, App. L), and (c) rests mainly on the crowd analysis.
issues.severity_disagreement: stat:M4 banded it major; meas:MV12 and design:m2 banded it minor. Minor is chosen because the paper already hedges the expert result as exploratory and the main regional claim rests on the crowd analysis (whose own defects are C01/C02). The residual overclaim is the Fig. 4 caption and the 'suggestive evidence' wording.
issues.suggested_fix: Replace the 36 tests with one ordinal mixed model on all 36 × 10 expert ratings, with a region effect and random effects for image and expert, or with a global permutation test that permutes region labels at the expert level. If per-image tests are kept, use exact or permutation p-values with BH/Holm adjustment and report Hodges-Lehmann shifts with CIs. Report the expert regional comparison as inconclusive, note that 3/36 does not exceed chance, and revise the Fig. 4 caption to match.

verdicts.reasoning:
The statistics in the issue hold up. I re-ran them (scripts/c20_check.py and c20_exact.py).

- **Count and multiplicity:** Appendix E has exactly 36 tests (18 subjects × Golden/Challenging), with three p-values below .05. P(X ≥ 3 | Bin(36, .05)) = 0.268. The minimum BH-adjusted p is 0.423 overall and 0.242 within Golden alone. The minimum Holm p is 0.652.
- **Exact test, no ties:** two-sided p is 0.0556 at U=22, 0.0317 at U=23, 0.0159 at U=24 and 0.0079 at U=25.
- **Tie configurations:** I searched all 5-vs-5 rating sets on a 1–10 scale under the tie- and continuity-corrected normal approximation. The number of sets that reproduce each reported (U, p) to six decimals matches the issue: 120, 3,528 and 1,260. The exact conditional p is 0.0476 for S13-Golden and 0.0238 for S14-Golden, and ranges from 0.0317 to 0.0714 for S14-Challenging. The claim that "multiplicity, not exactness, is the robust problem" is therefore correct.
- **Gap in the paper:** I searched the whole manuscript for a multiple-comparison correction, a note on non-independence, or a statement of the global-null expectation. There is none. The only "correction" hits are about photographic colour correction.
- **Same subject:** two of the three hits are Subject 14, Golden and Challenging, rated by the same 10 experts. Fig. 4 shows exactly those two.
- **Overclaim:** taken together, the expert data are consistent with no regional effect. Calling them "suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation" (§5) overstates them. §6 then reuses that wording as motivation ("We found suggestive evidence for regional differences in annotation in Section 5").

The issue misreads one point. The Fig. 4 caption does not generalise the expert result. The full sentence is "In large-scale experiments with trained annotators (§6), we found consistently measurable differences in annotator behavior based on region." It explicitly credits the "consistently measurable differences" to the crowd study in §6, not to the expert data in the figure. Putting that sentence in the caption invites readers to conflate the two studies, but that is a framing issue, not a textual overclaim. The issue calls the caption a "residual overclaim", and that part should be removed.

Several passages in the paper already soften the expert result:
- §4 calls the expert study "a qualitative survey".
- §5 says "suggestive".
- §6 says "Unlike the exploratory analysis of experts... in this setting we have enough statistical power", which implicitly concedes the expert study is underpowered.
- The Limitations call the expert analyses "exploratory" and "more limited".
- Appendix L says the expert portion is delineated "as exploratory" and used "to establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later in the paper".
- Appendix E lists all 36 tests, so readers can do the multiplicity arithmetic themselves.
- Contribution (c), the Abstract and the Discussion's regional claim all rest on the crowd MANOVA, not on the experts.

Hypothesis generation does not require surviving correction, so the issue's claim that the "hypothesis-generation narrative" is affected is weak.

What remains: an uncorrected "significant ... for three of the images" statement, "suggestive evidence" wording that the data do not support, and no acknowledgement that two of the hits are the same subject. That is minor.

verdicts.corrections:
1. **Fig. 4 caption:** the issue says the caption "generalises to 'consistently measurable differences'". That misreads it. The caption sentence begins "In large-scale experiments with trained annotators (§6)" and explicitly credits the differences to the crowd study, not to the expert data shown. At most the placement invites conflation. It should not be listed as the residual overclaim. The residual overclaim is the "suggestive evidence" wording in §5 and its reuse at the start of §6's "Regional Differences in Annotation" paragraph.
2. **"Three of the images":** the phrase is literally accurate, since S13-Golden, S14-Golden and S14-Challenging are three distinct images. The paper also discloses in the Fig. 4 caption that the two images shown are both Subject 14. The defect is that the main text does not acknowledge that the hits are non-independent, not that it hides the fact.
3. **Hypothesis-generation narrative:** listing it under "Affected claims" overstates things. Generating hypotheses from exploratory data does not require surviving multiplicity correction, and Appendix L frames the expert study exactly that way.
4. **Exact-test wording:** the "would not pass an exact test" claim attributed to meas:MV12 and design:m2 comes from other reviewers, not the paper. The paper never states which test variant it used. The issue's own correction (it holds only without ties) is accurate: under the configurations I enumerated, the exact p for S14-Challenging is 0.0317, 0.0397 or 0.0714.
5. **Verified numbers:** all of the issue's numerical claims reproduce. They are the binomial 0.268, BH 0.423 (0.242 within Golden), Holm 0.652, the exact no-ties p-values, and the configuration counts 120, 3,528 and 1,260 with their exact-p values or ranges.

verdicts.reasoning:
I reran every number with scipy (script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-connielam-Documents-Github-modlli-research/258e1bf5-b292-418f-9e28-a4893dc6037a/scratchpad/scripts/c20_check.py). The statistical core of the issue holds.

(1) Setup. The paper has five experts per market (§5, "a panel of five experts in photography in India and five ... in the United States"). Appendix E lists 18 subjects × 2 image sets = 36 tests. Three have p < .05, against 1.8 expected under the null. Binom P(X≥3 | 36, .05) = 0.268. Taking Golden alone, P(X≥2 | 18, .05) = 0.226.

(2) Correction. scipy BH gives a minimum adjusted p of 0.423 over all 36 tests and 0.242 within Golden. Holm gives a minimum of 0.652 over all 36 and 0.326 within Golden. Nothing survives under either family definition. Holm is valid under any dependence. Shared raters would most likely add positive dependence, which does not rescue the result.

(3) Method. Running scipy's asymptotic Mann-Whitney U (tie and continuity correction) on reconstructed tie configurations reproduces the reported p-values to six decimals: S13G 0.026888, S14G 0.018119, S14C 0.048632. The paper never says it used an exact test or any multiplicity correction; a search for Bonferroni, correction and FDR finds nothing relevant.

(4) Exact p-values. Without ties, the exact two-sided p is 0.0556 for U=22, 0.0317 for U=23, 0.0159 for U=24 and 0.0079 for U=25, which confirms the issue. Exact conditional permutation p over tie configurations that reproduce the reported (U, p):
- S13G: 0.0476 (120 configurations)
- S14G: 0.0238 (3,528)
- S14C: 0.032 to 0.071 (1,260; about two thirds below .05)
- S9G: 0.119
- S15G: 0.167

So the exact test removes at most S14-Challenging, and only for some tie patterns. The issue is right that multiplicity, not exactness, is the robust objection. The approximation is anti-conservative in every case checked.

(5) Dependence. Two of the three hits are Subject 14 (Golden and Challenging), rated by the same 10 experts. Fig. 4 plots exactly these two, so it is one subject shown twice, not two replications.

So by current methods standards, calling 3 of 36 uncorrected asymptotic hits "suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation" is an overstatement. The pattern is what noise alone would produce, and a competent methods reviewer would accept that point.

Where the issue overreaches:
- The Fig. 4 caption does not generalise the expert result. It explicitly credits the "consistently measurable differences" to "large-scale experiments with trained annotators (§6)". The real problem is only that this sentence sits next to the expert plots and could be read as backing them. That removes one of the two "residual overclaims" behind the severity.
- The paper labels the expert study exploratory in §6 ("Unlike the exploratory analysis of experts") and App. L (expert results "establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later"). Hypothesis generation needs no confirmatory evidence, so the hypothesis-generation narrative is not invalidated. Only the word "evidence" is too strong.
- Contribution (c) and the abstract's regional claim rest on the crowd MANOVA, not on these tests. The MST-E release is unaffected.

Severity is minor. The criticism is correct but bears only on hedged, exploratory material. It does not weaken a headline claim, which rests on the crowd analysis (whose own problems are C01/C02). Major, as stat:M4 proposed, is not justified.

issues.title: Expert accuracy figures fail GRIM-style checks against the stated denominators, and the image set behind them is unspecified
issues.claim: Only 18 subjects were rated in the expert study, and the text never says whether the 'within 1' and 'average median distance' figures refer to Golden, Challenging or both pooled. The India figures fit n=18 (16/18 = 88.9%; 14/18 = 0.78). The US 83.4% cannot be k/n for any small n (15/18 = 83.3%), and 0.84 cannot be reached with n=18 or 36, even allowing half-integer medians from skipped ratings; it is reachable with n=19 or 25. The likely causes are rounding or transcription errors or a different denominator. Either way the analysis set is underspecified. The direction of the conclusion is unchanged.
issues.paper_evidence: §5 p.7: “88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States”; “0.78 in India and 0.84 in the United States”. §5 footnote 4: “One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error.”
issues.external_evidence: No k/n with n < 60 falls in [0.8335, 0.8345) (stat:m1, design:m6); meas:MV13 (merged in C16) extends this to n < 80. 0.84 (in [0.835, 0.845)) is reachable for n ∈ {19, 25, 31, 32, 37, …} with integer distances and n ∈ {16, 19, 22, 25, …} with half-integer distances; neither set includes 18 or 36 (half-integer sums give 0.833 or 0.847/0.861). 88.9% is reachable for n ∈ {9, 18, 27, 36, …}. Relatedly, the crowd figure 0.78 cannot equal k/19 (15/19 = 0.789) (meas:MV4, merged in C04).
issues.affected_claims: Confidence in, and reproducibility of, the expert-alignment numbers behind (a). Not its direction.
issues.severity_disagreement: None; all three sources banded it minor.
issues.suggested_fix: State the image set and denominator for each expert metric, report k/n next to percentages, give per-subject expert medians so the figures can be checked, and correct the US figures.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the main text, footnotes, figure captions and Appendices B through L, including L "Addressing previous reviews". Nothing in them settles the issue.

1) Denominator. §5 says experts annotated "19 from the MST-E Golden Images or Challenging Image sets". Footnote 4 then removes one subject. Appendix E (Fig. 7a/7b) lists exactly 18 subjects per set, with S16 missing. The released metadata has 19 subjects (subject_0 to subject_18). So n = 18 per set, or 36 if the sets are pooled. The main text's "19" is itself inconsistent with the footnote.

2) The analysis set is never stated. The "Distance from Intended Annotations" paragraph in §5 gives one India figure and one US figure. It never says whether they come from Golden, Challenging, or both pooled. ICC is broken out by set (Fig. 3a) and the Mann-Whitney tests are broken out by set (Appendix E). Appendix F gives confusion matrices for the crowd annotators only and has no expert breakdown. Appendix L ("Analytic Clarifications") says the authors "more clearly define 'average median distance'", but it does not specify the image set for the expert numbers. The paper never addresses this point.

3) The arithmetic holds. I re-ran the checks in scratchpad/scripts/grim_c21.py:
- No k/n with n < 80 falls in [0.8335, 0.8345). 15/18 and 30/36 both give 83.33%, so the reported "83.4%" fits neither.
- §5 says "Each expert reviewed each image" and there were 5 experts per market, so each median is an integer. With integer sums, 0.84 is reachable only for n in {19, 25, 31, 32, 37, 38}. For n = 18 the neighbouring values are 0.833 and 0.889. For n = 36 they are 0.833 and 0.861, or 0.847 if half-integer sums are allowed.
- 88.9% = 16/18 and 0.78 = 14/18 both fit n = 18.
- The US pair (83.4%, 0.84) therefore fits neither n = 18 nor n = 36. 16/19 = 0.842 is possible, which points to a transcription or rounding error, or a mixed or stale denominator. The likely example is a 19-subject calculation made before the excluded subject was dropped.

4) Impact. The expert data are not released, so the numbers cannot be recomputed. The conclusion's direction (consensus within about 1 point of the oracle) holds under any nearby value. The expert study is explicitly labelled exploratory (Appendix L), and its headline claim is qualitative. Minor severity is appropriate.

Textual fidelity: the quoted passages are verbatim and in context. The issue reads the paper correctly. The one weak point is the crowd-related side note (see corrections). It does not affect C21's core claim.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§5 p.7: "a high percentage of the consensus annotations were with 1-point of discrepancy of the oracle annotations, 88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States" (verbatim).
§5 p.7: "0.78 in India and 0.84 in the United States" (verbatim; split across a line break).
§5 footnote 4, p.6: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error." (verbatim).
§5 p.6: "Experts were asked to annotate a total of 50 images, 19 from the MST-E Golden Images or Challenging Image sets".
§5 p.6: "Each expert reviewed each image, so we use a two-way random, single score ICC".
§4 p.5: "the average median distance, the expected difference between the median annotation from a group of annotators and the oracle computed across all images".
Appendix E, Fig. 7: 18 subject rows per set; S16 is absent.
Appendix L: "We also more clearly define 'average median distance'"; the set is not specified.
§6 p.8: "The distance was 0.78 for both well lit and poorly lit images."
verdicts.corrections:
1) Ambiguity of n: the main text says 19 MST-E images were used, and only footnote 4 and Appendix E (18 rows, S16 missing) establish that n = 18. The issue should cite Appendix E as the direct evidence for n = 18 and note the internal 19-vs-18 inconsistency in §5.

2) Half-integer case: five experts rated every image, so the expert medians are integers. The half-integer allowance is not needed for the expert figures. It only makes the conclusion more conservative.

3) Crowd 0.78 side note (merged into C04): its claim that 0.78 "cannot equal k/19" assumes the crowd figure is computed over the 19 Golden or Challenging images. §6 says "for both well lit and poorly lit images". The released metadata labels 893 images well_lit and 635 poorly_lit, so that figure may be computed over those image pools rather than over 19 subjects. The GRIM argument therefore does not establish an inconsistency for the crowd figure and should be dropped or hedged.

4) Severity: minor is correct. These are reproducibility and precision problems in an analysis the paper labels exploratory, and they do not change the direction of the conclusion.

verdicts.reasoning:
I reran the arithmetic (script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-connielam-Documents-Github-modlli-research/258e1bf5-b292-418f-9e28-a4893dc6037a/scratchpad/scripts/c21_grim.py).

1. Denominator. The paper itself confirms 18 subjects, and more directly than the footnote does. Appendix E (Figure 7a and 7b) lists 18 subjects in both the Golden table and the Challenging table, and S16 is missing from both. The issue rests on the footnote, but the appendix is the stronger evidence.

2. GRIM results under standard round-half rounding. India 88.9% = 16/18 and 0.78 = 14/18 both fit. US 83.4% fits no k/18 or k/36 (15/18 = 83.33%). US 0.84 fits no integer or half-integer sum over 18 or 36. Under conventional rounding, the issue's arithmetic is correct.

3. The issue misses a much simpler explanation. Both US figures equal the same fraction, 15/18 = 0.8333, rounded up: ceil to one decimal gives 83.4%, and ceil to two decimals gives 0.84. Under that same round-up rule, all four expert figures fit n = 18 with integer distances (16, 15, 14 and 15 out of 18). They also all fit pooled n = 36 (32, 30, 28 and 30). So the most economical reading is a rounding-direction slip of 0.001 to 0.007 on the US numbers. A different denominator (19 or 25) is less likely, and the appendix's 18-row tables argue against it. One small correction on the half-integer case: 30.5/36 = 0.847 truncates to 0.84, so "unreachable with n = 36" holds only under round-half rounding.

4. Underspecification. This is real but overstated. The §4 metric definition says the average median distance is "computed across all images", which points toward pooling Golden and Challenging. The §5 figures are not explicitly labelled by set. Every figure fits both n = 18 and n = 36, so which set was used changes no conclusion. It is a reporting-clarity issue only.

5. Materiality. The discrepancy sits in the third significant digit. Every reading of the numbers leaves both regions well above the "within 1-point" level and below a 1.0 average distance. This section is labelled exploratory, and the MST-E release does not depend on it. GRIM is a legitimate check, and a methods reviewer would accept it as a note on reporting precision. It does not weaken any core claim. The issue's "minor" band is the ceiling, and it is close to "none".

Verdict: partially upheld. The GRIM inconsistency under standard rounding is real, and the image set is not labelled in §5. The implied scope ("a different denominator", "the analysis set is underspecified") is overstated: the simplest explanation is 15/18 rounded upward, n = 18 is confirmed by Appendix E, and the metric definition points to pooling.
