§5 p.7: "0.78 in India and 0.84 in the United States" (confirmed).
§5 fn 4: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error." (confirmed; attached to the Challenging-session sentence)
§5 p.6: "Experts were asked to annotate a total of 50 images, 19 from the MST-E Golden Images or Challenging Image sets"
§4: "the average median distance... between the median annotation from a group of annotators and the oracle computed across all images"
App. E, Fig. 7(a)/(b): 18 subject rows per table (S0–S18 with S16 absent), for both Golden and Challenging.
verdicts.corrections: (1) The claim that 0.84 and 83.4% "cannot be reached with n=18 or 36" holds only under round-half rounding. If 15/18 = 0.8333 is rounded up, both US figures follow exactly, and all four expert figures then fit n = 18 (16, 15, 14, 15) or n = 36. Both US figures being the same fraction rounded up is the most plausible cause, more likely than a different denominator. (2) Under truncation, 30.5/36 = 0.847 also displays as 0.84, so the half-integer claim needs that qualifier. (3) n = 18 is directly confirmed by Appendix E, where both tables list 18 subjects and S16 is absent. That evidence is stronger than inferring it from the footnote. It also makes the n = 19 and n = 25 alternatives unlikely. (4) "The text never says" which set the figures use overstates the gap: the §4 metric definition says the distance is "computed across all images", which suggests pooling. The §5 figures are still not explicitly labelled. (5) Severity should be minor at most, close to none. The discrepancy is at most 0.007 in the third significant digit and changes no conclusion.

issues.title: Collected covariates and missingness (skips, difficulty ratings, body part, mask, pose) are never reported, analysed or released, despite bearing directly on the regional and lighting claims
issues.claim: The skip criterion is inconsistent ('no skin visible' in §6 vs 'too hard to annotate' in the data card), and skip counts by region, lighting or subject are never reported. Difficulty-dependent missingness could bias both the Challenging-condition and the regional results. Body part used and 5-point difficulty ratings were collected in both arms but never analysed. Body part is a direct alternative explanation for regional offsets: regions relying on the face rather than the arms or torso would produce systematic shifts without different 'mental models'. Difficulty and skips are the natural test of lighting invariance. Mask and pose are labelled in the dataset but enter no analysis. The released annotation CSV omits all of these, along with annotator IDs (C02, C17), so readers cannot check.
issues.paper_evidence: §6 p.7: “Annotators could select that an image was difficult to annotate for skin tone, and skip the task if no skin was visible.” App. C: “Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators.” §5 p.6: “to select which part of the person’s body they used in their assessment, and to rate on a 5-point scale the ease/difficulty of the annotation.” Data card: the released annotation fields are subject, image, region and annotation only.
issues.external_evidence: Released metadata: mask=1 on 155 rows. Pose has 4 levels (side 635, facing_camera 501, bottom 191, frontal 188). None enters any reported analysis.
issues.affected_claims: Alternative explanations for (c) (regional offsets) and (b) (lighting invariance). Reproducibility of the crowd-level inferences behind (a)–(c).
issues.severity_disagreement: None; both sources banded it minor.
issues.suggested_fix: Report skip and 'difficult' rates by region, lighting and subject, and run the main analyses under explicit missing-data assumptions (e.g. treating skips as informative). Report body-part distributions by region and lighting and adjust the regional comparisons for them. Add mask and pose as covariates. Release these fields with pseudonymous annotator IDs and timestamps.

verdicts.reasoning:
I read the whole manuscript: main text, limitations and ethics, the Appendix C data card, Appendices D–K and Appendix L ("Addressing previous reviews"). Nothing in it reports, analyses or releases skip counts, body-part selections, difficulty ratings, mask or pose, and nothing explains why these are left out. Appendix L covers the earlier reviews (citing the MST scale, the expert's identity, why photographers were chosen, the 19-subject limit, and the annotation release). It never mentions missingness or these covariates. The Limitations section lists factors not considered (annotator identity, task language, UI, other people in the image). Body part, difficulty, skips, pose and mask are not among them. So the core complaint holds: the paper collected these covariates and then dropped them without saying so.

The released metadata supports the issue and goes further. mask=1 on 155 rows is confirmed. Pose has 4 image levels (side 635, facing_camera 501, bottom 191, frontal 188) plus 31 rows marked 'video'. I matched the Golden/Challenging pairs against the metadata. Pose differs within 15 of the 18 matchable pairs. Mask differs in 2 pairs: subject_15's Challenging image is masked, and subject_16's Golden image is masked. Subject_18's Golden image is missing from the metadata file. §3 says the Challenging set "mirrored the Golden Images set with different lighting conditions", but the Golden-vs-Challenging contrast changes pose (and sometimes mask) along with lighting. That makes the issue's point about lighting invariance stronger: the paper never names or controls this confound.

The quotes are verbatim apart from ligatures and reflect their context fairly. The data card's annotation fields are exactly subject, image, region and annotation, so the omission of annotator IDs and covariates is confirmed.

Why only partially upheld:
1. Overstated: the 5-point difficulty scale is described only for the expert photographers (§5). For the crowd (§6), annotators "could select that an image was difficult", with no scale given. So "5-point difficulty ratings were collected in both arms" is wrong. Body part was collected in both arms, which is correct.
2. The skip-criterion "inconsistency" is mild. §6 describes a difficulty flag plus a skip option for images with no visible skin. The data card describes what happened (hard images were skipped). These can partly be reconciled, though the data card does suggest skips were driven by difficulty.
3. On annotator IDs, the ethics section gives a stated rationale: it chose "not to collect or release other sensitive information about ... our annotators, beyond general geographic region". That is a partial, stated justification, although pseudonymous IDs would hardly count as sensitive.
4. The body-part explanation for regional offsets would still be a region-driven difference. It weakens the "cultural mental model" reading of claim (c) but not the existence of regional differences.

Severity is minor. None of these points alone invalidates the ICC, MANOVA or oracle-distance results. They are reporting and transparency gaps, plus an unacknowledged confound, that weaken the interpretation of claims (b) and (c) and stop outside readers from checking them.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§6 p.7: "Annotators could select that an image was difficult to annotate for skin tone, and skip the task if no skin was visible." (verbatim)
§6 p.7: "report which part of the body they primarily used to make the selection (Face, Torso, Arms/Hands, Legs/Feet, or Other)" (crowd arm, body part only, no 5-point scale)
§5 p.6: "to select which part of the person's body they used in their assessment, and to rate on a 5-point scale the ease/difficulty of the annotation" (expert arm, verbatim)
App. C data card: "Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators. In those cases there will be less than 25 annotations." (verbatim)
App. C crowd fields: "subject ... image ... region ... annotation" (only four fields, confirmed)
§3: "We curated a corresponding Challenging Images set which mirrored the Golden Images set with different lighting conditions."
§3: "some subjects provided images of themselves with a facial mask"
§7 Ethics: "We chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about the subjects of the dataset or our annotators, beyond general geographic region"
§7 Limitations: "it does not consider other aspects of annotator identity and background, or other factors such as the language used in the task" (does not cover skips, body part or difficulty)
§7: "evaluate performance of models over varying lighting conditions and poses" (pose mentioned only as a use for model evaluation, never analysed)
App. L: no section on missingness, skips, body part, difficulty, pose or mask.
verdicts.corrections:
1. "5-point difficulty ratings were collected in both arms" is wrong. The 5-point ease/difficulty scale is described only for the expert photographers (§5). The crowd arm (§6) had only an option to mark an image as difficult, with no scale specified. Body part was collected in both arms.
2. "Pose has 4 levels" holds for images only. The metadata also has a 'video' pose value on 31 rows.
3. The skip-criterion inconsistency is mild, not a clear contradiction. §6 describes the instruction (skip if no skin is visible) alongside a separate difficulty flag. The data card describes the outcome (hard images were skipped).
4. The paper does give a privacy rationale for not releasing annotator information beyond region (§7 Ethics). It is weak for pseudonymous IDs, but it exists, and the issue should acknowledge it.
5. Body-part reliance would itself be a region-linked difference. It challenges the "mental model/cultural" interpretation of claim (c), not the existence of regional differences.
6. Addition that strengthens the issue: in the released metadata, Golden/Challenging pairs differ in pose in 15 of 18 matchable pairs and in mask status in 2 pairs (subject_15, subject_16). §3's description of the Challenging set as mirroring the Golden set "with different lighting conditions" therefore hides a pose/mask confound in the lighting-invariance comparison. Subject_18's Golden image is missing from the image-details CSV.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core factual claims hold. The paper collected several things it never reports or analyses: body part used (both arms), a 5-point ease/difficulty rating (experts), a difficulty flag and a skip option (crowd), and mask and pose labels (dataset). I searched the full text, including Appendices D, E, F and K, and found no skip counts, no body-part distribution, no difficulty summary, and no analysis that uses mask or pose. The data card lists only four crowd annotation fields: subject, image, region and annotation. I re-ran the counts on the released metadata. mask=1 is on 155 rows (137 well_lit, 17 poorly_lit, 1 video). Pose counts are side 635, facing_camera 501, bottom 191 and frontal 188, plus 31 video rows. Both match the issue.

By current reporting standards (missing data reported by condition; covariates that were collected are reported or their omission explained), this is a fair criticism. A competent methods reviewer would raise it.

It also connects to claim (b) more than the issue says. In the released Golden/Challenging pair list, 15 of the 18 Golden images I could match in the metadata are facing_camera. 16 of the 19 Challenging images are side or frontal. One Golden and one Challenging image have mask=1. So the lighting contrast is confounded with pose, and pose was never modelled. Skips in a dataset where every image shows the subject are most plausibly driven by difficulty, not by 'no skin visible'. If skips are concentrated in the Challenging set, they would remove the likely-discordant ratings and inflate Challenging-set ICC. That is a concrete and plausible bias direction, but the paper's text gives no magnitude, and the annotation CSV is not available to check.

Several parts are overstated, so I do not uphold the issue fully.
(1) The crowd arm did not collect a 5-point difficulty rating. §6 describes only an option to mark an image as difficult. The 5-point scale is in the expert study (§5) only.
(2) The 'inconsistent skip criterion' is more a loose wording difference than a contradiction. §6 describes a difficulty flag and a skip option separately, and the data card merges them. It is still worth fixing.
(3) Body part used does not threaten claim (c) that region has a significant effect on annotations. If regions favour different body parts, that is still a regional difference in annotation behaviour. It only weakens the interpretation that 'shared mental models' of skin tone differ by region, which the paper itself hedges ('may vary').
(4) Not analysing mask or pose is not a defect in itself for a Datasets & Benchmarks paper. The paper offers pose only as a downstream model-evaluation use. The pose concern matters only because of the Golden/Challenging confound described above.
(5) The missing annotator IDs belong to C02/C17, so they should not count twice here.

None of these omissions is shown to change a headline number, and the value of the MST-E release does not depend on them. Minor is the right severity.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§6 p.7: "Annotators could select that an image was difficult to annotate for skin tone, and skip the task if no skin was visible." — verified.
§6 p.7: "report which part of the body they primarily used to make the selection (Face, Torso, Arms/Hands, Legs/Feet, or Other)" — verified.
§5 p.6: "to select which part of the person's body they used in their assessment, and to rate on a 5-point scale the ease/difficulty" — verified (expert arm only).
App. C data card p.21: "Some images were too hard to annotate and were skipped by some annotators." — verified.
App. C data card crowd fields: subject, image, region, annotation — verified; no other fields listed.
§6 p.8: "the shared mental models of skin tone may vary significantly across different geographic regions." — verified (hedged).
§7 p.9: the dataset "can be used ... to evaluate performance of models over varying lighting conditions and poses" — verified (pose is offered only as a model-evaluation use).
Metadata check: mask=1 on 155 rows; pose: side 635, facing_camera 501, bottom 191, frontal 188, video 31 — verified.
Golden/Challenging pair list: 15 of the 18 matched Golden images are facing_camera; 16 of 19 Challenging images are side or frontal; one Golden and one Challenging image have mask=1.
verdicts.corrections:
(1) "5-point difficulty ratings were collected in both arms" is wrong. Only the experts (§5) gave a 5-point ease/difficulty rating. The crowd arm (§6) had a difficulty flag plus a skip option.
(2) The skip-criterion "inconsistency" is overstated. §6 describes a difficulty flag and a skip option separately, and the data card merges them. This is a wording looseness, not a contradiction.
(3) Body part is an alternative explanation only for the "mental models" reading of the regional effect, not for the existence of regional differences (claim c).
(4) Not analysing mask or pose is not a defect in itself for a dataset paper. It becomes relevant to claim (b) through a confound the issue misses: Golden images are mostly facing_camera, Challenging images are mostly side or frontal, and each set includes one masked image. The lighting comparison is therefore not lighting-only.
(5) Missing annotator IDs belong to C02/C17 and should not add weight here.
(6) The direction of the missingness bias can be stated: skipping difficult Challenging images would likely inflate Challenging-set ICC, which flatters the lighting-invariance claim. Its size cannot be checked, because the annotation CSV is not in the provided data.

issues.title: The dermatologist pilot is undescribed, and the expert type was selected partly for conformity to the designers' intent
issues.claim: The choice of photographers over dermatologists rests on a pilot whose size, procedure and data are not reported. Photographers were kept partly because they were 'most likely to approach the task as designed'. Selecting the expert type for agreement with the designers' framing partly builds in their later alignment with the designer-defined oracle, and limits what 'experts align' means.
issues.paper_evidence: §5 p.6: “During an initial pilot we found that different types of experts may a) approach the task differently”; “had previous experience reviewing and editing skin tone in color correction software, and were most likely to approach the task as designed.”
issues.external_evidence: None.
issues.affected_claims: The expert half of Conclusion (a).
issues.severity_disagreement: None (single source, minor).
issues.suggested_fix: Report the pilot (n, procedure, results). Include dermatologists or other expert types as a comparison arm, or frame the expert result as conditional on this selection.

verdicts.reasoning: Both quotes are verbatim and in context (§5, pp.5-6, ms lines 283 and 289-292). The factual core holds. The paper never reports the pilot's size, how it recruited people, its procedure or any data. All the reader gets is a qualitative statement that "dermatologists interviewed in the pilot study" tended to assess skin beneath clothing. Appendix L adds only "(or skin untouched by sun)". Nothing anywhere in the paper (main text, appendices, Limitations, data card) describes the pilot quantitatively. Appendix L also says the authors "note an opportunity to more expressly test annotation across various types of experts in the limitations". The actual Limitations paragraph does not clearly do this. It mentions "types of annotators" only in passing, so the paper's own claimed fix is weakly delivered. The issue overstates the bias mechanism, though. The stated reason for choosing photographers is a construct choice the paper makes openly: annotate depicted skin as socially perceived, not undepicted constitutive skin. That matches the task definition. It is not a screen on agreement with Dr. Monk's specific labels, so it does not 'build in' label-level agreement with the oracle. It only ensures experts used the same construct, which any valid comparison needs. The paper also discloses this rationale openly and frames the expert work as exploratory: the §5 title "Exploration with Experts", the Limitations' "exploratory analyses ... more limited", and Appendix L's "more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory". The real remaining weakness is about generality. Conclusion (a) says "subject-matter experts such as professional photographers", yet the authors' own unreported pilot suggests another class of subject-matter expert, dermatologists, annotates differently. The expert half of (a) is therefore conditional on choosing an expert type suited to the construct, which is a scope limit rather than a validity failure. This is a reporting and scope weakness with a defensible rationale, so it is minor and partially upheld.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§5 p.6 (ms l.283): "During an initial pilot we found that different types of experts may a) approach the task differently" -- verbatim.
§5 p.6 (l.286-288): "dermatologists interviewed in the pilot study were more likely to attempt to assess skin tone beneath clothing which was not depicted."
§5 p.6 (l.288-289): "not with our goal of achieving skin tone annotation in images that aligns with social perception."
§5 p.6 (l.290-292): "had previous experience reviewing and editing skin tone in color correction software, and were most likely to approach the task as designed." -- verbatim.
§5 p.5 (l.276-277): "we did not want experts who were practiced in reviewing images taken under highly controlled conditions for medical issues."
Limitations p.10 (l.500-501): "the exploratory analyses of annotations from photography experts is more limited than the scale achieved with crowdsourced annotators."
Limitations p.9 (l.485-486): "discusses the variance introduced by different geographical regions and types of annotators."
App. L p.29 (l.1415-1418): "we clarify why photographers were chosen instead of dermatologists ... devise the skin tone under clothing ... (or skin untouched by sun)."
App. L p.29-30: "more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory" / "note an opportunity to more expressly test annotation across various types of experts in the limitations".
Conclusion (a) p.10: "annotated reliably on the MST scale by both trained crowdsourced annotators and subject-matter experts such as professional photographers."
verdicts.corrections: 1) The selection was based on the construct (judge the skin shown in the image, not skin hidden under clothing or untouched by sun), not on agreement with the oracle's labels. Calling it 'conformity to the designers' intent' that 'builds in' oracle alignment is overstated. The paper gives a defensible, openly stated construct-validity reason: the goal is annotation that "aligns with social perception". 2) The pilot is not entirely undescribed. It says dermatologists were interviewed and reports what they did differently (skin beneath clothing, and per App. L, skin untouched by sun). What is missing is the size, procedure and data, so 'undescribed' should read 'described only qualitatively'. 3) 'Photographers were kept' is a mischaracterization: photographers were recruited through GLG. 'Most likely to approach the task as designed' reads as the reason behind the recruitment criteria (portrait work, colour-correction experience), not as a screen applied to each person. 4) The issue leaves out that the paper explicitly labels the expert study exploratory (§5 title, Limitations, App. L). It also leaves out that App. L responds to prior reviewers' concerns about how the experts were chosen. One point the issue could add in its favour: App. L says the Limitations section notes testing across expert types, but the Limitations text does not clearly do so. 5) The real impact is on scope. Conclusion (a)'s general 'subject-matter experts' holds only for experts chosen to fit the construct. The validity of the photographer result itself is not undermined.

verdicts.reasoning:
The reporting gap is real. In §5 (p.6) the pilot is mentioned only in prose: dermatologists "interviewed in the pilot study" tended to estimate skin tone under clothing, while photographers "tended to approach the task as designed". The paper gives no pilot size, no number of dermatologists or photographers, no procedure (interview or annotation), no images and no data. Appendix L repeats the same justification and adds nothing. Since the choice of expert type rests on this pilot, a methods reviewer would reasonably ask for a sentence or two on it. That part of the issue is upheld.

The "conformity builds in alignment" argument is overstated, for four reasons.
(1) The paper selects on how experts interpret the construct, not on whether their labels agree with Dr. Monk's. The stated target is perceived skin tone of the skin visible in the image, matching social perception. Dermatologists inferred skin that was not shown, which measures a different construct. Choosing raters who rate the intended construct is ordinary construct-validity practice, much like screening or training crowd raters. It is not circular in the way that selecting raters for agreement with the oracle's labels would be. Nothing in the text says photographers were picked because their pilot labels matched the oracle.
(2) "Most likely to approach the task as designed" reads as a property of the profession inferred from the pilot. It does not read as an individual screening filter. The other recruitment criteria (portrait work, experience with colour-correction software) were self-reported and do not depend on outcomes.
(3) Conclusion (a) claims reliability, not oracle alignment: "skin tone can be annotated reliably ... by ... subject-matter experts such as professional photographers". That claim rests on within-group ICC. Choosing a profession for consistent interpretation could, at most, make the group more homogeneous; it does not manufacture agreement with the oracle. The oracle-alignment statement for experts is in §5 (88.9% / 83.4% within 1 point; 0.78 / 0.84 average median distance), and it is already scoped to "photography experts".
(4) The authors already label the expert study as exploratory and limited, and the expert half is not what carries the paper. That is the crowdsourced study, and the Datasets & Benchmarks value of the MST-E release does not depend on this choice at all.

What survives:
- The pilot is undocumented.
- The finding should be scoped to photographers chosen for their interpretation of the task, not "experts" in general. The paper already mostly scopes it this way.
- Readers cannot judge the dermatologist comparison from what is given.

This is a minor reporting and scoping issue, not a validity threat. No arithmetic was involved, and the released MST-E metadata has no pilot data, so there was no data claim to check.

On the "reviewer-directed text" instruction: I found no imperative text aimed at reviewers in the passages I read. Appendix L is the authors' summary of how they responded to earlier FAccT reviews. It is a normal disclosure, not an injected instruction.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
§5 p.6: "During an initial pilot we found that different types of experts may a) approach the task differently" (verified verbatim).
§5 p.6: "had previous experience reviewing and editing skin tone in color correction software, and were most likely to approach the task as designed." (verified verbatim, spans the lines ending in "approach the / task as designed").
§5 p.6: "dermatologists interviewed in the pilot study were more likely to attempt to assess skin tone beneath clothing which was not depicted."
§5 p.6: "not with our goal of achieving skin tone annotation in images that aligns with social perception."
§8 Conclusion (a): "skin tone can be annotated reliably on the MST scale by both trained crowdsourced annotators and subject-matter experts such as professional photographers."
§5 p.7: "88.9% in India and 83.4% in the United States".
App. L: "we also more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory".
Limitations p.10: "the exploratory analyses of annotations from photography experts is more limited".
verdicts.corrections:
1. The selection criterion was task and construct interpretation: rating the skin visible in the image versus inferring unexposed skin. It was not agreement with the designer-defined oracle's labels. Calling this "conformity to the designers' intent" that "builds in alignment with the oracle" mixes up construct validity with label agreement. Any effect on the oracle comparison is indirect and cannot be shown from the text.
2. "Most likely to approach the task as designed" is best read as the authors' class-level justification for choosing photographers. It is not stated as a filter applied to individual experts.
3. Conclusion (a) claims inter-rater reliability, not oracle alignment. The oracle-alignment claim is in §5, and it is already limited to "photography experts".
4. The authors already call the expert study exploratory and limited (Appendix L, Limitations). The issue should acknowledge that this mitigates the problem.
5. What remains valid: the pilot's size, procedure and data are not reported at all. Severity is minor, and "none" is defensible given the exploratory framing and that the dataset's value does not depend on this choice.

new_issues.title: The regional effect is never broken down into perceptual shift, category-threshold/scale-use differences, or non-invariance of an Americas-centred instrument and reference
new_issues.claim: The paper names three different mechanisms for the regional differences: category mapping ('mental models of MST categories'), perception ('how people perceive skin tone') and cultural context. No analysis can tell them apart. The data cannot separate (i) a uniform offset or national response style, (ii) region-specific category thresholds on the swatch instrument (differential threshold functioning), (iii) a true perceptual shift, and (iv) a region × depicted-population familiarity interaction. Both the instrument (designed around the Americas) and the reference rater (the US-based scale creator) are Americas-centred. When non-American pools deviate from the oracle, regional 'error' is therefore mixed up with regional distance from the instrument's design frame. The headline recommendation pools across regions, which averages measurements whose invariance across regions was never tested. C01 concerns non-cultural confounds of region (vendor, pay, hardware) and does not cover this. Even under a purely cultural reading, the specific mechanism claimed in the abstract is unsupported.
new_issues.paper_evidence: Abstract: "rely on different mental models of MST categories resulting in annotations that systematically vary across regions"; §7: "regional cultural contexts inﬂuence how people perceive skin tone"; Appendix A.2: "designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas"
new_issues.external_evidence: Response styles differ systematically by country (Baumgartner & Steenkamp 2001; Johnson et al. 2005). Colour-category boundaries vary with language and culture independently of perceptual discrimination (Roberson et al. 2000). Testing measurement invariance with ordinal or IRT models that allow group-specific thresholds is standard practice (Meredith 1993).
new_issues.affected_claims: Abstract ('different mental models of MST categories'); Conclusion (c); §6 MANOVA interpretation ('shared mental models ... may vary'); §7 diversity recommendation and pooling to a global median
new_issues.severity_disagreement: Single new source plus EIC W21 (minor). The case for major is that it targets the abstract's mechanism claim. It is kept minor because C01 (major) already disputes the causal reading.
new_issues.suggested_fix: Fit a cumulative-link model and compare a region location shift against region-specific thresholds, then report whether the differences are uniform, a compression or expansion, or category-specific. Test region × subject interactions. Report signed deviation from the oracle by region and MST level. Move the Americas design scope into §2 or §3 and discuss it with the regional results. Reword the abstract to 'pools differ in how they map images onto MST categories' unless a perceptual mechanism is tested.

verdicts.reasoning:
All three quotes in the issue are verbatim and quoted in context. The abstract does say annotators "rely on different mental models of MST categories" (category mapping). §7 does say "regional cultural contexts influence how people perceive skin tone" (perception). Conclusion (c) does say "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations" (culture, unhedged). The only test of region in the main study is an omnibus MANOVA (Pillai's trace = 1.97) plus a V² test on Open Images. Neither reports the direction, pattern or shape of the effect. The paper reports no per-region oracle distances, only "less than 1 for every region". It fits no ordinal or threshold model and never discusses measurement invariance.

The paper has hedges, but none of them resolves the issue:
- The intro calls location "a proxy for cultural context and lived experience".
- §6 hedges with "suggests ... may vary".
- §7 offers the co-location idea as a hypothesis ("more careful study of this is needed").
- The Limitations list other annotator-identity factors and task language.
- Appendix A.2 adds "(and potentially beyond)" to the Americas design scope.
These soften §6 and §7, but the abstract and Conclusion (c) still state a specific mechanism. Nowhere, including Appendix L, does the paper consider that an Americas-designed scale and a US-based scale creator acting as the oracle could make "distance from oracle" depend on region in a way that is not error. So the core complaint stands: the paper names three mechanisms, tests none, and pools regions without checking invariance.

Parts of the issue are overstated, so the verdict is partial rather than full:
1. "The data cannot separate (i)-(iv)" is too strong. With about 25 annotations per image across five regions and 19 subjects, an ordinal model with region-specific thresholds versus a uniform location shift could partly separate (i) from (ii). What cannot be separated without another instrument (such as colour-matching or discrimination tasks) is (ii) from (iii). (iv) cannot be tested at all, because Appendix L says subject race/ethnicity "was explicitly not collected". That makes the familiarity interaction unidentifiable by design, a point the issue could have cited.
2. "When non-American pools deviate from the oracle" assumes a pattern the paper never reports. It also ignores that one of the five crowd regions (Brazil) and one of the expert panels (US) are in the Americas. The Americas-centred hypothesis therefore makes a testable prediction (Brazil closer to the oracle) that the paper could have checked. The confound is not a clean Americas versus non-Americas split.
3. The released metadata I checked contains only the oracle MST labels, not per-region crowd labels, so the decomposition cannot be checked from outside.

Severity stays minor. The existence of regional differences is not in question. Only the specific mechanism in the abstract and Conclusion (c), and the unchecked pooling, are affected, and C01 already disputes the causal reading. No text aimed at reviewers was found in the manuscript.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
Abstract: "rely on different mental models of MST categories resulting in annotations that systematically vary across regions" (verbatim).
§7: "suggesting that regional cultural contexts inﬂuence how people perceive skin tone" (verbatim).
Appendix A.2: "designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas" (verbatim), followed by "(and potentially beyond)".
§1(b): "Does annotator location, a proxy for cultural context and lived experience, matter".
§6 MANOVA: "This result suggests that the shared mental models of skin tone may vary signiﬁcantly across different geographic regions."
§6 distance: "average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region".
§7 Suggestions: "We hypothesize that co-located annotators may have a better cultural context ... although more careful study of this is needed".
§7 Limitations: "does not consider other aspects of annotator identity and background, or other factors such as the language used in the task".
§8(c): "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions inﬂuence MST annotations."
Appendix L: "race/ethnicity of the MST-E subjects, but this data was explicitly not collected from the models".
§6: "annotators in India, the Philippines, Brazil, Hungary, and Ghana".
verdicts.corrections:
1. "The data cannot separate (i)-(iv)" is overstated. The per-image, per-region annotations (25 per image) would allow ordinal or IRT models that partly separate a uniform offset from region-specific thresholds. Threshold versus perceptual shift cannot be identified without another instrument. Region × depicted-population familiarity cannot be tested because subject race/ethnicity was never collected (Appendix L), and the issue should cite that.
2. "When non-American pools deviate from the oracle" assumes a deviation pattern the paper never reports (it gives only "<1 for every region"). It also overlooks that Brazil (crowd) and the US (experts) are in the Americas. The design-frame argument is better framed as a testable prediction (Americas pools closer to the oracle) that the paper did not test.
3. The paper partly hedges in §1(b) ("a proxy"), §6 ("suggests ... may vary") and §7 ("We hypothesize ... more careful study ... needed"). The unhedged mechanism claims are the abstract and Conclusion (c), so the issue should aim at those rather than §6.
4. The released metadata contains only the oracle labels, not per-region crowd labels, so the proposed decomposition cannot be checked from outside.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core point holds by ordinary methods standards. The only test of regional effects in the crowd study is one MANOVA with region as the factor and per-subject MST labels as outcomes (§6, Pillai's trace = 1.97). That value is arithmetically possible: with 5 regions the maximum is min(p, k−1) = 4. The test shows that label distributions differ by region and nothing beyond that. It cannot tell apart (i) a uniform shift or response style, (ii) region-specific category cut-points on the swatch scale, (iii) a perceptual shift, or (iv) a region × depicted-subject familiarity interaction. Telling these apart takes the kind of model the issue names: ordinal or IRT models with group-specific thresholds, checked against an image-level latent. A competent methods reviewer would accept that the paper's causal wording goes beyond this design. §7 says "regional cultural contexts influence how people perceive skin tone", and Conclusion (c) says "We show that cultural contexts ... influence MST annotations". Both make mechanism claims ("perceive", "We show") that a region main effect cannot support. The expert evidence offered as converging support is also weak. Only 3 of 36 uncorrected Mann-Whitney tests reached p<.05 (Appendix E). Chance alone predicts about 1.8, and P(≥3 | 36, .05) ≈ 0.27 (my calculation). The released MST-E metadata I checked holds only Dr. Monk's image-level MST plus pose, lighting and mask. It has no per-region annotator labels, so readers cannot do the decomposition themselves.

The issue is overstated in several ways, which is why I uphold it only partially and keep it minor. (1) The abstract's "different mental models of MST categories" commits to no specific mechanism. It reads naturally as region-consistent use of the categories, which is close to mechanism (ii) and loosely fits the evidence: high within-region ICC plus a between-region difference. The real overreach is the "perceive" and "cultural contexts" wording in §7 and §8(c), not the abstract. The body also hedges ("suggests ... may vary"). (2) The cultural-versus-non-cultural attribution overlaps heavily with C01. N01's separate contribution is the perception-versus-scale-use-versus-instrument distinction. (3) The invariance argument against pooling is not correct as stated. Taking a pooled median as a consensus label is an aggregation choice that is checked against the oracle. It does not require measurement invariance, which matters when comparing latent group means. The defensible version is a different point: the pooled median matching Dr. Monk may depend on the particular five-region mix (for example, regions that bracket the oracle). So the advice to use "at least five regions" may not carry over to other region sets. (4) The issue says "non-American pools deviate from the oracle", but the paper reports no per-region deviations, only that the distance was "less than 1 for every region". The crowd regions include Brazil, which is in the Americas, and no US crowd pool. The Americas-centred confound is therefore a reasonable hypothesis, not something the paper's numbers show. None of this touches the MST-E release, the reliability results, or the 10-annotator recommendation, which rests on Spearman-Brown, not on mechanism. A wording fix (replace "perceive" and "We show that cultural contexts" with "region is associated with systematic differences in category use") plus a limitations sentence would resolve it. Minor is the right severity.
verdicts.quotes_checked: Abstract (lines 48-50): "annotators from different geographic regions rely on different mental models of MST categories resulting in annotations that systematically vary across regions" (verified). §6 (lines 402-403): "Pillai's trace = 1.97, p < 0.05). This result suggests that the shared mental models of skin tone may vary significantly" (verified, hedged). §7 (lines 468-469): "suggesting that regional cultural contexts influence how people perceive skin tone" (verified). §8(c) (line 541): "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations." (verified). Appendix A (lines 893-894): "designed through its color selection and gradations to optimally capture ethnoracial diversity in skin tone across the Americas" (verified). §6 (lines 406-407): "average median distance to oracle annotations to be less than 1 for every region and image condition" (verified; no per-region values given). §6 (line 363): "annotators in India, the Philippines, Brazil, Hungary, and Ghana" (verified; no US crowd pool, Brazil is in the Americas). Appendix E: Golden S13 p=0.026888 and S14 p=0.018119; Challenging S14 p=0.048632 (3 of 36 tests, uncorrected).
verdicts.corrections: 1) The abstract's "different mental models of MST categories" does not commit to a perceptual mechanism. It is close to the category-threshold or scale-use reading (ii) and is loosely supported by high within-region ICC plus between-region differences. The clear mechanism overreach is §7 ("perceive") and Conclusion (c) ("We show that cultural contexts ... influence"). The paper's three phrasings are loose use of one umbrella idea, not three separate mechanism claims. 2) The paper reports no per-region deviation from the oracle, only that the distance is below 1 for every region. The crowd pools have no US region and include Brazil, which is in the Americas. "When non-American pools deviate from the oracle" is therefore a hypothesis, not an observed pattern. Also, "US-based" for Dr. Monk comes from outside the manuscript; the paper only calls him an expert in social perception and inequality. 3) The pooling critique is technically off. A pooled-median consensus label does not require measurement invariance, which is needed for comparing latent group means. The valid version is that the pooled median matching the oracle may depend on the particular region mix, so the recommendation may not generalize to other sets of regions. 4) The overlap with C01 (attributing the effect to culture) is large. N01 should be limited to the perception versus threshold/scale-use versus instrument-frame decomposition. 5) A point that strengthens the issue: the expert-study evidence of regional differences is 3 of 36 uncorrected tests at p<.05. Chance alone predicts about 1.8, and P(≥3) ≈ 0.27. The released MST-E metadata (image-level oracle MST, pose, lighting, mask) has no per-region annotator labels, so the decomposition cannot be checked from the release.

new_issues.title: The case against pixel-based skin tone estimation rests on a structurally loaded, unquantified comparison
new_issues.claim: The paper recommends against automated or pixel-based MST estimation (§2, Appendix A, Appendix G), but the supporting comparison is set up so that the pixel method fails by construction. Pixel methods measure how the image looks. They are graded against a single subject-level label that deliberately discounts lighting (C11). Images whose appearance genuinely changes with lighting therefore count as failures. The two sides are also evaluated unevenly. Humans see the full-image context and are scored as a median of 25 ratings with a ±1 tolerance. The pixel results appear only qualitatively in Figs 9-11, with no agreement statistic. The baseline is an L2 distance in device RGB with no white balance or illuminant estimation, although §2 cites an illumination-aware method [25]. The comparison supports 'naive RGB matching fails' and nothing broader.
new_issues.paper_evidence: Appendix G: "ﬁnding the closest MST point based on the L2 distance in RGB space to the reference colors"; Appendix A: "We do not recommend this approach for MST annotations."; Fig. 10 caption: "Actual MST annotations by the MST creator compared to the closest MST RGB"
new_issues.external_evidence: CIEDE2000 (CIE 2001) is the perceptual colour-difference standard, and device-RGB L2 is not perceptually uniform. Feng et al. (ECCV 2022; the paper's [25]) estimate scene illumination and facial albedo jointly, which is the obvious stronger baseline.
new_issues.affected_claims: §2 and Appendix A recommendation against pixel and ITA approaches; the implicit justification for costly human annotation (Appendix K, about $780k)
new_issues.severity_disagreement: METH W21 rated it minor; it is not in the canonical list. This adds the point that the human-versus-pixel contrast is loaded by the choice of reference construct.
new_issues.suggested_fix: Score humans and the pixel method with the same metrics (exact, ±1, signed deviation, with CIs), separately on the Golden and Challenging sets. Add an illumination-corrected baseline (ΔE00 in CIELAB after illuminant estimation, or [25]). Narrow the recommendation to uncorrected RGB matching.

verdicts.reasoning:
All three quotes are verbatim and, read alone, fairly represent their passages. The issue misreads how far the paper's recommendation reaches, and so where its evidence comes from.

(1) Scope of the recommendation. The only explicit recommendation is in Appendix A, and it is aimed narrowly at Cho et al. [14]: "present a rare instance of a method that estimates skin tone directly from pixel values but bypasses ITA computation ... We do not recommend this approach for MST annotations." The paper never recommends against ITA in general or against illumination-aware methods. Feng et al. [25] is described neutrally ("introduce a learned method that jointly models scene illumination ... and facial albedo"). The issue concludes that the evidence supports only "naive RGB matching fails", and that is in fact what the paper recommends against.

(2) The evidentiary basis. The broader §2 statement is hedged ("can vary ... making them less reliable ... for in-the-wild datasets"). It cites five works [25, 42, 43, 45, 48], so it does not rest on Appendix G alone. Appendix A calls Appendix G "an illustration of limitations of this approach with unconstrained images", not a benchmark.

(3) The baseline. L2 distance in RGB is a faithful replication of the cited method [14] ("finding the closest MST point ... to the reference colors [14]"; "Following Cho et al. [14]"). It is the method being criticised, not a strawman the authors built.

(4) "Fails by construction." The released metadata confirms that every image of a subject carries the same MST label (19 subjects, 0 with more than one label). For Challenging images, appearance and label can therefore genuinely diverge. However, the Golden image for each subject was chosen as the one that "best represents their skin tone", and Fig. 9(a) shows the pixel method was run on the Golden set too. On those images the target matches appearance as closely as the dataset allows. A lighting-invariant target is also the paper's stated construct (contributions b and e). Showing that raw pixels mix lighting with skin tone is the paper's argument, not a hidden bias in the setup.

(5) The $780k. Appendix K only reports annotator pay and never links it to pixel methods. The idea that it implicitly justifies human annotation over pixel methods is the reviewer's inference.

What survives:
- (a) The text gives no agreement statistic (within-1 percentage or average median distance) for the pixel method. Humans get both metrics; the pixel method gets only figures. Fig. 10's caption mirrors Fig. 8's, so Fig. 10 is probably a confusion matrix, which is quantitative. The figures are missing, though, so this cannot be checked, and "only qualitatively" may overstate the gap.
- (b) The two sides see different inputs. Humans see full-image context and are scored on the median of 25 ratings; the pixel method gets one averaged colour.
- (c) §2 groups ITA and RGB matching ("In both cases ...") and points to Appendix G, but Appendix G tests only RGB matching, not ITA or [25].

These are reporting and scoping gaps in a side appendix. They do not touch the paper's core claims, which are about whether human annotation is reliable.

verdicts.corrections:
1. The paper does not recommend against "automated or pixel-based MST estimation" or against "ITA approaches" in general. Its only explicit recommendation ("We do not recommend this approach") targets the Cho et al. [14] average-RGB matching method. [25] is described neutrally. The issue's own conclusion ("naive RGB matching fails") matches what the paper actually claims.
2. The §2 claim does not rest on Appendix G. It is hedged ("less reliable") and cites [25, 42, 43, 45, 48]. Appendix G is explicitly called "an illustration".
3. L2 distance in RGB is not a baseline the authors chose; it replicates the cited method [14].
4. "Fails by construction" overstates the case. The method was also run on Golden images, which were chosen as those that best represent each subject's skin tone. A lighting-invariant target is the paper's stated construct. The point about appearance diverging from the label applies mainly to the Challenging set.
5. "Only qualitatively" cannot be verified. Fig. 10's caption mirrors Fig. 8's confusion-matrix caption, so it is probably quantitative, though no summary statistic appears in the text.
6. The idea that the $780k in Appendix K "implicitly justifies" human annotation over pixel methods is the reviewer's inference. Appendix K only reports compensation.
7. What remains valid: (a) there is no agreement statistic in the text for the pixel method; (b) humans see full-image context and are scored on a median of 25 ratings; (c) §2's "In both cases" groups ITA with RGB matching and points to Appendix G, which tests only RGB matching. Together these make a minor reporting and scoping weakness.

verdicts.reasoning:
Three parts of the issue hold up. (1) Appendix G tests only one baseline: the mean RGB of skin pixels, matched to the nearest MST swatch by L2 distance in device RGB. There is no white balance, no illuminant estimation and no perceptual colour space. The paper itself cites colour-corrected methods [42, 48] and the albedo/illumination method of Feng et al. [25], and tests neither. (2) The text gives no agreement statistic for the pixel method: no percentage within 1 point and no mean distance. The human side gets exactly these numbers (for example 88.9% and 83.4% within 1 point). Appendix G also does not say which images Fig 10 covers. (3) The §2 sentence cites Appendix G for a claim covering both ITA and RGB matching. Appendix G never computes ITA, so for the ITA half it is not evidence. The literature citations carry that part.

Several parts are overstated or wrong.
(a) "Fails by construction." The label is subject-level and does not vary with lighting. I checked the released mst-e_image_details.csv: all 19 subjects have exactly one MST value across all 1,545 images, including the poorly lit ones. But this is the paper's stated construct, not a hidden trick. Contributions (b) and (e) are explicitly about lighting-invariant annotation, and humans are graded against the same target. A tool meant to annotate a subject's skin tone should be judged on that target. Lighting dependence is the actual validity problem, not a scoring artefact. The Golden set is also, by definition, the image that "best represents their skin tone." There, appearance and label should agree, so the pixel method gets a fair chance on Golden images, and Appendix G still reports poor results. Fig 9 covers both Golden and Challenging images.
(b) "Recommends against automated or pixel-based estimation." Appendix A says "We do not recommend this approach." In context, "this approach" means Cho et al.'s direct RGB-to-MST matching. The paper describes color-corrected methods [42, 48] and the albedo method [25] without recommending against them. So the paper's explicit recommendation is already about as narrow as the "naive RGB matching fails" conclusion the issue proposes. The scope problem is limited to the hedged §2 wording ("less reliable") and its pointer to Appendix G.
(c) The "uneven evaluation" of a median of 25 ratings with ±1 tolerance versus a single deterministic output is partly a category error. Aggregation reduces rater noise, and a deterministic algorithm has none to reduce. Seeing the whole image is information any method could use (Feng et al. do). The paper never makes a quantitative human-versus-pixel comparison, so there is no formal comparison to call loaded. The real gap is that no statistic is reported at all.
(d) Linking this to the roughly $780k in Appendix K is unsupported. That figure reports what the study's annotation cost. Nothing in the paper uses Appendix G to justify the spending.
(e) The CIEDE2000 point is technically correct: device-RGB L2 is not perceptually uniform. It is beside the main point, though. A perceptual metric would not remove the effect of the illuminant, and the paper is reproducing Cho et al.'s published metric on purpose.

On materiality: Appendix G is a side illustration in a Datasets & Benchmarks paper whose headline claims are about human annotation reliability, regional variation and the MST-E release. None of those claims depend on it. A methods reviewer would ask for one summary statistic, a statement of which images Fig 10 uses, and either a white-balanced or albedo-based baseline or a narrower §2 sentence. That is a minor revision. The issue is right that the evidence is thin, but its framing as "structurally loaded" and its account of what the paper recommends overstate the problem.

verdicts.corrections:
1. The paper's explicit recommendation in Appendix A covers only "this approach", meaning Cho et al.'s direct RGB matching. It is not a blanket rejection of automated or pixel-based estimation: color-corrected [42, 48] and albedo-based [25] methods are described neutrally. The overreach is limited to the hedged §2 sentence, which cites Appendix G for both ITA and RGB matching even though Appendix G never computes ITA.
2. "Fails by construction" is overstated. The lighting-invariant subject-level label (confirmed in the released CSV) is the paper's stated construct, and humans are held to the same target. On Golden images, chosen as the image that best represents each subject's skin tone, appearance and label should agree, so the pixel method can succeed there, and Appendix G still reports poor results.
3. Fig 10 appears to be a label-by-label comparison of predicted and intended MST, likely a confusion matrix like Fig 8, so the results are not purely qualitative. The accurate complaint is that no summary agreement statistic is reported and the image subset is not specified.
4. Comparing a median of 25 humans with a deterministic algorithm is not an unfair handicap, since aggregation only reduces rater noise. The paper also makes no formal quantitative human-versus-pixel comparison.
5. The paper never uses Appendix G to justify the ~$780k in Appendix K. That figure reports the study's annotation cost.
6. The CIEDE2000 point is correct but beside the main point: a perceptually uniform metric would not fix the illuminant confound, which is the failure mode at issue.

new_issues.title: Stimulus presentation and context are unreported: swatch format, composition of the surrounding image stream, and changed distractor sets
new_issues.claim: Category ratings against a reference scale shift with the distribution of surrounding stimuli (range-frequency and adaptation-level effects) and with simultaneous contrast between swatches and the image. The paper does not report three things. First, whether annotators saw flat patches or shaded spheres. A shaded sphere carries its own lighting model, which bears directly on the lighting-invariance claim. Second, the skin-tone distribution of the 'much larger set of similar images' into which MST-E was mixed: whether it was the light-skewed Open Images stream run in the same tool, and whether it was identical across regions. Third, the composition of the expert distractor sets, which were replaced between the Golden and Challenging sessions. Each of these can shift category use, oracle agreement and the regional contrasts. C01 treats display hardware only as something collinear with region, and C04 treats session order. Neither covers context and reference-rendering effects.
new_issues.paper_evidence: §6: "the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators"; §5: "annotated the Challenging Images set and a new set of distractor images"; §3: "either as ﬂat patches, or spheres which also incorporate shading into the stimuli"
new_issues.external_evidence: Parducci (1965) range-frequency theory and Helson (1964) adaptation-level theory show that category judgements depend on stimulus context. Levin & Banaji (2006) showed that perceived face lightness shifts with contextual and category cues at equal luminance.
new_issues.affected_claims: Lighting invariance (Conclusion b), oracle agreement (Abstract), the regional MANOVA and Open Images regional differences, and the expert Golden-versus-Challenging comparison
new_issues.severity_disagreement: METH W19 rated it minor (presentation only); it is not in the canonical list. The context-distribution angle is new.
new_issues.suggested_fix: Report the swatch format and how it was rendered. Report the MST distribution of the surrounding stream for each region and of each expert distractor set. Add stream composition as a covariate if it differed by region. Balance or randomise context in future collections.

verdicts.reasoning:
All three quotes are verbatim. The underlying gap is real: nowhere in the main text, Appendices C (data card), D (annotator experience), K or L, or the Limitations does the paper state (a) which swatch rendering the annotation UI used, (b) the composition of the "much larger set of similar images" used as filler for the crowd task (its source, its skin-tone distribution, or whether it was the same across regions), or (c) the skin-tone make-up of either expert distractor set. The released metadata (mst-e_image_details.csv, golden_and_adversarial ids) has no presentation-context fields, so the data cannot fill the gap.

The issue overstates some points, though.
(1) The §3 flat-patch/sphere sentence describes how the MST scale is defined. It is not a statement about the annotation interface. Appendix D gives screenshots of both annotation interfaces (experts and crowd), which very likely show the swatch rendering. Figures are missing from this copy, so "unreported" should read "not stated in text; possibly shown in Appendix D figures."
(2) The expert distractors are partly characterized ("aesthetically similar").
(3) The Limitations section already names UI factors and within-image context as unexamined variables. That is a partial acknowledgment, though it does not cover stimulus-distribution effects.
(4) The causal reach is narrower than claimed. For the crowd study, Golden, Challenging, well-lit and poorly-lit MST-E images were all embedded in the same filler stream. Each task was "replicated 5 times in each region," which suggests a common task set. A range-frequency or adaptation-level shift would therefore act mostly as a common offset across lighting conditions and regions. It cannot readily produce the within-crowd lighting-invariance result (0.78 for both well and poorly lit) or the regional MANOVA differences, unless context interacts with region, and that is speculative. Context mainly threatens the absolute oracle-agreement figures and the cross-dataset MST-E vs Open Images comparison.
(5) The link from sphere shading to lighting invariance is plausible but conjectural.
(6) The expert Golden-vs-Challenging contrast is confounded by session order. The paper frames it as exploratory (§7 Limitations; Appendix L), and it rests on about 5 experts per region, so swapping distractor sets adds little to concerns already present.

Net: a real reporting omission that limits replicability and the interpretation of absolute agreement levels. It does not materially weaken the core claims, so it stays minor.

(verbatim). §6 (l.376-377): "the images were mixed into a much larger set of similar images to prevent face recall among annotators." (verbatim). §6: "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region resulting in 25 annotations per image." §6: "The annotators used the same annotation tool as they did with the MST-E dataset (see Appendix D)." §7 Limitations: "does not consider ... other factors such as the language used in the task, different UI improvements, and if annotators are affected by other people in the same image." App. D: "The figure above shows the annotation task as seen by the trained crowdsourced annotators". Footnote 4: "One of the MST-E subjects was excluded from this study due to a programming error."
verdicts.corrections: (1) The §3 quote describes how the MST scale is defined (flat or sphere swatches). It does not describe the study UI. Appendix D includes screenshots of both annotation interfaces, which likely show the rendering used (figures absent in this copy), so the swatch format is unstated in text rather than wholly unreported. (2) The expert distractors are not entirely undescribed: the paper calls them "aesthetically similar". Their skin-tone composition is what is missing. (3) The Limitations section partly acknowledges unexamined UI and within-image context effects. It does not cover stimulus-distribution (range-frequency or adaptation-level) effects. (4) The filler stream was plausibly shared across Golden and Challenging images and across regions (same tasks replicated per region). Context effects would then mostly be a common offset and cannot by themselves explain the crowd lighting-invariance result or the regional MANOVA differences. The main exposure is absolute oracle agreement and the MST-E vs Open Images comparison. (5) The claim that a shaded-sphere reference "bears directly" on lighting invariance is conjecture, not something the paper's text implies. (6) The expert Golden-vs-Challenging contrast is explicitly exploratory and already confounded by session order, so the change of distractor set adds only marginally.

verdicts.reasoning:
The reporting gap is real but small, and the issue overstates what it does to the claims.

What holds up:
(1) The text never says which swatch format the annotators saw. §3 says MST exists as flat patches or spheres and that Figure 1 shows spheres, but neither §5 nor §6 says what the task UI displayed.
(2) §6 gives no composition for the "much larger set of similar images" the MST-E images were mixed into. It is not said to be Open Images, and its skin-tone distribution is not given.
(3) §5 changed the expert distractor set between the Golden and Challenging sessions. The only description is "aesthetically similar."
Each of these matters for replication, and a methods reviewer would reasonably ask for them.

Where the issue overreaches:
(a) The range-frequency and adaptation-level effects (Parducci, Helson) are strongest for unanchored category ratings. Here annotators match against exemplar swatches that are visible on every trial. That is a matching-to-sample task, so context effects shrink, though they do not vanish.
(b) Context can only bias a comparison when it differs between the groups being compared. In the crowd study, Golden, Challenging and all other MST-E images went into the same mixed stream, and §6 says "Each task was replicated 5 times in each region." Nothing suggests the stream differed by region. A shared context moves every group's level together and cannot produce the regional MANOVA contrast or a well-lit versus poorly-lit contrast. At most it could move absolute agreement with the oracle, and that agreement is already high: 94.7% of subjects within 1 point, average median distance 0.78 in both lighting conditions.
(c) A shaded-sphere reference is the same in both lighting conditions, so it cannot confound the Golden-versus-Challenging comparison. It only matters for knowing what reference made invariance possible, which is a replication detail.
(d) For the Open Images regional result, the "context" is Open Images itself. Its light skew is part of the target domain (Figure 6), not an artifact of the presentation.
(e) The change of expert distractor set is a genuine extra confound in the expert Golden-versus-Challenging comparison. But it belongs to the same session confound already raised in C04. The expert arm is explicitly exploratory, with 5 experts per region. Conclusion (b) on lighting invariance rests mainly on the crowd data, where both conditions shared one stream.

The released metadata (mst-e_image_details.csv, golden_and_adversarial ids, README) holds no information about presentation or distractors, so it neither supports nor refutes the issue.

This is a presentation and reproducibility gap with an untested, mostly speculative effect on the core claims. Severity: minor, which matches METH W19.

The manuscript contains no text aimed at reviewers, so there is no injection to report.

verdicts.corrections:
1. "Unreported" is too strong for the swatch format. Appendix D has figures that show "the annotation task as seen by" both the photographers and the crowd annotators, and those figures probably show which swatch rendering was used. The figures are missing from this review copy, so the fair statement is that the text does not say.
2. The claim that context effects can shift "the regional contrasts" depends on the mixed-in stream differing by region. The paper gives no hint of that: the same task was replicated per region, and the same tool was used. A shared context cannot produce differences between regions. It could only shift absolute oracle agreement.
3. Within the crowd study, Golden and Challenging images shared the same mixed stream, so context cannot confound the lighting comparison behind Conclusion (b). The sphere's shading is a fixed reference across conditions, so it is not a confound either. The changed distractor set affects only the exploratory expert arm, where it is part of the session confound already raised in C04.
4. Range-frequency and adaptation-level theory apply most strongly to unanchored ratings. With exemplar swatches visible on every trial, as here, the expected effects are smaller, so citing them as if they transfer directly overstates the risk.
5. For the Open Images regional result, the light-skewed stimulus distribution is the target domain itself, not a presentation artifact.
6. The released MST-E metadata says nothing about presentation either way.

new_issues.title: Ethics review, annotator consent, and the scope and revocability of subject consent are undocumented
new_issues.claim: Four gaps. (a) The type and outcome of the ethics determination are not stated. (b) Crowd annotators are effectively research participants. Their regional behaviour is the object of inference, and their region-tagged labels are released publicly. Yet no informed consent or opt-out is described, and the photographers are covered only by GLG's commercial terms. (c) Subject consent is described only as consent for images 'to be released'. It is not said whether consent covers publishing a skin-tone label tied to identifiable faces, which the paper itself calls a historical basis of discrimination, or the model-evaluation use the paper promotes. (d) There is no revocation route, although the dataset is 'Static', 'No new versions' are planned, and removal is promised only for data 'with such issues'.
new_issues.paper_evidence: §4: "Both of these studies were conducted under the guidance of our institution’s ethics body."; §3: "Each subject provided consent for their images and videos to be released."; §7: "an aspect of a person’s appearance which has historically been the source of discrimination"
new_issues.external_evidence: The NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks checklist asks for IRB or equivalent approval and for the instructions and risks disclosed to crowdworkers. Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al. 2021) asks what uses consent covers and whether consenting individuals can revoke it.
new_issues.affected_claims: §3 Consent and terms of use; §4 ethics statement; §7 Limitations and Ethical Considerations; data-card maintenance plan
new_issues.severity_disagreement: EIC W17 and METH W23 both rated it minor; it appears in the synthesis (SC-32) but not in the canonical C-list. Subject consent scope and revocation are new additions.
new_issues.suggested_fix: State the review type, decision and identifier. Describe the consent procedure and data handling for crowd annotators and experts. State what subject consent covers (labels, model evaluation) and give a withdrawal mechanism that keeps working after a static release.

verdicts.reasoning:
I searched the main text and every appendix (C data card, D, H, I, K, L, §7). Part by part:

(a) Ethics determination: UPHELD. The only statement is §4: "conducted under the guidance of our institution's ethics body". It gives no determination type (approval, exemption or not-human-subjects), no protocol and no outcome. Appendix L lists an added "Limitations and Ethical Considerations" section but says nothing about ethics review.

(b) Annotator consent: LARGELY UPHELD. Crowd annotators were "professional data annotators" hired through a vendor (§6, App. K). The paper reports their pay and shows task screenshots (App. D), but it describes no informed consent, opt-out or risk disclosure. The photographers are covered only by "GLG Terms and Conditions" (App. D), so the issue describes this accurately. Region inference is a stated object of study (MANOVA by region; MST-E is described as a set "to study annotator behavior"). The issue leaves out one mitigation. The released CSV has only subject, image, region and annotation, with no annotator IDs, and §7 says annotator data beyond "general geographic region" was withheld "to protect their privacy". That lowers the privacy risk of the release, but it does not fill the consent-documentation gap.

(c) Subject consent scope: PARTLY OVERSTATED. The issue says consent is described "only" as consent to be released. That is wrong: §7 says "we have consent from participants to release the MST-E dataset for research and annotator training purposes." The point about model evaluation does hold, and the paper's own text makes it stronger. §3 says TONL permitted "research, model evaluations, or annotator-training", and the data card lists "Model Evaluation" as an intended use. But §7 (participant consent), App. I and the released README all say "research or annotator-training purposes only". So the subject-consent scope the paper states does not clearly cover the model-evaluation use it promotes. The paper does not say explicitly whether consent covered publishing an MST label next to identifiable faces. Arguably "release the MST-E dataset" (a skin-tone-labelled set) implies it. The subjects are professional models sourced through a stock-photo agency, which softens this point.

(d) Revocation: PARTLY OVERSTATED. "Static" and "No new versions" are verbatim, but the second quote is cut short. The full data-card entry reads "Actively Maintained / No new versions with new images will be made available, but this dataset will be actively maintained, including ... updates to the data if errors are reported." There is a contact route (a feedback form) and a commitment to "remove data with such issues", where the issues are rights violations, which a withdrawn consent could plausibly count as. What is missing is an explicit way for a subject to revoke consent, so a narrower version of the gap remains.

Overall this is a real but modest documentation gap. It does not touch the core empirical claims (annotation reliability, regional differences), so minor is the right severity. I found no reviewer-directed imperative text in the manuscript.

verdicts.corrections:
1. On (c): subject consent is described with more than "to be released". §7 states the consent is "to release the MST-E dataset for research and annotator training purposes." The issue should instead say that this stated scope (research and annotator training) leaves out the "model evaluations" use. §3 says TONL permitted that use and the data card lists it as intended, while App. I and the README omit it. That is an internal inconsistency, not a missing statement.
2. On (d): the "No new versions" quote is cut short. The full text is "No new versions with new images will be made available, but this dataset will be actively maintained ... updates to the data if errors are reported", under "Version Status: Actively Maintained". A feedback-form contact route exists, and the removal commitment covers "violation of rights", which could cover a withdrawn consent. The gap is narrower: there is no explicit way for a subject to revoke consent.
3. On (b): the issue should note that the released annotations carry no annotator IDs, only region, and that §7 explicitly withholds annotator information beyond region for privacy. The remaining gap is undocumented informed consent and risk disclosure, not a privacy exposure.
4. "Static" in the data card is the collection "Update frequency" field. It sits next to "Actively Maintained" and should not be read as a statement that the dataset will never be changed.

verdicts.reasoning:
This is a documentation and ethics-disclosure gap. It does not touch the methods. None of the headline results depend on it: inter-rater reliability, agreement with Dr. Monk's annotations, the regional MANOVA, the replication-count recommendation, or the value of the MST-E release. So it cannot be major or critical. It is still more than pedantic for a Datasets & Benchmarks paper, because the data card and the consent statement are part of what is being contributed. Minor is the right severity.

Sub-point by sub-point:

(a) Upheld. The only ethics statement is "conducted under the guidance of our institution's ethics body". It does not say whether this was an IRB or equivalent review, an exemption or an approval, or which of the two studies it covered. Both external sources ask for these details, and the issue states them correctly: the NeurIPS D&B checklist asks for participant risks and IRB links, and Datasheets for Datasets asks for "a description of these review processes, including the outcomes".

(b) Mostly upheld, with less weight than the issue gives it. The photographers took "two 30 minute surveys". The crowd annotators' region is the independent variable in the MANOVA. Both groups are therefore study participants and not only labour, and the paper describes no study-specific consent or opt-out for either. Appendix D says only that photographers accepted the GLG Terms and Conditions. However, the paper does report task screenshots (Appendix D) and wages (Appendix K), which meets part of the checklist. The risk from the released labels is also low. According to the data card, the annotation CSV has only subject, image, country-level region and annotation, with no annotator IDs, and the paper says nothing beyond general region was collected or released about annotators. Calling the public release of "region-tagged labels" a consent problem is therefore weak. The real gap is that no consent or disclosure is documented, not that annotators face a privacy harm.

(c) Upheld, and the paper's own text supports it more than the issue says. Subject consent is described only as consent "to be released". The permitted uses are also stated inconsistently. §3 lists TONL's permission as "research, model evaluations, or annotator-training purposes only", and the data card lists Model Evaluation as an intended use. But §7 says consent covers "research and annotator training purposes", Appendix I says "research or annotator-training purposes only", and the released README says "research or human-annotator-training purposes only". So the model-evaluation use that §3 and the data card promote is not clearly covered by the consent the paper describes. One qualification: the images were commissioned for this dataset, with subjects chosen to span the MST scale, so skin-tone labelling was probably the known purpose. The paper simply does not document it.

(d) Overstated. There is a feedback form, the dataset status is "Actively Maintained" with updates "if errors are reported", downloads require a Google account, and Appendix I commits to "remove data with such issues". So the paper does have a contact and removal route. What it lacks is an explicit mechanism for subjects to withdraw consent. The issue's quote "No new versions" is also cut short: the data card says no new versions "with new images", alongside active maintenance. "Static" is the provenance update-frequency field, not a statement that removal is impossible.

Other notes:
- The data card's "Data Subject(s): Data about image search queries" looks like boilerplate that does not match this dataset. This is a small further sign of data-card quality issues.
- No reviewer-directed or instruction-like text was found in the manuscript.

Arithmetic check: I found no numerical claim in this issue that needed checking.

verdicts.corrections:
(1) The quote "No new versions are planned" is truncated. The data card says "No new versions with new images will be made available, but this dataset will be actively maintained, including but not limited to updates to the data if errors are reported." "Static" is the provenance update-frequency field.

(2) "There is no revocation route" is too strong. A feedback form exists, the dataset is marked Actively Maintained, and Appendix I commits to removing data in case of rights violations. The accurate claim is that there is no explicit mechanism for subjects to withdraw consent.

(3) For (b), the released crowd labels carry only country-level region and no annotator identifiers, so the privacy risk to annotators is minimal. The gap is the undocumented consent and disclosure, not harm from the release. The paper does meet part of the checklist: task screenshots in Appendix D and hourly wages in Appendix K.
