The permitted uses are inconsistent across the paper. §3 and the data card include model evaluation. §7, Appendix I and the released README limit use to research and annotator training. So the model-evaluation use the paper promotes is not clearly within the consent it describes.

(5) The severity rationale should state that none of the headline empirical claims depend on this issue.

new_issues.title: The design claim that MST-E helps annotators 'decouple skin tone from race' cannot be verified, cannot be delivered with this subject set, and is never tested
new_issues.claim: §3 justifies the subject mix as helping annotators decouple skin tone from race, and §7 and Conclusion (e) recommend MST-E for annotator training. The authors cite evidence that inferred race shifts perceived skin tone. Three problems. Subject ethnicity was explicitly not collected, so neither the authors nor users can confirm that ethnicity varies within any MST level. With one subject at MST7 and at MST10, and at most three at any level, little or no within-level ethnic contrast can exist. No analysis checks whether annotators' deviations from the oracle track perceived ethnicity. The regional pattern on Subject 14 is equally consistent with a race-inference or familiarity effect. C10 and C18 address small n for category-level and general claims. This issue concerns a specific purpose claim the release is built on.
new_issues.paper_evidence: §3: "include individuals of different ethnicities and gender identities to help human annotators decouple the concept of skin tone from race"; Appendix L: "this data was explicitly not collected from the models"; §1: "the inferred race/ethnicity of an individual [30] can affect the perception of skin tone"
new_issues.external_evidence: Levin & Banaji (2006, JEP: General) showed that faces with race-typed features are perceived as lighter or darker at identical luminance. Testing for decoupling therefore needs contrasts of ethnicity within a tone level.
new_issues.affected_claims: §3 dataset design rationale; §7 'Train annotators ... MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training'; Conclusion (e)
new_issues.severity_disagreement: Single source. It overlaps C10, C12 and C18 in subject count but is aimed at the decoupling purpose claim.
new_issues.suggested_fix: Remove or qualify the decoupling claim. If it is kept, collect perceived-ethnicity labels (or self-identification with consent), test whether residuals against the oracle vary by perceived group within MST level and by region, and in future versions add several ethnicities per MST level.

verdicts.reasoning:
The three quotes are verbatim and in context. The decoupling rationale appears exactly once, as a design-intent sentence in §3. The paper never tests it, and nothing in the main text, the Limitations section, the Appendix C data card or Appendix L qualifies it. Appendix L confirms that race/ethnicity "was explicitly not collected from the models." The Limitations section says only that the authors "chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about the subjects." So the core charge stands: the claim is asserted, cannot be checked against released metadata, and is not evaluated. I counted subjects per level in the released metadata (mst-e_image_details.csv, unique MST per subject): MST1=2, MST2=3, MST3=2, MST4=2, MST5=2, MST6=2, MST7=1, MST8=2, MST9=2, MST10=1. That confirms one subject each at MST7 and MST10 and at most three at any level.

The issue overreaches in three places:
(1) §7 and Conclusion (e) do not rest on the decoupling claim. The §7 bullet recommends training "across the full MST spectrum in a variety of conditions." Conclusion (e) is about invariance "to lighting conditions." The data card's motivating factors list MST coverage, lighting invariance and fairness research, not race decoupling. Listing these as affected claims inflates the issue's scope.
(2) "Cannot be delivered with this subject set" is too strong. Eight of ten levels have two or three subjects, so some within-level contrast is possible. Adjacent-level pairs of differing appearance could also serve a training purpose. The real problem is that the contrast cannot be verified, not that it is impossible.
(3) Saying the Subject 14 regional pattern is "equally consistent" with race inference is speculative. The paper already presents the expert result only as "suggestive evidence" and hedges its cultural-context explanation ("more careful study of this is needed"). This is an alternative explanation the paper does not rule out. It is not a misreading.

Because the decoupling claim is one design-rationale sentence and no core empirical claim depends on it, the severity is minor. The paper does not address it, so the issue is partially upheld rather than refuted.
verdicts.quotes_checked: §3 (l.215-216): "include individuals of different ethnicities and gender identities to help human annotators decouple the concept of skin tone from race" (verbatim). §1 (l.98-99): "the inferred race/ethnicity of an individual [30] can affect the perception of skin tone" (verbatim). Appendix L (l.1446-1448): "demographic details like race/ethnicity of the MST-E subjects, but this data was explicitly not collected from the models" (verbatim). Limitations (l.511-512): "We chose not to collect or release other sensitive information about the subjects of the dataset". §7 (l.530-531): "Train annotators with examples of individuals across the full MST spectrum in a variety of conditions. The MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training." Conclusion (e) (l.545-546): "help practitioners train annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions". §5 (l.344-345): "provide suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation". Appendix C data card (l.1095-1112): the motivating factors are MST span, MST-scale training, lighting invariance and fairness research. Race decoupling is not listed.
verdicts.corrections:
1. The affected-claims list is overstated. §7's training recommendation and Conclusion (e) do not use the decoupling rationale: §7 is about MST-spectrum coverage and capture conditions, and (e) is about lighting invariance. The decoupling claim appears only in §3, so only the §3 design rationale is directly affected.
2. "Cannot be delivered" is too strong. The released metadata shows two subjects at 7 of the levels and three at MST2. Only MST7 and MST10 have one subject. Some within-level ethnic contrast is possible but cannot be verified, because ethnicity was not collected.
3. "Equally consistent" for Subject 14 is an unproven alternative explanation, not a demonstrated equivalence. The paper already labels the expert regional finding "suggestive."
4. Saying the release is "built on" the decoupling purpose overstates it. The paper's stated goal for the dataset (§3, l.209-210) is consistent annotation across capture conditions, and decoupling is a secondary rationale.

verdicts.reasoning:
The issue's factual core holds. §3 gives the design rationale that varying ethnicity helps annotators separate skin tone from race. Appendix L says race/ethnicity was "explicitly not collected", and the Limitations section confirms that no sensitive subject information was collected. So the claim of ethnic diversity in §3 is an assertion that users cannot check. No analysis in the paper relates annotator deviations to the subjects' perceived race or ethnicity. I checked the subject-per-level counts in the released mst-e_image_details.csv: MST1 has 2, MST2 3, MST3 2, MST4 2, MST5 2, MST6 2, MST7 1, MST8 2, MST9 2 and MST10 1, for a total of 19. The issue's arithmetic is correct: one subject at MST7 and at MST10, and at most three at any level.

Several parts of the issue are overstated:
(1) Misattribution. §7 recommends training with "examples of individuals across the full MST spectrum in a variety of conditions". Conclusion (e) recommends training annotators "to be invariant to lighting conditions". Neither one repeats the race-decoupling purpose, so the purpose claim appears once, as a single sentence of design intent in §3. It is not a headline or tested contribution, and none of the paper's five contributions (a–e) depends on it.
(2) "Cannot be delivered with this subject set" contradicts the issue's own premise. If ethnicity is unknown, the reviewer cannot say there is no ethnic contrast within a level either. Eight of the ten levels have two or three subjects, so contrast within a level is possible there. It is ruled out only at MST7 and MST10. Decoupling can also be shown across levels, by showing people a viewer would place in the same race category at different MST levels. That needs no contrast within a level.
(3) "Never tested" is true, but the paper never claims it was tested. It is a stated design goal of a dataset release. A Datasets & Benchmarks reviewer would ask for softer wording, or for an aggregate description of the subjects' perceived diversity in the data card. That reviewer would not treat the point as a methodological flaw.
(4) The alternative explanation for Subject 14 is speculative. If annotators in different regions infer race differently, that is one route by which cultural context could work, not a separate confound. The paper also presents the expert result only as "suggestive evidence".

What remains valid is a documentation and wording problem in a dataset paper: a purpose claim about race and ethnicity that is not substantiated, made about subjects whose ethnicity was not recorded. Minor is the right severity, at the low end. It does not weaken any core claim or the value of the release.

The MST-E dataset can be used to perform this training." | Conclusion (e) (l.545-546): "release the MST-E dataset to help practitioners train annotators to be invariant to lighting conditions" | §5 (l.343-344): "provide suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation"
verdicts.corrections:
1. §7 and Conclusion (e) do not recommend MST-E for race decoupling. They recommend it for training across the MST spectrum and for invariance to lighting. Only one sentence, in §3, makes the decoupling claim, so it should not be listed among the "affected claims" as if it ran through the paper.
2. "Cannot be delivered" and "little or no within-level ethnic contrast can exist" are overstated and contradict the issue's own point that ethnicity is unknown. The released metadata shows 2 or 3 subjects at 8 of the 10 levels. Contrast within a level is impossible only at MST7 and MST10, where there is one subject each. Decoupling can also be taught by showing people of one perceived race at different MST levels.
3. "Never tested" is accurate, but the paper never claims to have tested this. It is design intent, not an empirical claim.
4. The race-inference explanation for Subject 14 is speculation, and it is not a separate confound: race inference that differs by region would be one way cultural context works. The paper already frames the Subject 14 result as only suggestive.
5. The counts in the issue are correct: one subject each at MST7 and MST10, and a maximum of 3, at MST2.

new_issues.title: The crowd and Open Images results are framed as confirmatory hypothesis tests, but the hypotheses were not pre-specified and the exploratory framing was added after the fact
new_issues.claim: The paper presents the crowd study as testing hypotheses generated by the exploratory expert study, and reports the Open Images results as 'consistent with our hypotheses'. Appendix L shows the exploratory label was introduced in response to a prior rejection. No collection dates show that the expert study came before the crowd and Open Images collections. There is no pre-specified analysis plan or power analysis. Many analytic paths were open: median versus other aggregators, ±1 versus exact agreement, three image subsets, five regions plus a global pool, ICC forms, MANOVA, χ² and V². 'Consistent with our hypotheses' therefore carries no confirmatory weight. C02 covers the unsupported power claim for the MANOVA. This issue covers the sequencing and pre-specification of the whole crowd analysis.
new_issues.paper_evidence: Appendix L: "use the results from this work to establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later in the paper"; §6: "Consistent with our hypotheses, we ﬁnd a high intraclass correlation across markets"
new_issues.external_evidence: Kerr (1998) on HARKing; Gelman & Loken (2013) on the garden of forking paths; Nosek et al. (2018) on preregistration as the basis for confirmatory claims.
new_issues.affected_claims: §6 regional and Open Images 'hypothesis' framing; Appendix L's exploratory-to-confirmatory narrative; Conclusion (c)
new_issues.severity_disagreement: Single source. The power-claim part overlaps C02.
new_issues.suggested_fix: Give collection dates for the expert, MST-E crowd and Open Images studies. Present the crowd and Open Images analyses as exploratory unless a pre-specified plan exists. List every analysis run, and correct for multiplicity where claims rest on several tests.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the issue holds. Nothing in the paper mentions preregistration, a pre-specified analysis plan, or a power analysis. §6 asserts "enough statistical power to explicitly test" and Appendix L calls the crowd work "properly powered analyses", but neither gives any justification for that. Appendix L also shows the expert-generates-hypotheses / crowd-tests-them story was strengthened while revising after the FAccT rejection.

The paper's own text makes the sequencing concern stronger than the issue states it:
(1) §5 says India was chosen for the expert panel "because we later recruit crowdsource annotators from this market". So the crowd markets were planned when the expert study was designed, not derived from its results. The crowd pool also excludes the US, one of the two expert markets.
(2) Appendix L says "In this submission, and the prior one" and "we separated the analyses by sample in this version of paper". That implies both the expert and crowd samples were already in the rejected FAccT version. The "hypotheses from exploratory study" story is therefore a later reframing of data already in hand.
(3) The MST-E image filenames in the released metadata are dated 2022-09-22, so all collection happened in a short window before the FAccT 2023 submission. No annotation dates are released, so the order of collection cannot be checked.

The Open Images "expectation" sentence comes directly before the result it "confirms". Its hypotheses come from the MST-E crowd results, not the expert study. "Consistent with our hypotheses" therefore adds no confirmatory weight.

The issue overstates the paper's framing in three ways:
(a) The paper never uses "confirmatory". It titles §6 "Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations", so the crowd study is itself labelled exploratory. The confirmatory language is limited to "explicitly test", "properly powered" and "consistent with our hypotheses".
(b) Appendix L says "more clearly delineate the expert portion ... as exploratory", not that the label was introduced for the first time.
(c) The forking-paths list is inflated:
- The ICC form is set by the design and justified: two-way random for the fully crossed experts, one-way random for the non-crossed crowd.
- The ±1 threshold and median consensus are stated up front in §4 and tied to prior work [33, 34]. The Limitations section returns to the threshold choice.
- Every region, the global pool and all three image subsets are reported in Fig. 3(b), not chosen selectively.
The real flexibility is limited to the choice and poor specification of the regional tests: MANOVA, a χ² comparison of ICCs, and an unexplained V². The MANOVA power claim overlaps C02.

The regional-effect and reliability results are probably robust, since the effects are large and every subset is reported. The lack of pre-specification therefore weakens the rhetoric rather than the main findings. Conclusion (c)'s causal wording ("cultural contexts ... influence") is a separate problem.

Severity: minor.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
Appendix L (Expert Annotation Exploration): "We also more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory and use the results from this work to establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later in the paper" — verbatim, apart from a page break before "analyses".
§6 Extension to In-the-Wild: "Consistent with our hypotheses, we ﬁnd a high intraclass correlation across markets ranging from 0.875 to 0.91" — verbatim.
§6 Extension: "Even in these uncontrolled settings we expect that crowdsource annotators will still consistently annotate skin tone".
§6 Regional Differences: "in this setting we have enough statistical power to explicitly test the effect of the annotator's region".
§6 heading: "6 Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations".
§5: "Experts in India were selected because we later recruit crowdsource annotators from this market."
§5 end: "suggestive evidence that geographic location affects skin tone annotation, which we explore further and at scale".
Appendix L: "In this submission, and the prior one, we focus on people's ability to annotate skin tone".
Appendix L: "we separated the analyses by sample in this version of paper to better delineate the separate analyses".
§4: "when calculating the consensus MST annotation for an image we use the median MST annotation from the responses".
Data card: "Date of Collection: 2022".
No reviewer-directed imperative text was found in the manuscript.
verdicts.corrections:
1. The paper does not call the crowd or Open Images analyses "confirmatory". §6 is titled "Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations". The confirmatory tone comes only from "explicitly test", "properly powered" and "consistent with our hypotheses".
2. Appendix L says the authors "more clearly delineate" the expert portion as exploratory. It does not show the label was introduced for the first time after the rejection.
3. The forking-paths list is overstated:
- The ICC forms (two-way vs one-way random) follow from the study design and are justified.
- The median aggregator and the ±1 threshold are fixed in §4 and anchored to prior work [33, 34].
- All five regions, the global pool and the three image subsets are reported, not selected.
The real analytic flexibility is in the regional tests (MANOVA, the χ² comparison of ICCs, and the unexplained V²).
4. The sequencing point should be strengthened with the paper's own text. §5 ("we later recruit crowdsource annotators from this market") shows the crowd study was planned when the expert study was designed. Appendix L ("In this submission, and the prior one"; "separated the analyses by sample in this version") implies both samples were already in the prior submission. The hypothesis-generation narrative is therefore a reframing after the data were collected.
5. The Open Images hypotheses come from the MST-E crowd results, not the expert study.
6. The unsupported power claim overlaps C02 and should not be counted twice.

verdicts.reasoning:
The issue's main point holds. Nothing in the paper shows pre-registration, a written analysis plan, or a power analysis. The OI 'hypotheses' appear only in prose immediately before the results ('we expect that...'). Appendix L says the experts-generate-hypotheses-for-powered-analyses narrative was written in response to the FAccT 2023 rejection. The FAccT version already contained the crowd analyses ('we separated the analyses by sample in this version'), so the sequencing was assigned afterwards, at the writing stage. The released metadata fits this: all 1542 image or video filenames carry the capture date 20220922. The expert study, the crowd collection and the OI collection therefore all happened between late September 2022 and the FAccT 2023 deadline. The paper gives no annotation-collection dates (only 'Date of Collection: 2022'). By Nosek et al. (2018) standards, 'consistent with our hypotheses' and 'explicitly test' carry no confirmatory weight. §5 even says India was chosen for the experts 'because we later recruit crowdsource annotators from this market', so the crowd design was fixed before or independently of the expert results. That cuts against the claim that the expert study generated the crowd hypotheses.

Several parts of the issue are overstated, and it matters little to the headline claims.
(1) The paper never uses the words 'confirmatory' or 'pre-registered'. §6 is titled 'Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations', and the abstract says only that it 'find[s] evidence' of regional differences. Only the OI paragraph uses 'hypotheses'. The MST-E crowd analysis is framed as a 'test', not as hypothesis confirmation.
(2) Most of the listed forks were not open at analysis time, or were reported exhaustively:
- The median consensus and the ±1 threshold are fixed globally in §4 and justified by prior work [33,34].
- The ICC forms follow from the design: two-way for fully crossed experts, one-way for non-crossed crowd raters, per Shrout–Fleiss and Koo–Li.
- The Golden and Challenging subsets were defined by Dr. Monk before annotation.
- All three subsets and all five regions plus the global pool are reported, not a selected subset.
The real loose ends are narrower: different test families (MANOVA, χ², V²) for the same regional question, and no stated reason for choosing them.
(3) Gelman–Loken forking paths threaten results near the significance threshold. The reliability results are ICC 0.82–0.96 tested against ICC=0, and no reasonable analytic choice would overturn them. The OI regional test (V²=0.0766 on about 86,809 faces) would reach significance under almost any specification. The weaknesses of the regional claim are therefore effect size, rater non-independence, region standing in for 'culture', and the unsupported power claim (C02). They are not HARKing.
(4) MST-E's value as a D&B release does not depend on the confirmatory status of these analyses.

Arithmetic checked: 94.7% = 18/19, which is correct. A Pillai trace of 1.97 is within the bound min(19 DVs, 5−1)=4.

Net: this is a fair note on wording and transparency. It should ask the authors to call the crowd and OI analyses exploratory or post hoc, remove 'consistent with our hypotheses' and 'explicitly test', and state the collection order. It does not materially weaken a core claim. Minor severity is right, but only on narrower grounds than the issue gives.
verdicts.quotes_checked:
Appendix L (p.29-30): "We also more clearly delineate the expert portion of the paper as exploratory and use the results from this work to establish hypotheses for the properly powered analyses later in the paper."
§6 OI paragraph (p.8): "Consistent with our hypotheses, we find a high intraclass correlation across markets ranging from 0.875 to 0.91."
§6 OI (p.8): "Even in these uncontrolled settings we expect that crowdsource annotators will still consistently annotate skin tone"
§6 Regional (p.8): "in this setting we have enough statistical power to explicitly test the effect of the annotator's region on MST annotation."
§6 heading (p.7): "6 Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations"
§5 (p.5): "Experts in India were selected because we later recruit crowdsource annotators from this market."
§4 (p.5): "when calculating the consensus MST annotation for an image we use the median MST annotation from the responses."
Appendix L (p.30): "we separated the analyses by sample in this version of paper to better delineate the separate analyses"
Datasheet: "Date of Collection: 2022"
Conclusion (c): "We show that cultural contexts across geographical regions influence MST annotations."
verdicts.corrections:
1. 'Appendix L shows the exploratory label was introduced in response to a prior rejection' is overstated. Appendix L says the authors 'more clearly delineate' the expert portion as exploratory, which means the label was sharpened, not newly introduced. What was clearly added in revision is the hypothesis-generation narrative.
2. The paper does not uniformly frame the crowd study as confirmatory. §6 is titled 'Exploration of Crowdsourced Annotations', and 'hypotheses' appears only in the OI paragraph.
3. Most of the listed 'analytic paths' were not open forks:
- The median aggregator and the ±1 threshold are fixed in §4 and cited to prior work.
- The ICC forms are dictated by crossed versus non-crossed rater designs.
- The Golden and Challenging subsets were defined before annotation.
- All subsets and regions are reported.
Only the choice among MANOVA, χ² and V² for the regional question is a plausible fork.
4. Forking paths cannot plausibly explain the headline results: the ICCs are 0.82–0.96, and the OI test has N≈86.8k. The weaknesses of the regional claim (effect size, rater non-independence, region used as a proxy for culture, the power claim) belong to other issues, such as C02.
5. The released metadata supplies a timeline the issue lacks. Every MST-E image was captured on 2022-09-22, so all annotation studies took place in a short window before the FAccT 2023 submission. The exact order of the expert and crowd collections remains undocumented.

strengths.title: External reference standard beyond inter-rater reliability
strengths.evidence: §4 p.5 recognises that “Typically, the only available indicator of annotation quality is a measure of inter-rater reliability” and scores consensus against the scale creator's labels using both a within-1 rate and average median distance. Framing these as 'oracle or intended annotations' rather than objective truth is defensible for an instrument defined by its designer. The results are far above chance (94.7% within-1 against a 28–37% chance or constant-guess baseline), and App. G adds a pixel-based baseline showing that automated MST estimation fails. The metrics are coarse (C05), but accuracy and bias questions become addressable in principle.

strengths.title: High replication across five regions, with raw crowd annotations and per-image capture metadata released
strengths.evidence: 25 annotations per image across 5 regions (§6), released at storage.googleapis.com/mste/mste_annotations.csv in response to FAccT reviewers (Apps C, L), together with per-image pose, lighting and mask labels. That supports the mixed-model, k-rater resampling, signed-bias, exact-agreement and stratified reanalyses this review requests, though missing annotator IDs limit annotator-level work (C02, C17).

strengths.title: Tight within-subject temporal control
strengths.evidence: §3: “All images and videos of a subject were collected within a short timespan of 4 hours”. Released filename timestamps show each subject's shoot lasted only 6.6–18.4 minutes. That rules out tanning or seasonal change and makes a subject-level reference the right target for within-subject lighting and pose contrasts (the external-validity limits are in C18).

strengths.title: Transparent reporting and candid limitations
strengths.evidence: App. E (Fig. 7) gives U and p for all 36 expert comparisons, not only the significant ones, which is what made the multiplicity and exact-test checks in C20 possible. §5 calls the expert result 'suggestive evidence', and App. L delineates the expert portion as exploratory. App. K reports pay per region and total spend; subject consent and TONL permission are stated. The Limitations acknowledge unmodelled annotator background and task language, the borrowed ±1 threshold, untested downstream usefulness and the 19-subject limit. App. L documents responses to prior reviews.

strengths.title: Explicit attempts to limit memory and context effects
strengths.evidence: §6: crowd MST-E images were mixed into a larger image set “to prevent face recall”, and annotators saw the thumbnail together with the full image so they could judge lighting context. §5: experts had a one-week gap and new distractors between sets. These efforts are unquantified (C04), but the design concern is recognised.

strengths.title: ICC forms match the rating designs
strengths.evidence: Two-way random for the fully crossed expert design and one-way random for the crowd, where raters differ per image, follow McGraw & Wong [56]. The one-way form is the conservative choice when raters are not crossed (§5 p.6, §6 p.7).

strengths.title: Robust consensus statistic for ordinal labels
strengths.evidence: §4 p.5 uses the median rather than the mean as the consensus, which suits ordinal 10-level ratings with outliers.

strengths.title: Explicit construct reasoning about rater type
strengths.evidence: §5 uses pilot evidence to explain why photographers rather than dermatologists were used. That is unusual and valuable, even though it exposes the construct tension in C11 and the undescribed pilot in C23.

strengths.title: In-the-wild scale-up
strengths.evidence: 86,809 Open Images faces were annotated (§6). That extends the study beyond a controlled dataset, even though only reliability could be assessed there (C07).

strengths.title: Released oracle labels match the paper
strengths.evidence: The subject-level MST values in mst-e_image_details.csv match App. E's MST column for every subject listed. The data card's per-MST image and video tables match the released files when MP4s are counted as videos.

open_questions: What is the unit of observation in the region MANOVA (annotator, image, annotation or index-matched row), and what N, F, df and exact p go with Pillai's trace = 1.97? Did any crowd annotator rate all 19 subjects? Which regions shift lighter or darker, by how much, and at which scale positions?
How many unique crowd annotators were in each regional pool, how many ratings did each contribute, did all pools share one vendor, and can pseudonymous annotator IDs be released?

Were training materials, instruction language, UI and display hardware identical across the five vendor pools? What did crowd training consist of (materials, duration, feedback, qualification), and did it include any MST-E subjects, Golden images or oracle labels?

How many of the author's pre-annotations did Dr. Monk change? Did he see them before rating? Did he judge the 19 values from photos or in person? Is any test-retest or second-expert check of the oracle available?
Is the expert ICC(2,1) absolute agreement or consistency? What are the numeric expert ICCs with CIs, and were the 31 distractor images included?
Which test produced χ² = 0.26, p = 0.99 (back-calculation implies df≈4)? Is 'V² = 0.0766' Cramér's V or its square, and what were N and the table dimensions?
Which ICC (per-region or global pool; Golden, Challenging or per-subject) went into Spearman-Brown, and what reliability target justified '10 ratings per image'?

Which image set and denominator do the expert 88.9%/83.4% and 0.78/0.84 refer to? Is 'average median distance' signed or absolute, and is it averaged over images, subjects or Golden/Challenging items? (0.78 cannot be k/19; 0.84 and 83.4% cannot be k/18 or k/36.)

How were the 19 Challenging images chosen, and why does pose differ from the Golden image in 15 of 18 pairs if the set 'mirrored' the Golden set? Who assigned the well_lit/poorly_lit and pose labels, by what criteria, and how reliably? Are the 635 poorly_lit rows the same images as the 635 'side'-pose rows?

What are the skip and 'difficult' rates by region × lighting, and which body parts did each region rely on? How were medians computed when skips left an even number of labels or fewer than 5 ratings per region?
How many images of the same subject did a typical crowd annotator see, and in what order? Does agreement differ between first and later exposures to a subject?
Which subject fell outside ±1 for the global crowd pool, at what scale position, and in which direction?

Was Subject 16 (excluded from the expert study, and the subject whose Golden image is labelled mask=1) also excluded from the crowd Golden/Challenging comparisons? Is the 'programming error' related to this metadata?
Did the India crowd shift in the same direction as the India photographers on S14? That would cross-validate the expert hint with the released data.

Does mste_annotations.csv contain separate rows for the 22 DNG duplicates, the three duplicated IDs and the malformed 'bottom' row? If so, how were they shown to annotators, and how do per-subject ICC and average median distance change after de-duplication? How was the headline '1515 images / 31 videos' computed?

Were all MST-E captures made on one Google Pixel model at one location with one lighting rig? Could a single computational-photography pipeline (auto-exposure, white balance, any skin-tone-aware rendering) inflate cross-lighting consistency and limit generalisation?

Which face detector, face-size threshold and Open Images split defined the 41,471 images and 86,809 faces, how many annotations per face were collected, and what is the detector's recall by skin tone?

Caveat on the Mann-Whitney exactness point: the reported p-values are reproduced exactly by the tie- and continuity-corrected normal approximation, but with ties the exact conditional p for U=22 can fall anywhere in 0.032–0.071, while U=23/24 stay below .05. The robust problem is multiplicity, not exactness (stat lens correction of lead F6).

Verification gap: no lens downloaded mste_annotations.csv (no permission was given). A direct reanalysis of that file (ICCs, k-rater resampling, single- vs mixed-region panels, signed regional offsets, lighting × region effects) would settle C04, C05, C06, C08 and C09 empirically, apart from annotator-level questions that need IDs.
critic_gaps: Sequential, fatigue and drift effects in monthly-contract annotators: no separate issue. Repeated exposure and session order fall under C04. Rater IDs and timestamps that would allow a drift analysis fall under C17. There is no evidence beyond those.
Skipped and 'difficult' responses as informative missingness are fully covered by C22.
Oracle ties where lighting genuinely changes apparent tone are covered by C11, with reference reliability under C03.

Open Images 'face thumbnail' unit versus MST-E 'per-subject' unit: covered by C05 (aggregated per-subject metrics), C07 (target variance and clustering) and C09. One residual point could fold into C09. The §6 advice that one rater per region suffices for 'a consensus across multiple images' assumes several images of each identity, which in-the-wild fairness data rarely have and Open Images did not test.

The closing sentence of the conclusion ('fine-grained skin tone annotation ... is possible') is in practice covered by C05, C06 and C14, but none of them names it as an affected claim. Suggest adding it to C06 or C14. No analysis shows that adjacent MST levels can be told apart, for example by reliability after collapsing to 5 or 6 bins, or by separation of ordinal thresholds.

MST-E as a benchmark: covered by C10, C15 and C19. Residual items that could fold into C16: the 31 released videos are never annotated or analysed in any experiment, yet they are promoted for evaluation. The taxonomy and labelling provenance of the released lighting and pose fields are also unstated.
The regional pay gap (about $6/h in India versus about $19/h in Hungary) is reported openly. Its role as a confound is already in C01, so it is not raised as an ethics issue.

Abstract and conclusion claims not yet scrutinised: the specific mechanism wording 'rely on different mental models of MST categories' (N01), and the dataset-purpose claim that MST-E helps annotators 'decouple the concept of skin tone from race' (N05). Conclusion (d) extends the suggestions to 'subjective annotations' in general, which C08 covers in part. The parenthetical 'even annotating one's own skin tone' in the conclusion has no evidence, but it is trivial.
Verification limits: Figs 3, 5, 6 and 8 and the Appendix D task screenshots are absent from the extraction. The swatch format (flat or sphere) in N03 may be visible in Appendix D.
No imperative text aimed at reviewers was found in the manuscript.

sources.citation: Barrett, Chen & Zhang (2023). Skin Deep: Investigating Subjectivity in Skin Tone Annotations for Computer Vision Benchmark Datasets. FAccT '23. doi:10.1145/3593013.3594114
sources.verified_how: WebFetch saved the arXiv PDF and I extracted the full text with pypdf; I read the methods and results (Sec. 3–5). I confirmed the DOI through the Crossref API.
sources.methodological_relevance: The authors surveyed prior skin-tone annotation work and ran 8 interface conditions (FST vs MST, light-to-dark vs dark-to-light ordering, face vs skin-patch images) with 165 US annotators who gave ranges on a continuous scale. Image type significantly affected agreement. Scale order, and the scale-by-image-type interaction, significantly affected individual uncertainty. Self-reported annotator skin tone showed a weak, non-significant pull toward the annotator's own tone. In the literature review, 41 papers documented their annotation procedure ambiguously and 34 of those reported no uncertainty analysis.

sources.citation: Thong, Joniak & Xiang (2023). Beyond Skin Tone: A Multidimensional Measure of Apparent Skin Color. ICCV 2023
sources.verified_how: I extracted all 15 pages of the local PDF with pypdf in the scratchpad venv (python -I) and read Sec. 2–5 and supplementary A.1–A.3. I also confirmed its OpenReview archive listing (LeoCw2Ijpx) through the search API.
sources.methodological_relevance: Argues that apparent skin colour has two dimensions: perceptual lightness L* and hue angle h*, running red to yellow. Unidimensional scales (FST, and MST, which it cites as concurrent work alongside Schumann et al.) miss hue. Its CIELAB pipeline clusters skin pixels and keeps the 3 lightest of 5 clusters. A relighting test (Fig. S3) shows L* moves by up to about 6 units under relighting while h* stays stable. It cites annotator demographics and background as a source of score bias and recommends automatic colorimetric scores to reduce annotator subjectivity.

sources.citation: Cook, Howard, Rabbitt, Shuggi, Sirotin, Tipton & Vemury (2024 preprint; 2025 journal). Colorimetric skin tone scale for improved accuracy and reduced perceptual bias of human skin tone annotations. arXiv:2410.21005; published as ACM Journal on Responsible Computing 2(2), 2025, doi:10.1145/3730409
sources.verified_how: I downloaded the arXiv PDF into an isolated directory, extracted it with pypdf and read Sec. 2.6, 3.2 and 4. I confirmed the journal version's metadata through the Crossref API. The paper cites Schumann et al. as its ref. [33].
sources.methodological_relevance: Raters were measured with a calibrated colorimeter. In Study 2, about 760 raters used MST and about 763 used CST to rate 8 subjects, each photographed on 3 cameras. Findings: (a) a large subject-race bias at equal measured lightness of about 2.1 MST steps (about 17.6 L*). (b) Raters of every race were similarly biased, even with about 250 diverse raters per image. The authors say this directly contradicts Schumann et al.'s suggestion that more, and more diverse, raters overcome bias. (c) Rater race also had an effect, about 2.7 L* on MST. (d) Scale background (white vs grey) and test location shifted ratings by the equivalent of about 3–6 L*, and screens were uncalibrated. (e) Across devices, ratings varied about 5–6 L* while image lightness varied about 23 L*, so humans partly compensate for exposure. (f) MST swatches were colorimetrically inaccurate for lighter skin, and MST's per-device ICC dropped to 0.81. The analysis used linear mixed-effects models with rater and image factors.

sources.citation: Cu, Dundas, et al. (2025). Validity of two subjective skin tone scales and its implications on healthcare model fairness. npj Digital Medicine 8:595. doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01975-7
sources.verified_how: I read the PMC article with WebFetch and also pulled the full-text XML through the Europe PMC REST API.
sources.methodological_relevance: Three annotators rated 810 facial-region images from 90 VA inpatients in triplicate on FST and MST. For MST, inter-annotator ICC(2,k) was 0.64 (95% CI 0.02–0.85), Krippendorff's alpha 0.41, and pairwise weighted kappa 0.30–0.64; within-rater Cronbach's alpha was 0.88–0.93. Annotators clustered toward the middle of the scale. Darker self-reports received lighter annotator scores (mixed-model beta = -0.82 for MST). Displays and lighting were not standardized. The paper cites Schumann et al. for the influence of cultural experience on ratings.

sources.citation: Weir, Li, et al. (2025). Evaluating skin tone scales for dermatologic dataset labeling: a prospective-comparative study. npj Digital Medicine 8:787. doi:10.1038/s41746-025-02245-2
sources.verified_how: PMC and nature.com blocked or redirected automated fetches, so I retrieved the full text through the Europe PMC REST API and read the methods, results and discussion.
sources.methodological_relevance: 64 patients were assessed by 2 raters under standardized in-person lighting. In-person MST weighted kappa was 0.75 across all sites. Agreement between photo-based and in-person MST depended on the lighting mode, cross-polarized vs white light (best sites kappa about 0.65–0.74). Triplicate colorimeter ITA had ICC 0.98. The authors stress that high inter-rater reliability does not establish accuracy when there is no ground truth. They cite Schumann et al.'s regional finding as evidence of cultural influence.

sources.methodological_relevance: Three board-certified dermatologists rated FST on 320 images. They agreed exactly on only 50–55% of images but within one unit on 92–94%. Crowd consensus came within one unit of each expert on 79–94% of images. The design benchmarks method-vs-expert agreement against expert-vs-expert agreement, with multiple experts and no single oracle.

The paper notes that ICC(k) and Spearman–Brown assume a one-way random-effects model with interchangeable raters, and that the mean is the only aggregator whose reliability can be derived analytically.

literature.openreview_summary:
I could not read the official NeurIPS 2023 D&B reviews, author responses or meta-review. The forum exists: id L9I9FhHfS3, decision 'NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Poster', confirmed through the OpenReview search API. But every request for the forum page or its notes (api2 and api v1) returned HTTP 403 ChallengeRequiredError, and the browser pane showed a 'Verifying your browser' check. Completing bot-detection is off-limits, so I stopped there. Wayback had no snapshot and its CDX service was offline. What I could verify is review metadata from the Paper Copilot dump of OpenReview: 4 reviewers (ph2V, jgJ9, 8mCy, JyxF), ratings 6/6/6/7 (mean 6.25, a borderline-to-weak accept), confidence 4/4/3/5. The 'improvement' fields are the longest parts of the reviews (28–216 words), the 'correctness' fields are short (1–73 words), the authors replied to all four reviewers, and three reviewers followed up. I cannot paraphrase the reviewers' specific methodological criticisms or the meta-review without the text. Treat any claim about their content as unverified.

The nearest proxy is the manuscript's own Appendix L. It is the authors' self-reported summary of reviews from an earlier rejection at FAccT 2023, not the NeurIPS reviews. As paraphrased by the authors, the FAccT reviewers raised these points:
(1) The MST scale lacked a citation. The authors now cite the MST white paper.
(2) The anonymous 'MST expert' who supplied ground truth had unclear credentials, for a construct the paper itself calls subjective. The authors' answer was to name Dr. Monk, the scale's creator and a co-author. That fixes disclosure, but it leaves a single-oracle, author-affiliated reference standard. Validity is not addressed.
(3) Why a 10-point scale? The authors declared this out of scope.
(4) The expert panel was small and its selection was questioned. The authors justified photographers over dermatologists and relabelled the expert study as 'exploratory, hypothesis-generating', yet it still drives a featured figure and the regional narrative.
(5) Analyses needed clarifying ('average median distance', the 1-point threshold). The authors added definitions and citations.
(6) The scope needed narrowing, and limitations and ethics sections were missing. Both were added.
(7) Only 19 subjects. Acknowledged, not fixed.
(8) No subject race or ethnicity. Not collected.
(9) The annotations should be released. Released as mste_annotations.csv.
No imperative text aimed at reviewers or AI tools was found in the manuscript.
implications: Validity claim 'a diverse pool's median matches the creator's intent' (Sec. 6, 7): Cook et al. (arXiv:2410.21005; ACM JRC 2025) found that with about 250 diverse raters per image and a calibrated colorimeter as ground truth, raters of all races shared a subject-race bias of about 2.1 MST steps (about 17.6 L*) at equal measured lightness. The authors explicitly say this contradicts the paper's advice that more and more diverse raters overcome bias. A shared perceptual bias survives median aggregation, and the paper's single human oracle (Dr. Monk) cannot detect it, because the oracle is subject to the same percept. MST-E has no colorimetric or spectrophotometric measurement of its 19 subjects, so 'alignment with intent' is not accuracy.

Single oracle and lenient 'within 1' metric (Sec. 4–6): Groh et al. (CSCW 2022, the paper's ref [34]) benchmark crowd-vs-expert agreement against expert-vs-expert agreement among three experts. Their experts agreed exactly on only 50–55% of FST images but within one unit on 92–94%. So 'within 1' is lenient even on a 6-point scale. On the 10-point MST it accepts a 3-category window (30% of the scale), and the paper's 94.7% (18/19 subjects) has no expert-expert reference to calibrate against. The paper should report exact agreement, signed error by MST level, and agreement with a second independent MST expert. The paper also presents [33]/[34] as setting a 1-point 'guardrail' for average median distance. Groh used within-one as one descriptive rate alongside exact agreement, not as a threshold on mean distance.

Reliability reporting (Fig. 3, Fig. 5): Cu et al. (npj Digit Med 2025) found MST inter-annotator ICC(2,k) of 0.64 with 95% CI 0.02–0.85, Krippendorff's alpha 0.41, and central-tendency compression on clinical face images. Weir et al. (npj Digit Med 2025) found in-person MST kappa 0.75, and photo-based agreement that depended on lighting mode. MST reliability is therefore highly context-dependent, and confidence intervals can be very wide at small n. The paper reports ICC point estimates with only 'p<0.05' (testing ICC≠0, which is uninformative) for n=19 subjects and one image per subject in the Golden and Challenging sets. CIs and alternative ordinal indices (weighted kappa, alpha) are needed. The medRxiv MST-Derm preprint (2026) already cites the paper's 0.86–0.94 ICCs as the scale's general reliability, so the lack of uncertainty quantification propagates downstream.

Spearman–Brown / replication recommendation (Fig. 5, '1 per region suffices', '10 raters'): Wong & Paritosh (ACL 2022) show that ICC(k) and Spearman–Brown assume a one-way random-effects model with interchangeable raters and apply to mean aggregation. The paper pools k across regions while also claiming regions differ systematically, which violates interchangeability. It also aggregates with the median, not the mean. SB-projected values are consistency, not accuracy against the oracle, and cannot show that a fixed regional mix reduces bias. With 25 labels per image, empirical kRR and oracle error as a function of k (resampling within and across regions) could be computed directly. That needs per-annotator IDs, which the public CSV (unchanged since 7 Jun 2023) lacks.

MANOVA for regional effects and metric treatment of ordinal labels (Sec. 6, Pillai's trace = 1.97): Liddell & Kruschke (JESP 2018) show that metric analyses of ordinal data can yield false positives, missed effects and reversed directions. Nelson & Edwards (Stat Med 2015), Nelson, Mitani & Edwards (Stat Med 2017) and Mitani et al. (Ann Epidemiol 2017) provide ordinal GLMM agreement measures. These handle unbalanced many-rater designs (as here, where different crowd raters label each image), are robust to prevalence and marginals, and test rater-group covariates such as region. A cumulative-link mixed model would give region offsets in MST units with CIs and per-region agreement, replacing the MANOVA. It would use crossed random effects for subject/image and annotator, plus fixed effects for region, lighting and MST level. The MANOVA has an unclear unit of analysis, assumes multivariate normality for 10-level bounded data, and reports no F, df or N. MST steps are also not equal intervals in colour space (Cook et al.: on average about 7.4–8.5 L* per step, with inaccurate light swatches). That undermines the ICC, the 'average median distance', and the claim that equal distances (0.78 vs 0.78) show lighting invariance.

'Annotators learn to be invariant to lighting' (Sec. 6–8): Cook et al. give partial support. Human ratings varied only about 5–6 L* across cameras whose image lightness differed about 23 L*, so raters do compensate for exposure. But compensation was incomplete and device effects remained. Weir et al. found photo-based MST agreement varied by lighting mode, and Thong et al. (ICCV 2023) show relighting moves L* by up to about 6 units. The paper's evidence is one author-curated 'Challenging' image per subject, with no quantified illumination, plus a descriptive equality of distances. The Google blog reports 'no significant difference' without naming any test. The invariance claim needs an explicit lighting-by-subject model on all MST-E images, using the released lighting field, with measured exposure or L* as a covariate.

Display and viewing-condition confound in the regional effect (Sec. 6; Limitations): Reinecke et al. (CHI 2016) show that ambient and monitor brightness significantly change colour discrimination in uncontrolled online settings. Cook et al. found that the scale's background colour (white vs grey) and test location shifted ratings by the equivalent of about 3–6 L*, with uncalibrated screens. The paper does not report display hardware, calibration, ambient conditions, or the background the MST swatches were shown on, for vendor pools in five countries. Region is fully confounded with vendor site, device fleet and environment, so 'cultural mental models' is one explanation among several. The paper's limitations list language and UI but not displays.

Interface and design dependence of 'reliable annotation' (Sec. 6–7 recommendations): Barrett et al. (FAccT 2023) show that scale order and image context (face vs skin patch) significantly change agreement and individual uncertainty. They also recommend recording annotator positionality, such as self-reported skin tone. The paper tests a single fixed UI: thumbnail plus full-image context, presumably light-to-dark order, with no ordering or anchor variants. It records only region, so its reliability and region findings hold only for that configuration, and rater-level positionality effects cannot be examined. FACET (ICCV 2023) shows an alternative that keeps uncertainty: multi-select MST per annotator, with all raters' labels released.

Scale dimensionality and the pixel-based baseline (Appendix G): Thong et al. show that apparent skin colour varies in hue (red to yellow) independently of lightness, and that unidimensional tone scales miss it. Regional disagreement could reflect different weighting of hue vs lightness when mapping to MST's 1-D swatches, which the paper cannot detect. Appendix G dismisses pixel methods using a raw RGB average and L2 distance to MST swatches. Thong et al. (CIELAB L*/h*, clustering, excluding shadowed clusters) and Cook et al. (CIELAB ΔE against calibrated swatches) describe stronger colorimetric baselines. Appendix G is therefore a weak strawman and does not establish that human annotation is preferable.

Scale-inclusivity grounding: Heldreth et al. (ACM JRC 2024, overlapping authors) support MST's inclusivity only through perceived representation in a US-only survey. The paper's annotators were in India, the Philippines, Brazil, Hungary and Ghana, and no evidence is cited that MST's anchor colours are perceived equivalently across those populations. Cook et al. found MST swatches colorimetrically inaccurate for lighter skin, and MST more affected by rater race than a colorimetric scale. That matters for interpreting both the regional offsets and the light-end skew in Open Images.

Reproducibility and release hygiene: the annotations CSV is still publicly listed at the URL given in the paper. An unauthenticated HEAD returned 200 (text/csv, 373,628 bytes, last modified 7 Jun 2023), and I did not download it. The MST-E page links only the image zip. Because the file has not changed since mid-2023, the lack of annotator IDs, which blocks rater-effect, kRR and mixed-model reanalysis, persists. The image zip also answers an unauthenticated HEAD with 200, which conflicts with the paper's claim that anonymous access is not allowed and a Google account is required. I verified this at HEAD level only.

Review process: the NeurIPS review texts were unreachable behind OpenReview's bot check. The ratings (6/6/6/7) suggest moderate support with improvement-focused reviews. Appendix L shows that the earlier FAccT reviewers' central validity concerns were addressed by disclosure or relabelling, not new analysis: the oracle's credentials and the single expert, the expert-panel size, and the analytic definitions. A methodology review should not assume these issues were resolved.
